## original-en · typhoeus · 8:11

This said, a double wreath Evander twin’d, And poplars black and white his temples bind. Then brims his ample bowl. With like design The rest invoke the gods, with sprinkled wine. Meantime the sun descended from the skies, And the bright evening star began to rise. And now the priests, Potitius at their head, In skins of beasts involv’d, the long procession led; Held high the flaming tapers in their hands, As custom had prescrib’d their holy bands; Then with a second course the tables load, And with full chargers offer to the god. The Salii sing, and cense his altars round With Saban smoke, their heads with poplar bound One choir of old, another of the young, To dance, and bear the burthen of the song. The lay records the labours, and the praise, And all th’ immortal acts of Hercules: First, how the mighty babe, when swath’d in bands, The serpents strangled with his infant hands; Then, as in years and matchless force he grew, Th’ Oechalian walls, and Trojan, overthrew. Besides, a thousand hazards they relate, Procur’d by Juno’s and Eurystheus’ hate: “Thy hands, unconquer’d hero, could subdue The cloud-born Centaurs, and the monster crew: Nor thy resistless arm the bull withstood, Nor he, the roaring terror of the wood. The triple porter of the Stygian seat, With lolling tongue, lay fawning at thy feet, And, seiz’d with fear, forgot his mangled meat. Th’ infernal waters trembled at thy sight; Thee, god, no face of danger could affright; Not huge Typhoeus, nor th’ unnumber’d snake, Increas’d with hissing heads, in Lerna’s lake. Hail, Jove’s undoubted son! an added grace To heav’n and the great author of thy race! Receive the grateful off’rings which we pay, And smile propitious on thy solemn day!” In numbers thus they sung; above the rest, The den and death of Cacus crown the feast. The woods to hollow vales convey the sound, The vales to hills, and hills the notes rebound. The rites perform’d, the cheerful train retire.

A monster named among the terrors Hercules did not fear.

## original-en · trojans · 1:0

The Trojans, after a seven years’ voyage, set sail for Italy, but are overtaken by a dreadful storm, which Aeolus raises at the request of Juno. The tempest sinks one, and scatters the rest. Neptune drives off the winds, and calms the sea. Aeneas, with his own ship and six more, arrives safe at an African port. Venus complains to Jupiter of her son’s misfortunes. Jupiter comforts her, and sends Mercury to procure him a kind reception among the Carthaginians. Aeneas, going out to discover the country, meets his mother in the shape of a huntress, who conveys him in a cloud to Carthage, where he sees his friends whom he thought lost, and receives a kind entertainment from the queen. Dido, by device of Venus, begins to have a passion for him, and, after some discourse with him, desires the history of his adventures since the siege of Troy, which is the subject of the two following books.

Aeneas’s people, the survivors of Troy; also called Dardans, Phrygians and Teucrians.

## original-en · latins · 5:25

Th’ unfledg’d commanders and their martial train First make the circuit of the sandy plain Around their sires, and, at th’ appointed sign, Drawn up in beauteous order, form a line. The second signal sounds, the troop divides In three distinguish’d parts, with three distinguish’d guides Again they close, and once again disjoin; In troop to troop oppos’d, and line to line. They meet; they wheel; they throw their darts afar With harmless rage and well-dissembled war. Then in a round the mingled bodies run: Flying they follow, and pursuing shun; Broken, they break; and, rallying, they renew In other forms the military shew. At last, in order, undiscern’d they join, And march together in a friendly line. And, as the Cretan labyrinth of old, With wand’ring ways and many a winding fold, Involv’d the weary feet, without redress, In a round error, which denied recess; So fought the Trojan boys in warlike play, Turn’d and return’d, and still a diff’rent way. Thus dolphins in the deep each other chase In circles, when they swim around the wat’ry race. This game, these carousels, Ascanius taught; And, building Alba, to the Latins brought; Shew’d what he learn’d: the Latin sires impart To their succeeding sons the graceful art; From these imperial Rome receiv’d the game, Which Troy, the youths the Trojan troop, they name.

Latinus’s people, whose land the Trojans are fated to hold.

## original-en · rutulians · 8:7

Conducted to the grove, Aeneas broke The silence first, and thus the king bespoke: “Best of the Greeks, to whom, by fate’s command, I bear these peaceful branches in my hand, Undaunted I approach you, tho’ I know Your birth is Grecian, and your land my foe; From Atreus tho’ your ancient lineage came, And both the brother kings your kindred claim; Yet, my self-conscious worth, your high renown, Your virtue, thro’ the neighb’ring nations blown, Our fathers’ mingled blood, Apollo’s voice, Have led me hither, less by need than choice. Our founder Dardanus, as fame has sung, And Greeks acknowledge, from Electra sprung: Electra from the loins of Atlas came; Atlas, whose head sustains the starry frame. Your sire is Mercury, whom long before On cold Cyllene’s top fair Maia bore. Maia the fair, on fame if we rely, Was Atlas’ daughter, who sustains the sky. Thus from one common source our streams divide; Ours is the Trojan, yours th’ Arcadian side. Rais’d by these hopes, I sent no news before, Nor ask’d your leave, nor did your faith implore; But come, without a pledge, my own ambassador. The same Rutulians, who with arms pursue The Trojan race, are equal foes to you. Our host expell’d, what farther force can stay The victor troops from universal sway? Then will they stretch their pow’r athwart the land, And either sea from side to side command. Receive our offer’d faith, and give us thine; Ours is a gen’rous and experienc’d line: We want not hearts nor bodies for the war; In council cautious, and in fields we dare.”

Turnus’s people, of Ardea.

## original-en · tyrians · 1:24

They climb the next ascent, and, looking down, Now at a nearer distance view the town. The prince with wonder sees the stately tow’rs, Which late were huts and shepherds’ homely bow’rs, The gates and streets; and hears, from ev’ry part, The noise and busy concourse of the mart. The toiling Tyrians on each other call To ply their labour: some extend the wall; Some build the citadel; the brawny throng Or dig, or push unwieldly stones along. Some for their dwellings choose a spot of ground, Which, first design’d, with ditches they surround. Some laws ordain; and some attend the choice Of holy senates, and elect by voice. Here some design a mole, while others there Lay deep foundations for a theatre; From marble quarries mighty columns hew, For ornaments of scenes, and future view. Such is their toil, and such their busy pains, As exercise the bees in flow’ry plains, When winter past, and summer scarce begun, Invites them forth to labour in the sun; Some lead their youth abroad, while some condense Their liquid store, and some in cells dispense; Some at the gate stand ready to receive The golden burthen, and their friends relieve; All with united force, combine to drive The lazy drones from the laborious hive: With envy stung, they view each other’s deeds; The fragrant work with diligence proceeds. “Thrice happy you, whose walls already rise!” Aeneas said, and view’d, with lifted eyes, Their lofty tow’rs; then, ent’ring at the gate, Conceal’d in clouds (prodigious to relate) He mix’d, unmark’d, among the busy throng, Borne by the tide, and pass’d unseen along.

Dido’s people, the settlers of Carthage.

## original-en · greeks · 1:25

Full in the centre of the town there stood, Thick set with trees, a venerable wood. The Tyrians, landing near this holy ground, And digging here, a prosp’rous omen found: From under earth a courser’s head they drew, Their growth and future fortune to foreshew. This fated sign their foundress Juno gave, Of a soil fruitful, and a people brave. Sidonian Dido here with solemn state Did Juno’s temple build, and consecrate, Enrich’d with gifts, and with a golden shrine; But more the goddess made the place divine. On brazen steps the marble threshold rose, And brazen plates the cedar beams inclose: The rafters are with brazen cov’rings crown’d; The lofty doors on brazen hinges sound. What first Aeneas in this place beheld, Reviv’d his courage, and his fear expell’d. For while, expecting there the queen, he rais’d His wond’ring eyes, and round the temple gaz’d, Admir’d the fortune of the rising town, The striving artists, and their arts’ renown; He saw, in order painted on the wall, Whatever did unhappy Troy befall: The wars that fame around the world had blown, All to the life, and ev’ry leader known. There Agamemnon, Priam here, he spies, And fierce Achilles, who both kings defies. He stopp’d, and weeping said: “O friend! ev’n here The monuments of Trojan woes appear! Our known disasters fill ev’n foreign lands: See there, where old unhappy Priam stands! Ev’n the mute walls relate the warrior’s fame, And Trojan griefs the Tyrians’ pity claim.” He said, his tears a ready passage find, Devouring what he saw so well design’d, And with an empty picture fed his mind: For there he saw the fainting Grecians yield, And here the trembling Trojans quit the field, Pursued by fierce Achilles thro’ the plain, On his high chariot driving o’er the slain. The tents of Rhesus next, his grief renew, By their white sails betray’d to nightly view; And wakeful Diomede, whose cruel sword The sentries slew, nor spar’d their slumb’ring lord, Then took the fiery steeds, ere yet the food Of Troy they taste, or drink the Xanthian flood. Elsewhere he saw where Troilus defied Achilles, and unequal combat tried; Then, where the boy disarm’d, with loosen’d reins, Was by his horses hurried o’er the plains, Hung by the neck and hair, and dragg’d around: The hostile spear, yet sticking in his wound, With tracks of blood inscrib’d the dusty ground. Meantime the Trojan dames, oppress’d with woe, To Pallas’ fane in long procession go, In hopes to reconcile their heav’nly foe. They weep, they beat their breasts, they rend their hair, And rich embroider’d vests for presents bear; But the stern goddess stands unmov’d with pray’r. Thrice round the Trojan walls Achilles drew The corpse of Hector, whom in fight he slew. Here Priam sues; and there, for sums of gold, The lifeless body of his son is sold. So sad an object, and so well express’d, Drew sighs and groans from the griev’d hero’s breast, To see the figure of his lifeless friend, And his old sire his helpless hand extend. Himself he saw amidst the Grecian train, Mix’d in the bloody battle on the plain; And swarthy Memnon in his arms he knew, His pompous ensigns, and his Indian crew. Penthisilea there, with haughty grace, Leads to the wars an Amazonian race: In their right hands a pointed dart they wield; The left, for ward, sustains the lunar shield. Athwart her breast a golden belt she throws, Amidst the press alone provokes a thousand foes, And dares her maiden arms to manly force oppose.

The army that took Troy; the poem also calls them Grecians, Argives and Danaans.

## original-en · arcadians · 8:13

Thus, walking on, he spoke, and shew’d the gate, Since call’d Carmental by the Roman state; Where stood an altar, sacred to the name Of old Carmenta, the prophetic dame, Who to her son foretold th’ Aenean race, Sublime in fame, and Rome’s imperial place: Then shews the forest, which, in after times, Fierce Romulus for perpetrated crimes A sacred refuge made; with this, the shrine Where Pan below the rock had rites divine: Then tells of Argus’ death, his murder’d guest, Whose grave and tomb his innocence attest. Thence, to the steep Tarpeian rock he leads; Now roof’d with gold, then thatch’d with homely reeds. A reverent fear (such superstition reigns Among the rude) ev’n then possess’d the swains. Some god, they knew—what god, they could not tell— Did there amidst the sacred horror dwell. Th’ Arcadians thought him Jove; and said they saw The mighty Thund’rer with majestic awe, Who took his shield, and dealt his bolts around, And scatter’d tempests on the teeming ground. Then saw two heaps of ruins, (once they stood Two stately towns, on either side the flood,) Saturnia’s and Janiculum’s remains; And either place the founder’s name retains. Discoursing thus together, they resort Where poor Evander kept his country court. They view’d the ground of Rome’s litigious hall; (Once oxen low’d, where now the lawyers bawl;) Then, stooping, thro’ the narrow gate they press’d, When thus the king bespoke his Trojan guest: “Mean as it is, this palace, and this door, Receiv’d Alcides, then a conqueror. Dare to be poor; accept our homely food, Which feasted him, and emulate a god.” Then underneath a lowly roof he led The weary prince, and laid him on a bed; The stuffing leaves, with hides of bears o’erspread. Now night had shed her silver dews around, And with her sable wings embrac’d the ground, When love’s fair goddess, anxious for her son, (New tumults rising, and new wars begun,) Couch’d with her husband in his golden bed, With these alluring words invokes his aid; And, that her pleasing speech his mind may move, Inspires each accent with the charms of love: “While cruel fate conspir’d with Grecian pow’rs, To level with the ground the Trojan tow’rs, I ask’d not aid th’ unhappy to restore, Nor did the succour of thy skill implore; Nor urg’d the labours of my lord in vain, A sinking empire longer to sustain, Tho’ much I ow’d to Priam’s house, and more The dangers of Aeneas did deplore. But now, by Jove’s command, and fate’s decree, His race is doom’d to reign in Italy: With humble suit I beg thy needful art, O still propitious pow’r, that rules my heart! A mother kneels a suppliant for her son. By Thetis and Aurora thou wert won To forge impenetrable shields, and grace With fated arms a less illustrious race. Behold, what haughty nations are combin’d Against the relics of the Phrygian kind, With fire and sword my people to destroy, And conquer Venus twice, in conqu’ring Troy.” She said; and straight her arms, of snowy hue, About her unresolving husband threw. Her soft embraces soon infuse desire; His bones and marrow sudden warmth inspire; And all the godhead feels the wonted fire. Not half so swift the rattling thunder flies, Or forky lightnings flash along the skies. The goddess, proud of her successful wiles, And conscious of her form, in secret smiles.

Evander’s people at Pallanteum.

## original-en · tuscans · 8:0

The war being now begun, both the generals make all possible preparations. Turnus sends to Diomedes. Aeneas goes in person to beg succours from Evander and the Tuscans. Evander receives him kindly, furnishes him with men, and sends his son Pallas with him. Vulcan, at the request of Venus, makes arms for her son Aeneas, and draws on his shield the most memorable actions of his posterity.

The Etruscan people who rise against Mezentius and join Aeneas.

## original-en · volscians · 7:45

Last, from the Volscians fair Camilla came, And led her warlike troops, a warrior dame; Unbred to spinning, in the loom unskill’d, She chose the nobler Pallas of the field. Mix’d with the first, the fierce Virago fought, Sustain’d the toils of arms, the danger sought, Outstripp’d the winds in speed upon the plain, Flew o’er the fields, nor hurt the bearded grain: She swept the seas, and, as she skimm’d along, Her flying feet unbath’d on billows hung. Men, boys, and women, stupid with surprise, Where’er she passes, fix their wond’ring eyes: Longing they look, and, gaping at the sight, Devour her o’er and o’er with vast delight; Her purple habit sits with such a grace On her smooth shoulders, and so suits her face; Her head with ringlets of her hair is crown’d, And in a golden caul the curls are bound. She shakes her myrtle jav’lin; and, behind, Her Lycian quiver dances in the wind.

Camilla’s people.

## original-en · italians · 1:27

“O Queen! indulg’d by favour of the gods To found an empire in these new abodes, To build a town, with statutes to restrain The wild inhabitants beneath thy reign, We wretched Trojans, toss’d on ev’ry shore, From sea to sea, thy clemency implore. Forbid the fires our shipping to deface! Receive th’ unhappy fugitives to grace, And spare the remnant of a pious race! We come not with design of wasteful prey, To drive the country, force the swains away: Nor such our strength, nor such is our desire; The vanquish’d dare not to such thoughts aspire. A land there is, Hesperia nam’d of old; The soil is fruitful, and the men are bold Th’ Oenotrians held it once, by common fame Now call’d Italia, from the leader’s name. To that sweet region was our voyage bent, When winds and ev’ry warring element Disturb’d our course, and, far from sight of land, Cast our torn vessels on the moving sand: The sea came on; the South, with mighty roar, Dispers’d and dash’d the rest upon the rocky shore. Those few you see escap’d the storm, and fear, Unless you interpose, a shipwreck here. What men, what monsters, what inhuman race, What laws, what barb’rous customs of the place, Shut up a desert shore to drowning men, And drive us to the cruel seas again? If our hard fortune no compassion draws, Nor hospitable rights, nor human laws, The gods are just, and will revenge our cause. Aeneas was our prince: a juster lord, Or nobler warrior, never drew a sword; Observant of the right, religious of his word. If yet he lives, and draws this vital air, Nor we, his friends, of safety shall despair; Nor you, great queen, these offices repent, Which he will equal, and perhaps augment. We want not cities, nor Sicilian coasts, Where King Acestes Trojan lineage boasts. Permit our ships a shelter on your shores, Refitted from your woods with planks and oars, That, if our prince be safe, we may renew Our destin’d course, and Italy pursue. But if, O best of men, the Fates ordain That thou art swallow’d in the Libyan main, And if our young Iulus be no more, Dismiss our navy from your friendly shore, That we to good Acestes may return, And with our friends our common losses mourn.” Thus spoke Ilioneus: the Trojan crew With cries and clamours his request renew.

The peoples of Italy taken together; also called Ausonians and Oenotrians.

## modern-en · aeneas · 1:0

The Trojans, after a seven years' voyage, set sail for Italy, but are overtaken by a dreadful storm, which Aeolus raises at the request of Juno. The tempest sinks one ship and scatters the rest. Neptune drives off the winds and calms the sea. Aeneas, with his own ship and six more, arrives safe at an African port. Venus complains to Jupiter of her son's misfortunes. Jupiter comforts her, and sends Mercury to secure him a kind reception among the Carthaginians. Aeneas, going out to discover the country, meets his mother in the shape of a huntress, who conveys him in a cloud to Carthage, where he sees his friends whom he thought lost, and receives a kind welcome from the queen. Dido, by a device of Venus, begins to feel a passion for him, and, after some conversation, asks to hear the history of his adventures since the siege of Troy, which becomes the subject of the two following books.

Son of Venus and Anchises, leader of the Trojan survivors and the man the poem follows from burning Troy to Italy.

## modern-en · ascanius · 1:17

"Daughter, dismiss your fears. The fates of your descendants stand fixed and unchanged, as you desire. You shall behold the Lavinian walls you wish for; and when Aeneas, ripe for heaven, is called by fate, you shall bear him up, sublime, to me. No counsel has reversed my firm decree. And lest new fears disturb your happy state, know that I have searched the mystic rolls of Fate. Your son (nor is the appointed season far off) shall wage successful war in Italy, tame fierce nations in the bloody field, impose sovereign laws, and build cities, until, every foe subdued, the sun has run its annual race three times through the signs. This is his appointed time. Then Ascanius, now called Iulus, shall begin his reign. He shall wear the crown for thirty rolling years, and then shall transfer the seat from Lavinium, and with hard labor shall build Alba Longa. The throne shall be filled by his successors for three hundred more years, and then Ilia the fair shall be seen, a priestess and a queen, who, filled with the seed of Mars, shall in due time bring forth twin boys at a single birth. A tawny wolf shall suckle the royal babes. Then Romulus shall gain his grandfather's throne, shall found towers of war, shall call the people Romans, and the city Rome. To them I assign no bounds of empire, nor term of years to their immortal line. Even haughty Juno, who now turmoils earth, seas, and heaven, and Jove himself, with endless broils, shall be reconciled at last, and join her friendly power to cherish and advance the Trojan line. The subject world shall acknowledge Rome's dominion, and lying prostrate shall adore the nation of the toga. An age is ripening in revolving fate when Troy shall overturn the Grecian state, and her conquering sons shall call for sweet revenge, to crush the people who conspired at her fall. Then Caesar shall arise from the Julian stock, whose empire shall be bounded only by ocean, and whose fame only by the skies; whom, laden with eastern spoils, our heaven, the just reward of human toils, shall securely receive with divine rites, and incense shall rise before his sacred shrine. Then dire debate and impious war shall cease, and the stern age shall be softened into peace. Then banished Faith shall return once more, and Vestal fires shall burn in hallowed temples; and Remus with Quirinus shall sustain the righteous laws, and restrain fraud and force. Janus himself shall stand before his shrine and guard the dreadful gates, with bolts and iron bars: within remains Fury, imprisoned, bound in brazen chains; high on a trophy of useless weapons he sits, and threatens the world with vain alarms."

Aeneas’s young son, also called Iulus, from whom Rome’s Julian line is traced.

She spoke, and led her guest to the palace; then offered incense and proclaimed a feast. Nor yet less careful for his absent friends, she sent twice ten fat oxen to the ships; besides a hundred boars, and a hundred lambs, with bleating cries, attending their milky dams; and jars of generous wine and spacious bowls she gave, to cheer the drooping souls of the sailors. Now purple hangings clothed the palace walls, and splendid halls served up sumptuous feasts. They dined on richly wrought Tyrian carpets; the sideboards shone with loads of massive plate, and antique vases all embossed with gold (the gold itself less valuable than the workmanship), of curious work, where on the sides were seen the battles and figures of illustrious men, from their first founder to the present queen.

Aeneas’s father, carried out of Troy on his son’s shoulders.

Smeared as she was with black Gorgonian blood, the Fury sprang above the Stygian flood; and on her wicker wings, sublime through night, she took her flight to the Latian palace. There she sought the queen's apartment, stood before the peaceful threshold, and besieged the door. Restless Amata lay, her swelling breast fired with disdain over Turnus' dispossession, and over the new nuptials of the Trojan guest. From her black bloody locks the Fury shook her darling plague, the favorite of her snakes; with her full force she threw the poisonous dart, and fixed it deep within Amata's heart, that, thus envenomed, she might kindle rage, and sacrifice to strife her house and her husband's age. Unseen, unfelt, the fiery serpent skimmed between her linen and her naked limbs, inspiring his baleful breath as he glided; now like a chain around her neck he rode; now like a fillet he repaired to her head, and folded her hair with his circling coils. At first the silent venom slid with ease, and seized her cooler senses by degrees; then, before the infected mass was fired too far, in plaintive accents she began the war, and thus bespoke her husband: "Shall," she said, "a wandering prince enjoy Lavinia's bed? If nature does not plead in a parent's heart, pity my tears, and pity her desert. I know, my dearest lord, the time will come when you would, in vain, reverse your cruel doom; the faithless pirate will soon set to sea, and bear the royal virgin far away! A guest like him, a Trojan guest before, in the show of friendship sought the Spartan shore, and ravished Helen from her husband. Resume your ancient care; and, if the god your sire, and you, resolve on foreign blood, know that all are foreign, in a larger sense, who are not born your subjects, or derived from here. An azure robe was spread over his body; a wreath of shady reeds adorned his head. Thus, manifest to sight, the god appeared, and with these pleasing words cheered his sorrow: "Undoubted offspring of ethereal race, O long expected in this promised place, who has borne your banished gods through the foes, restored them to their hearths and old abodes: this is your happy home, the clime where fate ordains you to restore the Trojan state. ## modern-en · priam · 1:25

In the very center of the town stood a venerable wood, thick with trees. The Tyrians, landing near this holy ground and digging here, had found a prosperous omen: from beneath the earth they drew out a horse's head, which foreshadowed their growth and future fortune. Juno, the foundress, had given them this fated sign of a fruitful soil and a brave people. Here Sidonian Dido built and consecrated Juno's temple with solemn state, enriched with gifts and with a golden shrine; but the goddess made the place still more divine. On brazen steps the marble threshold rose, and brazen plates enclosed the cedar beams. The rafters were crowned with brazen coverings, and the lofty doors sounded on brazen hinges. What Aeneas first beheld in this place revived his courage and drove away his fear. For while, awaiting the queen, he raised his wondering eyes and gazed around the temple, admiring the fortune of the rising town, the competing artists, and the fame of their art, he saw, in order painted on the wall, all that had befallen unhappy Troy: the wars that fame had blown around the world, every scene true to life, every leader known. There he sees Agamemnon, and here Priam, and fierce Achilles, who defies them both. He stopped, and weeping, said: "O friend! Even here monuments of Trojan suffering appear! Our known disasters fill even foreign lands: see there, where old unhappy Priam stands! Even the mute walls relate the warrior's fame, and Trojan griefs stir Tyrian pity!" He said, and his tears found a ready passage, as he devoured with his eyes the scenes so well depicted, and fed his mind with an empty picture. For there he saw the fainting Greeks yielding, and there the trembling Trojans quitting the field, pursued by fierce Achilles across the plain as he drove his high chariot over the slain. Next came the tents of Rhesus, and his grief was renewed, their white sails betraying them to nightly view, and wakeful Diomede, whose cruel sword slew the sentries and did not spare their slumbering lord; then he took the fiery steeds before they tasted the food of Troy or drank from the river Xanthus. Elsewhere he saw where Troilus defied Achilles, and tried unequal combat; then, where the boy, disarmed, with loosened reins, was hurried over the plain by his horses, hung by the neck and hair, and dragged around, the hostile spear still sticking in his wound, inscribing the dusty ground with tracks of blood. Meanwhile the Trojan matrons, oppressed with woe, went in long procession to the temple of Pallas, hoping to reconcile their heavenly enemy. They wept, beat their breasts, tore their hair, and bore richly embroidered vests as offerings; but the stern goddess stood unmoved by prayer. Three times Achilles dragged Hector's corpse around the Trojan walls, whom he had slain in combat. Here Priam was suing; and there, for sums of gold, the lifeless body of his son was being sold. So sad an object, and so well expressed, drew sighs and groans from the grieving hero's breast, to see the figure of his lifeless friend, and his old father stretching out his helpless hand. He saw himself also amid the Grecian train, mingled in the bloody battle on the plain; and he knew swarthy Memnon in his armor, his pompous ensigns, and his Indian crew. There was Penthesilea, leading an Amazonian race to war with haughty grace; in their right hands they wielded a pointed dart, and their left sustained the lunar shield for defense. She threw a golden belt across her breast, and alone among the press she provoked a thousand foes, daring to oppose her maiden arms to manly force.

The old king of Troy, killed at his own altar on the night the city fell.

Again I thought on my forsaken wife, and trembled for my son's abandoned life. I looked about, but found myself alone, deserted at my hour of need! My friends were gone. Some, spent with toil, some oppressed with despair, had leaped headlong from the heights; the flames consumed the rest. Thus, wandering on my way without a guide, I spied graceless Helen in the porch of Vesta's temple. There she lurked alone, sitting muffled, and, as much as she could, unknown. But by the flames that cast their blaze around, I recognized that common bane of Greece and Troy. For now that Ilium burned, she dreaded the Trojan sword; and more dreaded the vengeance of her injured lord; even those gods she had taken refuge with abhorred her. Trembling with rage, I regarded the strumpet, resolved to give her guilt its due reward: ‘Shall she sail triumphant before the wind, and leave unhappy Troy behind her in flames? Shall she see again her kingdom and her friends, attended in state with a captive crew, while unavenged the good old Priam falls, and Grecian fires consume the Trojan walls? For this were the Phrygian fields and the Xanthian flood swollen with bodies and drunk with blood? True, a soldier can gain small honor, and can boast no conquest, from killing a woman: yet the deed shall not pass without applause, the vengeance being taken in so just a cause. The punished crime shall set my soul at ease, and appease the murmuring ghosts of my friends.' Thus while I raved, a gleam of pleasing light spread over the place; and, shining heavenly bright, my mother stood revealed before my sight. Never did her eyes appear so radiant; not her own star confessed so clear a light. Great in her charms, as when she looks upon the gods above, and breathes herself into their love. She held my hand, to break the destined blow; then from her rosy lips began to speak: ‘My son, from where comes this madness, this neglect of my commands, and of those whom I protect? Why this unmanly rage? Recall to mind whom you forsake, what pledges you leave behind. Look whether your helpless father yet survives, or if Ascanius or Creüsa lives. Around your house the greedy Greeks are roving; and these would have perished in the nightly war, but for my presence and protecting care. Not Helen's face, nor Paris, is at fault; but this destruction was brought by the gods. Now cast your eyes around, while I dissolve the mists and films that wrap mortal eyes; I will purge the dross from your sight, and make you see the shape of each avenging deity. Enlightened thus, fulfill my just commands, and do not fear obedience to your mother's will. Where that disordered heap of ruin lies—stones rent from stones, where clouds of dust arise—amid that smother Neptune holds his place, drives his mace below the wall's foundations, and heaves the building from its solid base. Look, where, in arms, imperial Juno stands, full in the Scaean gate, with loud commands, urging on shore the tardy Grecian bands. See! Pallas, proud of her snaky buckler, bestrides the tower, refulgent through the cloud. See! Jove supplies new courage to the foe, and arms the partial deities against the town. Haste from here, my son; end this fruitless labor. Haste, where your trembling spouse and sire await you. Haste; and a mother's care shall befriend your passage.' She said, and swiftly vanished from my sight, obscure in clouds and gloomy shades of night. I looked, I listened: I heard dreadful sounds; and the dire forms of hostile gods appeared. I saw Troy sunk in flames, nor could I prevent it; and Ilium rent from its old foundations, rent like a mountain ash, which had dared the winds, and stood the sturdy strokes of laboring hinds. About its roots the cruel axe resounds; the stumps are pierced with oft-repeated wounds: the war is felt on high; the nodding crown now threatens a fall, and throws down its leafy honors. At last, though late, it yielded to their united force, and mourned with mortal groans its approaching fate. The roots could no longer sustain its upper load, and down it fell, and spread a ruin across the plain.

Aeneas’s first wife, lost in the sack of Troy; her ghost sends him on to Italy.

No vessels were in view; but on the plain three stately stags, with branching heads, led a lordly train; the more ignoble herd followed their stately steps, grazing slowly along. He halted; and while they fed in security below, he took the quiver and the trusty bow that Achates was used to carry. First he laid the leaders low, and then pierced the rest; nor did he cease from his arrows until seven mighty bodies stained the shaded plain with their blood. For the seven ships he made an equal share, and returned to the port in triumph from the hunt. He broached the jars of generous wine—Acestes' gift, when the fleet left his Trinacrian shores—and prepared for the feast, sharing the wine equally with the venison. While he dealt it round, the pious chief allayed the common grief with cheerful words: "Endure, and conquer! Jove will soon dispose our past and present sufferings to future good. With me you have survived the rocks of Scylla, and defied the inhuman Cyclops and his den. What greater ills can you endure after that? Take courage again and put away care; an hour will come when it will be a pleasure to recall your past sorrows, as blessings sent by Fate. Through various hazards and events we move to Latium and the realms foreordained by Jove. There we are called (that is the promise of the skies), where Trojan kingdoms may rise once again. ## modern-en · serestus · 1:31

"He whom you seek am I—tossed by tempests, and saved from shipwreck on your Libyan coast. I present before your throne, gracious queen, a prince who owes his life to you alone. Fair majesty, the refuge and redress of those whom fate pursues and wants oppress, you, who employ your pious offices to save the remnants of abandoned Troy—receive the shipwrecked on your friendly shore, relieve the poor with hospitable rites, take into your town a wandering company, and entertain strangers in your palace. What thanks can wretched fugitives return, who, scattered through the world, mourn in exile? The gods, if gods are inclined to goodness, and if acts of mercy touch their heavenly minds, and, more than all the gods, your generous heart, conscious of its worth, shall requite its own desert! This age is happy in you, and so is this earth, and parents more than mortal gave you birth. While rolling rivers shall run into seas, and the radiant sun shall course around the vault of heaven, while trees shall shade the mountain tops, your honor, name, and praise shall never die. Whatever abode my fortune has assigned me, your image shall be present to my mind." Having said this, he turned with pious haste and joyfully embraced his waiting friends. With his right hand he honored Ilioneus, and with his left Serestus; then pressed Cloanthus and noble Gyas to his breast; and so by turns he greeted the rest.

A Trojan captain who walks the camp with Mnestheus. Dryden spells him Serestus once and Seresthus elsewhere.

By chance Aeneas turned his eyes another way, and unexpectedly saw his friends—Antheus, grave Sergestus, strong Cloanthus, and behind them a mighty Trojan throng, whom the tempest had lately tossed on the waves and scattered widely on another shore. Then to the king: "Forbear your empty vaunts; I hope for success, and cannot fear fate; alive or dead, I shall deserve a name; Jove is impartial, and to both the same." While, at the Lemnian god's command, they thus urged their labors, and plied the Aeolian forge, the cheerful morn saluted Evander's eyes, and the songs of chirping birds invited him to rise. He left his lowly bed: his buskins met above his ankles; sandals sheathed his feet; he set his trusty sword upon his side, and threw a panther's hide over his shoulder. Two menial dogs pressed before their master. Thus clad, and thus guarded, he sought his kingly guest. Mindful of promised aid, he mended his pace, but met Aeneas in the middle space. Young Pallas attended his father's steps, and true Achates waited on his friend. They joined their hands; they chose a secret seat. The Arcadian first renewed their former talk: "Undaunted prince, I never can believe the Trojan empire lost, while you survive. Command the assistance of a faithful friend; but the succors I can send are feeble. Our narrow kingdom here is bounded by the Tiber; on that other side the Latian state surrounds us, insults our walls, and wastes our fruitful grounds. But I prepare mighty nations to join their arms with yours, and to aid your just design. You come, as if sent by your better genius, and fortune seems to favor your intent. Not far from here stands a hilly town, of ancient building, and of high renown, torn from the Tuscans by the Lydian race, who gave the place the name of Caere, once called Agyllina. It flourished long, strong in pride of wealth and in warlike people, until cursed Mezentius, in a fatal hour, assumed the crown, with arbitrary power. What words can paint those execrable times, the subjects' sufferings, and the tyrant's crimes? That blood, those murders, O you gods, visit back on his own head, and on his impious race! The living and the dead were coupled at his command, face to face, and hand to hand, till, choked with stench, tied in loathed embraces, the lingering wretches pined away and died. Thus plunged in ills, and meditating more—the people's patience, tired, no longer bore the raging monster; but they beset his house with arms, and threatened vengeance and destruction. They fired his palace; while the flame ascended, they forced his guards, and executed his friends. He cleaved the crowd, and, favored by the night, directed his flight to Turnus' friendly court. Set on fire by just revenge, the Tuscans require their king's punishment by lawful arms: their numerous troops, now mustered on the strand, shall submit to your command by my counsel. Their navy swarms upon the coasts; they cry to hoist their anchors, but the gods deny. An ancient augur, skilled in future fate, restrains their hate with these foreboding words: 'You brave in arms, you Lydian blood, the flower of Tuscan youth, and choice of all their power, whom just revenge against Mezentius arms, to seek your tyrant's death by lawful arms: know this—no native of our land may lead this powerful people; seek a foreign head.' Awed by these words, they still abide in camps, and await with longing looks their promised guide. Tarchon, the Tuscan chief, has sent me their crown, and every regal ornament: the people join their own desire with his; and all require my conduct, as their king. But the chill blood that creeps within my veins, and age, and listless limbs unfit for pains, and a soul conscious of its own decay, have forced me to refuse imperial sway. My Pallas would be more fit to mount the throne, and should, but he is a Sabine mother's son, and half a native; but in you combine a manly vigor and a foreign line. Where Fate and smiling Fortune show the way, pursue the ready path to sovereign sway. The staff of my declining days, my son, shall make your good or ill success his own; in fighting fields, from you, he shall learn to dare, and serve the hard apprenticeship of war; view your matchless courage and your conduct, and early begin to admire and copy you. Besides, he shall command two hundred horse; though few, a warlike and well-chosen band. These are enlisted in my name; and my son has added as many more in his own."

The Etruscan chief who brings his people to Aeneas.

With both hands he labored at the knots; his holy fillets were stained by their blue venom; his roaring filled the flitting air around him. Each called on his fellow for help; at last the fatal fabric mounted the walls, big with destruction. Boys crowned with chaplets, and choirs of virgins, sang and danced around it. Thus raised aloft, and then descending down, it passed in over our heads and threatened the town. O sacred city, built by hands divine! O valiant heroes of the Trojan line! We adorned the temples with branches, and in jollity we wasted the day ordained to be our last. Meanwhile the rapid heavens rolled down the light, and night rushed upon the shaded ocean. Our men, feeling secure, kept no guards nor sentries, but easy sleep compelled their weary limbs. The Greeks had embarked their naval forces from Tenedos, and sought our well-known shores, safe under cover of the silent night, and guided by the imperial galley's light. ## modern-en · achilles · 1:25

In the very center of the town stood a venerable wood, thick with trees. The Tyrians, landing near this holy ground and digging here, had found a prosperous omen: from beneath the earth they drew out a horse's head, which foreshadowed their growth and future fortune. Juno, the foundress, had given them this fated sign of a fruitful soil and a brave people. Here Sidonian Dido built and consecrated Juno's temple with solemn state, enriched with gifts and with a golden shrine; but the goddess made the place still more divine. On brazen steps the marble threshold rose, and brazen plates enclosed the cedar beams. The rafters were crowned with brazen coverings, and the lofty doors sounded on brazen hinges. What Aeneas first beheld in this place revived his courage and drove away his fear. For while, awaiting the queen, he raised his wondering eyes and gazed around the temple, admiring the fortune of the rising town, the competing artists, and the fame of their art, he saw, in order painted on the wall, all that had befallen unhappy Troy: the wars that fame had blown around the world, every scene true to life, every leader known. There he sees Agamemnon, and here Priam, and fierce Achilles, who defies them both. He stopped, and weeping, said: "O friend! Even here monuments of Trojan suffering appear! Our known disasters fill even foreign lands: see there, where old unhappy Priam stands! Even the mute walls relate the warrior's fame, and Trojan griefs stir Tyrian pity!" He said, and his tears found a ready passage, as he devoured with his eyes the scenes so well depicted, and fed his mind with an empty picture. For there he saw the fainting Greeks yielding, and there the trembling Trojans quitting the field, pursued by fierce Achilles across the plain as he drove his high chariot over the slain. Next came the tents of Rhesus, and his grief was renewed, their white sails betraying them to nightly view, and wakeful Diomede, whose cruel sword slew the sentries and did not spare their slumbering lord; then he took the fiery steeds before they tasted the food of Troy or drank from the river Xanthus. Elsewhere he saw where Troilus defied Achilles, and tried unequal combat; then, where the boy, disarmed, with loosened reins, was hurried over the plain by his horses, hung by the neck and hair, and dragged around, the hostile spear still sticking in his wound, inscribing the dusty ground with tracks of blood. Meanwhile the Trojan matrons, oppressed with woe, went in long procession to the temple of Pallas, hoping to reconcile their heavenly enemy. They wept, beat their breasts, tore their hair, and bore richly embroidered vests as offerings; but the stern goddess stood unmoved by prayer. Three times Achilles dragged Hector's corpse around the Trojan walls, whom he had slain in combat. Here Priam was suing; and there, for sums of gold, the lifeless body of his son was being sold. So sad an object, and so well expressed, drew sighs and groans from the grieving hero's breast, to see the figure of his lifeless friend, and his old father stretching out his helpless hand. He saw himself also amid the Grecian train, mingled in the bloody battle on the plain; and he knew swarthy Memnon in his armor, his pompous ensigns, and his Indian crew. There was Penthesilea, leading an Amazonian race to war with haughty grace; in their right hands they wielded a pointed dart, and their left sustained the lunar shield for defense. She threw a golden belt across her breast, and alone among the press she provoked a thousand foes, daring to oppose her maiden arms to manly force.

The greatest of the Greeks at Troy, dead before the poem begins; also called Pelides.

## modern-en · aeolus · 1:0

The Trojans, after a seven years' voyage, set sail for Italy, but are overtaken by a dreadful storm, which Aeolus raises at the request of Juno. The tempest sinks one ship and scatters the rest. Neptune drives off the winds and calms the sea. Aeneas, with his own ship and six more, arrives safe at an African port. Venus complains to Jupiter of her son's misfortunes. Jupiter comforts her, and sends Mercury to secure him a kind reception among the Carthaginians. Aeneas, going out to discover the country, meets his mother in the shape of a huntress, who conveys him in a cloud to Carthage, where he sees his friends whom he thought lost, and receives a kind welcome from the queen. Dido, by a device of Venus, begins to feel a passion for him, and, after some conversation, asks to hear the history of his adventures since the siege of Troy, which becomes the subject of the two following books.

King of the winds, who looses the storm at Juno’s request.

Whatever befalls, your life shall be my care; we shall share one death, or one deliverance. My hand shall lead our little son; and you, my faithful consort, shall follow in our steps. Next, you, my servants, heed my strict commands: outside the walls there stands a ruined temple, once hallowed to Ceres; a cypress tree nearby shoots up its venerable head on high, kept holy by long religion. There bend your steps, and let us meet in divided parties. Our country gods, the relics, and the bands, take, father, in your guiltless hands: it would be impious for me to bear holy things, red as I am with slaughter, fresh from war, until I cleanse in some living stream the guilt of dire debate and blood spilled in battle.' So, arranging all that prudence could provide, I clothed my shoulders with a lion's hide and yellow spoils; then on my bending back I took the welcome load of my dear father; while Ascanius hung on my better hand, and tripped along with unequal paces. Creüsa kept behind; by choice we strayed through every dark and every devious way. I, who just before had been so bold and dauntless, who bore the Grecian darts and the shock of lances, was now seized with fear at every shadow—not for myself, but for the charge I bore. At last, arrived near the ruined gate, I felt secure, and deemed all the danger past, when we heard a frightful noise of trampling feet. My father, looking through the shadows, cried out in fear: ‘Haste, haste, my son, the foes are near; I see their swords and shining armor.' Some hostile god, for some unknown offense, had surely bereft my mind of better sense. Stung with spite, and furious with despair, she struck her trembling breast, and tore her hair. “And shall the ungrateful traitor go,” she said, “my land forsaken, and my love betrayed? What have I said? Where am I? Fury turns my brain; and my distempered bosom burns. Then, when I gave my person and my throne, this hate, this rage, should have been shown more timely. I should have torn him piecemeal; strewn his scattered limbs in the floods, or left them exposed in woods; destroyed his friends and son; and, from the fire, set the reeking boy before the sire. Events are doubtful, which wait on battles: yet where is the doubt, to souls secure of fate? My Tyrians, at their injured queen's command, would have tossed their fires amid the Trojan band; at once extinguished all the faithless name; and I myself, in vengeance of my shame, would have fallen upon the pile, to mend the funeral flame. First, let him see his friends slain in battle, and lament their untimely fate in vain; and when, at length, the cruel war shall cease, may he buy his peace on hard conditions: nor let him then enjoy supreme command; but fall, untimely, by some hostile hand, and lie unburied on the barren sand! Three more ships fierce Eurus, in his angry mood, dashed on the shallows of the shifting sand, and left them stranded in mid-ocean. Orontes' ship, that bore the Lycian crew—a horrid sight, even in the hero's view—was overwhelmed from stem to stern; the trembling pilot, torn from his rudder, was hurled headlong; three times the ship was tossed around, then broke apart at once, and was lost in the deep. Here and there above the waves were seen weapons, pictures, precious goods, and floating men. Even the stoutest vessel gave way to the storm, and sucked in the rushing sea through loosened planks. Ilioneus was her captain; and old Alethes, faithful Achates, and young bold Abas suffered no less. Their ships, with gaping seams, let in the flood of brine.

The north wind.

## modern-en · triton · 1:10

Meanwhile imperial Neptune heard the sound of raging billows breaking on the ground. Displeased, and fearing for his watery reign, he raised his awful head above the sea, serene in majesty, and rolled his eyes over the space of earth, seas, and skies. He saw the Trojan fleet scattered and distressed, oppressed by stormy winds and wintry sky. Well the god knew his sister's envy, and what her aims and her schemes pursued. He summoned Eurus and the western blast, cast an angry glance on both, and then rebuked them thus: "Audacious winds! From where comes this bold attempt, this rebel insolence? Is it for you to ravage seas and land, unauthorized by my supreme command? To raise such mountains on the troubled sea? Whom I—but first it is fitting to restrain the waves; and then you shall be taught obedience to my rule. Hence! Carry my royal mandate to your lord. The realms of ocean and the fields of air are mine, not his. By fatal lot the liquid empire and the trident of the sea fell to me. His power is confined to hollow caverns. There let him reign, the jailer of the winds, summoning his breathing subjects with hoarse commands, and boasting and blustering in his empty hall." He spoke; and as he spoke, he smoothed the sea, dispelled the darkness, and restored the day. Cymothoe and Triton, and the sea-green train of lovely nymphs, the daughters of the main, cleared the vessels from the rocks with their hands. The god himself, with his ready trident, opened the deep, spread out the shifting sands, and heaved the ships off the shoals. Wherever he guided his finny coursers and rode in triumph, the waves grew smooth and the sea subsided. As when a riot rises among an ignoble crowd, their motions are mad, and their tongues are loud; stones and firebrands fly in rattling volleys, and every rustic weapon that fury can supply; but if some grave and pious man appears, they hush their noise and lend a listening ear; he soothes their angry mood with sober words, and quenches their inborn desire for blood—so, when the Father of the Flood appeared, and raised his sovereign trident over the seas, their fury fell. He skimmed the liquid plains, high on his chariot, and with loosened reins he moved along majestic, maintaining awful peace. The weary Trojans plied their shattered oars toward the nearest land, and reached the Libyan shores.

A sea god who heaves the stranded ships off the rocks.

Down through the crannies of the living walls, crystal streams descend in murmuring falls. No hawsers are needed here to bind the vessels, nor any toothed anchors; for they fear no storms. ## modern-en · doto · 9:6

It is said that, when the chief prepared his flight, and felled his timber from Mount Ida's height, the grandam goddess then approached her son, and with a mother's majesty began: "Grant me," she said, "the sole request I bring, since conquering heaven has owned you for its king. On Ida's brows, for ages past, there stood a shady wood, filled with firs and maples; and on the summit rose a sacred grove, where I was worshiped with religious love. Those woods, that holy grove, my long delight, I gave to the Trojan prince, to speed his flight. Now, filled with fear, I come on their behalf; let neither winds overset, nor waves entomb, the floating forests of the sacred pine; but let their safety be mine." Then thus replied her awful son, who rolls the radiant stars, and controls heaven and earth: "How dare you, mother, demand endless date for vessels molded by a mortal hand? What then is fate? Shall bold Aeneas ride, certain of safety, on the uncertain tide? Yet, what I can, I grant: when, wafted over, the chief is landed on the Latian shore, whatever ships escape the raging storms shall, at my command, change their fading forms to divine nymphs, and plow the watery way, like Doto and the daughters of the sea." To seal his sacred vow, he swore by Styx, the lake of liquid pitch, the dreary shore, and Phlegethon's innavigable flood, and the black regions of his brother god. He said, and shook the skies with his imperial nod.

A sea nymph, named when the ships are promised her shape.

## modern-en · harpies · 3:11

“He said; and we obeyed with glad consent, forsook the seat, and, leaving a few behind, spread our sails before the willing wind. Now our galleys moved out of the sight of land, with only seas around and skies above, when a burst of rain descended over our heads, and night enveloped the main with sable clouds. The ruffling winds raised the foamy billows; the scattered fleet was forced into several ways; the face of heaven was ravished from our eyes, and roaring thunder flew in redoubled peals. Cast from our course, we wandered in the dark. No stars to guide, no point of land to mark. Even Palinurus found no distinction between night and day; such darkness reigned around. Three starless nights the doubtful navy strayed, without distinction, and three sunless days. The fourth renewed the light; and from our shrouds we viewed a rising land, like distant clouds. The mountain tops confirmed the pleasing sight, and curling smoke ascended from their height. The canvas fell; the sailors plied their oars; from the rude strokes the whirling waters flew. At length I landed upon the Strophades, safe from the danger of the stormy seas. Those isles are encompassed by the Ionian main, the dire abode where the foul Harpies reign, forced by the winged warriors to return to their old homes, and leave their costly fare. More fierce monsters offended Heaven never sent from hell's abyss for human punishment: with virgin faces, but with wombs obscene, foul paunches, and still unclean with ordure; with claws for hands, and looks forever lean.

The foul bird-women of the Strophades, who befoul the Trojans’ meal.

## modern-en · celaeno · 3:12

“We landed at the port, and soon beheld fat herds of oxen grazing the flowery field, and wanton goats straying without a keeper. With our weapons we attacked the welcome prey, then called the gods as partners of our feast, and Jove himself, the chief invited guest. We spread the tables on the greensward ground; we fed with hunger, and the bowls went round. When from the mountain tops, with hideous cry and clattering wings, the hungry Harpies flew; they snatched the meat, defiling all they found, and, parting, left a loathsome stench behind. Close by a hollow rock, we sat down again, dressed the dinner anew, and refitted the beds, secure from sight, beneath a pleasing shade where tufted trees made a native arbor. Again the holy fires burned on the altars; and once again the ravenous birds returned, whether from the dark recesses where they lie, or from another quarter of the sky; with filthy claws they repeated their odious meal, and mixed their loathsome ordures with their meat. I bade my friends then prepare for vengeance, and to wage war with the hellish nation. They, as commanded, provided for the fight, and hid their glittering weapons in the grass. Then, when along the crooked shore we heard their clattering wings, and saw the foes appear, Misenus sounded a charge: we took the alarm, and armed our strong hands with swords and bucklers. In this new kind of combat all employed their utmost force, to destroy the monsters. In vain; the fated skin is proof against wounds; and the shining sword rebounded from their plumes. At length, rebuffed, they left their mangled prey, and displayed their stretched pinions to the skies. Yet one remained, the messenger of Fate: high on a craggy cliff sat Celaeno, and thus delivered her dismal errand: ‘What! Not contented with our slain oxen, do you dare to maintain an impious war with Heaven, and drive the Harpies from their native realm? Heed therefore what I say; and keep in mind what Jove decrees, what Phoebus has designed, and what I, the Furies' queen, relate from both: You seek the Italian shores, foredoomed by fate: the Italian shores are granted you to find, and a safe passage to the port assigned. But know that before you build your promised walls, my curses shall be severely fulfilled. Fierce famine shall be your lot for this misdeed—reduced to grinding the plates on which you feed.' She said, and flew to the neighboring forest. Our courage failed us, and our fears renewed. Hopeless to win by war, we fell to prayers, and humbly called upon the offended Harpies, and whether they were gods or obscene birds, we preferred our vows for pardon and for peace. But old Anchises, offering sacrifice and lifting up to heaven his hands and eyes, adored the greater gods: ‘Avert,' he said, ‘these omens; render vain this prophecy, and free a pious people from the impending curse!'

The Harpies’ leader, who prophesies that hunger will make the Trojans eat their tables.

## modern-en · charon · 6:11

Just in the gate and in the jaws of hell, revengeful Cares and sullen Sorrows dwell, and pale Diseases, and repining Age, Want, Fear, and Famine's unresisted rage; here Toils, and Death, and Death's half-brother, Sleep, terrible forms to view, keep their sentry; with the anxious Pleasures of a guilty mind, deep Frauds before, and open Force behind; the Furies' iron beds; and Strife, that shakes her hissing tresses and unfolds her snakes. Full in the midst of this infernal road, an elm displays her dusky arms abroad: the God of Sleep there hides his heavy head, and empty dreams are spread on every leaf. Of various forms, unnumbered specters more, Centaurs, and double shapes, besiege the door. Before the passage, horrid Hydra stands, and Briareus with all his hundred hands; Gorgons, Geryon with his triple frame; and vain Chimaera vomits empty flame. The chief unsheathed his shining steel, prepared, though seized with sudden fear, to force the guard, offering his brandished weapon at their face; had not the Sibyl stopped his eager pace, and told him what those empty phantoms were: forms without bodies, and impassive air. Hence to deep Acheron they took their way, whose troubled eddies, thick with ooze and clay, are whirled aloft, and lost in Cocytus. There Charon stands, who rules the dreary coast: a sordid god: down from his hoary chin a length of beard descends, uncombed, unclean; his eyes, like hollow furnaces on fire; a girdle, foul with grease, binds his obscene attire. He spreads his canvas; with his pole he steers; he bears the freights of flitting ghosts in his thin bottom. He looked old in years; yet in his years were seen a youthful vigor and autumnal green. An airy crowd came rushing where he stood, which filled the margin of the fatal flood: husbands and wives, boys and unmarried maids, and the more majestic shades of mighty heroes, and youths, entombed before their fathers' eyes, with hollow groans, and shrieks, and feeble cries. Thick as the leaves in autumn strew the woods, or fowls, forced by winter, forsake the floods, and wing their hasty flight to happier lands; such, and so thick, the shivering army stood, and pressed for passage with extended hands. Now these, now those, the surly boatman bore: the rest he drove to a distance from the shore. The hero, who beheld with wondering eyes the tumult mixed with shrieks, laments, and cries, asked of his guide what the rude concourse meant; why the thronging people bent toward the shore; what forms of law were used among the ghosts; why some were ferried over, and some refused.

The ferryman of the dead.

## modern-en · cerberus · 6:15

No sooner had they landed, than in his den they found the triple porter of the Stygian sound, grim Cerberus, who soon began to rear his crested snakes, and armed his bristling hair. The prudent Sibyl had prepared beforehand a sop, steeped in honey, to charm the guard; which, mixed with powerful drugs, she cast before his greedy grinning jaws, just opened to roar. With three enormous mouths he gaped; and straightway, pressed with hunger, devoured the pleasing bait. Long draughts of sleep enslaved his monstrous limbs; he reeled, and, falling, filled the spacious cave. The keeper charmed, the chief without delay passed on, and took the irremeable way. Before the gates, the cries of babes newly born, whom fate had torn from their tender mothers, assaulted his ears: then those, whom the form of laws condemned to die, when traitors judged their cause. Nor do they lack lots, nor judges to review the wrongful sentence, and award a new. Minos, the strict inquisitor, appears; and hears lives and crimes, with his assessors. He rolls the blended balls round in his urn, absolves the just, and dooms the guilty souls. The next, in place and punishment, are they who prodigally throw their souls away; fools, who, repining at their wretched state, and loathing anxious life, suborned their fate. With late repentance now they would retrieve the bodies they forsook, and wish to live; they desire to bear their pains and poverty, to view the light of heaven, and breathe the vital air: but fate forbids; the Stygian floods oppose, and with circling streams enclose the captive souls.

The three-headed dog at the gate of the underworld.

## modern-en · fame · 4:14

The loud report spread through Libyan cities. Fame, the great ill, grows from small beginnings: swift from the first; and every moment brings new vigor to her flights, new pinions to her wings. Soon the pigmy grows to gigantic size; her feet on earth, her forehead in the skies. Enraged against the gods, revengeful Earth produced her as the last of the Titanian birth. Swift is her walk, swifter still her winged haste: a monstrous phantom, horrible and vast. As many plumes as raise her lofty flight, so many piercing eyes enlarge her sight; millions of opening mouths belong to Fame, and every mouth is furnished with a tongue, and the flying plague is hung round with listening ears. She fills the peaceful universe with cries; no slumbers ever close her wakeful eyes; by day, from lofty towers she shows her head, and spreads disastrous news through trembling crowds; she haunts the courts with informers and royal spies; she relates things done, she feigns things not done, and mingles truth with lies.

Rumour personified, the swiftest of evils, who grows as she goes and spreads the news of Dido and Aeneas.

## modern-en · hymen · 4:9

“Mine,” said imperial Juno, “shall be the care; time now urges to perfect this affair: attend my counsel, and share the secret. There, while the huntsmen pitch their toils around, and cheerful horns resound from side to side, a pitchy cloud shall cover all the plain with hail, and thunder, and tempestuous rain; the fearful train shall take their speedy flight, dispersed, and all involved in gloomy night; one cave shall afford a grateful shelter to the fair princess and the Trojan lord. The god of marriage, invoked for the union in the cave.

## modern-en · faunus · 7:4

Latinus, old and mild, had long possessed the Latin scepter, and had blessed his people. His father was Faunus; his mother a Laurentian dame, fair Marica by name. But Faunus came from Picus; Picus drew his birth from Saturn, if records be true. Thus King Latinus, in the third degree, had Saturn as author of his family. But this old peaceful prince, as Heaven decreed, was blessed with no male issue to succeed: his sons in blooming youth were snatched by fate; one only daughter inherited the royal state. Fired with her love, and led by ambition, the neighboring princes courted her nuptial bed. Among the crowd, but far above the rest, young Turnus addressed himself to the beauteous maid. Turnus, for high descent and graceful mien, was first, and favored by the Latian queen; with him she strove to join Lavinia's hand, but dire portents withstood the purposed match.

A god of the Latin woods, Latinus’s father.

## modern-en · janus · 1:17

"Daughter, dismiss your fears. The fates of your descendants stand fixed and unchanged, as you desire. You shall behold the Lavinian walls you wish for; and when Aeneas, ripe for heaven, is called by fate, you shall bear him up, sublime, to me. No counsel has reversed my firm decree. And lest new fears disturb your happy state, know that I have searched the mystic rolls of Fate. Your son (nor is the appointed season far off) shall wage successful war in Italy, tame fierce nations in the bloody field, impose sovereign laws, and build cities, until, every foe subdued, the sun has run its annual race three times through the signs. This is his appointed time. Then Ascanius, now called Iulus, shall begin his reign. He shall wear the crown for thirty rolling years, and then shall transfer the seat from Lavinium, and with hard labor shall build Alba Longa. The throne shall be filled by his successors for three hundred more years, and then Ilia the fair shall be seen, a priestess and a queen, who, filled with the seed of Mars, shall in due time bring forth twin boys at a single birth. A tawny wolf shall suckle the royal babes. Then Romulus shall gain his grandfather's throne, shall found towers of war, shall call the people Romans, and the city Rome. To them I assign no bounds of empire, nor term of years to their immortal line. Even haughty Juno, who now turmoils earth, seas, and heaven, and Jove himself, with endless broils, shall be reconciled at last, and join her friendly power to cherish and advance the Trojan line. The subject world shall acknowledge Rome's dominion, and lying prostrate shall adore the nation of the toga. An age is ripening in revolving fate when Troy shall overturn the Grecian state, and her conquering sons shall call for sweet revenge, to crush the people who conspired at her fall. Then Caesar shall arise from the Julian stock, whose empire shall be bounded only by ocean, and whose fame only by the skies; whom, laden with eastern spoils, our heaven, the just reward of human toils, shall securely receive with divine rites, and incense shall rise before his sacred shrine. Then dire debate and impious war shall cease, and the stern age shall be softened into peace. Then banished Faith shall return once more, and Vestal fires shall burn in hallowed temples; and Remus with Quirinus shall sustain the righteous laws, and restrain fraud and force. Janus himself shall stand before his shrine and guard the dreadful gates, with bolts and iron bars: within remains Fury, imprisoned, bound in brazen chains; high on a trophy of useless weapons he sits, and threatens the world with vain alarms."

The two-faced god whose gates stand open in war.

She saw the Trojan and his joyful train descending upon the shore, deserting the main, designing a town, and, with unhoped success, the ambassadors returning with a promised peace. Then, pierced with pain, she shook her haughty head, sighed from her inward soul, and thus she said: "O hated offspring of my Phrygian foes! O fates of Troy, that oppose Juno's fates! Could they not fall unpitied on the plain, but revive slain, and, taken, escape again? When execrable Troy lay in ashes, through fires and swords and seas they forced their way. Then vanquished Juno must contend in vain, her rage disarmed, her empire at an end. Is all my fury spent, breathless and tired? Or does my glutted spleen at length relent? As if it were too little to chase them from their town, I pursued their exiled race through the seas; I engaged the heavens, opposed the stormy main; but billows roared, and tempests raged in vain. What have my Scyllas and my Syrtes done, when they overpass these, and shun those? On Tiber's shores they land, secure of fate, triumphant over the storms and over Juno's hate. Mars could bathe the Centaurs in mutual blood, and Jove himself gave way to Cynthia's wrath, who sent the tusky boar to Calydon; what great offense had either people done? But I, the consort of the Thunderer, have waged a long and unsuccessful war, with various arts and arms have toiled in vain, and at length am foiled by a mortal man. If native power does not prevail, shall I doubt to seek needful succor from without? If Jove and Heaven deny my just desires, Hell shall supply the power of Heaven and Jove. Grant that the Fates have firmed, by their decree, that the Trojan race shall reign in Italy; at least I can defer the nuptial day, and delay the peace with protracted wars. The dear alliance shall be bought with blood, and both peoples brought near destruction; so shall the son-in-law and father join, with ruin, war, and the waste of either line. O fatal maid, your marriage is endowed with Phrygian, Latian, and Rutulian blood! Bellona leads you to your lover's hand; another queen brings forth another brand, to burn another land with foreign fires! A second Paris, differing only in name, shall fire his country with a second flame."

The war goddess, who leads the bride to her wedding.

Then he told of Argus' death, his murdered guest, whose grave and tomb attest his innocence. Thence he led to the steep Tarpeian rock, now roofed with gold, then thatched with homely reeds. A reverent fear (such superstition reigns among the rude) possessed the swains even then. Some god, they knew—what god, they could not tell—dwelt there amidst the sacred horror. The Arcadians thought him Jove; and they said they saw the mighty Thunderer with majestic awe, who took his shield, and dealt his bolts around, and scattered tempests on the teeming ground. Then they saw two heaps of ruins (once they stood as two stately towns, on either side of the flood), the remains of Saturnia and of Janiculum; each place retained the founder's name. Thus discoursing together, they arrived where poor Evander kept his country court. They viewed the ground of Rome's litigious hall (once oxen lowed, where now the lawyers bawl); then, stooping, they pressed through the narrow gate, when thus the king bespoke his Trojan guest: "Mean as it is, this palace, and this door, received Alcides, then a conqueror. Dare to be poor; accept our homely food, which feasted him, and emulate a god." Then beneath a lowly roof he led the weary prince, and laid him on a bed—the stuffing leaves, overspread with hides of bears. Now night had shed her silver dews around, and with her sable wings embraced the ground, when love's fair goddess, anxious for her son (new tumults rising, and new wars begun), couched with her husband in his golden bed, with these alluring words invokes his aid; and, so that her pleasing speech may move his mind, she inspires each accent with the charms of love: "While cruel fate conspired with Grecian powers to level with the ground the Trojan towers, I asked not aid to restore the unhappy, nor did I implore the succor of your skill; nor did I urge in vain the labors of my lord, to sustain a sinking empire longer, though I owed much to Priam's house, and more, deplored the dangers of Aeneas. But now, by Jove's command, and fate's decree, his race is doomed to reign in Italy. With humble suit I beg your needful art, O power still propitious, that rules my heart! A mother kneels a suppliant for her son. By Thetis and Aurora you were won to forge impenetrable shields, and to grace a less illustrious race with fated arms. Behold what haughty nations are combined against the relics of the Phrygian kind, to destroy my people with fire and sword, and to conquer Venus twice, in conquering Troy." She said; and straightaway she threw her snow-white arms about her unresolving husband. Her soft embraces soon infused desire; his bones and marrow inspired sudden warmth; and all the godhead felt the wonted fire. Not half so swift flies the rattling thunder, nor forky lightnings flash along the skies. The goddess, proud of her successful wiles, and conscious of her form, smiled in secret.

Evander’s mother, a prophetess who foretold the Roman race.

It was night; and weary nature had lulled asleep the birds of the air, and the fishes of the deep, and beasts, and mortal men. The Trojan chief lay on Tiber's banks, oppressed with grief, and found a late relief in silent slumber. Then, through the shadows of the poplar wood, arose the father of the Roman flood. An azure robe was spread over his body; a wreath of shady reeds adorned his head. Thus, manifest to sight, the god appeared, and with these pleasing words cheered his sorrow: "Undoubted offspring of ethereal race, O long expected in this promised place, who has borne your banished gods through the foes, restored them to their hearths and old abodes: this is your happy home, the clime where fate ordains you to restore the Trojan state. Fear not! The war shall end in lasting peace, and all the rage of haughty Juno shall cease. And, so that this nightly vision may not seem the effect of fancy, or an idle dream, a sow shall lie along beneath an oak, all white herself, and white her thirty young. When thirty rolling years have run their race, your son Ascanius, on this empty space, shall build a royal town, of lasting fame, which from this omen shall receive its name. Time shall approve the truth. For what remains, and how to crown your pains with sure success, attend next with patience. A banished band, driven with Evander from the Arcadian land, have planted here, and placed their walls on high; their founder calls their town Pallanteum, derived from Pallas, his great-grandsire's name. But the fierce Latians claim old possession, infesting the new colony with war. Make these your friends, and rely on their aid. I submit my streams to your free passage. Wake, son of Venus, from your pleasing dreams; and, when the setting stars are lost in day, pay your just devotion to Juno's power; appease the wrathful queen with sacrifice: her pride at length shall fall, her fury cease. When you return victorious from the war, perform your vows to me with grateful care. I am the god whose yellow water flows around these fields, and fattens as it goes: my name is Tiber; among the rolling floods I am renowned on earth, esteemed among the gods. This is my certain seat. In times to come, my waves shall wash the walls of mighty Rome."

The river of Latium, who rises in a dream to tell Aeneas he has reached his promised land.

The goblet went around; Iopas brought his golden lyre, and sang what ancient Atlas had taught him: the various labors of the wandering moon, and whence the eclipses of the sun proceed; the origin of men and beasts; and whence the rains arise, and fires dispense their warmth; and how the fixed and wandering stars dispose their influence; what shakes the solid earth; what cause delays the summer nights and shortens winter days. The Tyrians praised the song with peals of shouts, and those peals were echoed by the Trojan throng. The unhappy queen prolonged the night with talk, and drank large drafts of love with vast delight. She inquired much of Priam, and more of Hector; then asked what arms the swarthy Memnon wore, and what troops he had landed on the Trojan shore; the steeds of Diomede varied the discourse, and fierce Achilles, with his matchless force. At length, as fate and her ill stars required, she desired to hear the whole series of the war. "Relate fully, my godlike guest," she said, "the Grecian stratagems, the town betrayed, the fatal issue of so long a war, your flight, your wanderings, and your woes. Now smiling hope, with sweet vicissitude, renewed his joys within the hero's mind. He called to raise the masts, to display the sheets; the cheerful crew obeyed with diligence; they scudded before the wind, and sailed in open sea. Ahead of all the master pilot steered; and, as he led, the following navy veered. The steeds of Night had traveled half the sky, the drowsy rowers lay on their benches, when the soft God of Sleep, with easy flight, descended, and drew a trail of light behind. You, Palinurus, are his destined prey; he takes his fatal way to you alone. He bears dire dreams to you, and iron sleep; and, lighting on your prow, he wears the form of Phorbas. Then thus the traitor god began his tale: “The winds, my friend, inspire a pleasing gale; the ships, without your care, sail securely. Now steal an hour of sweet repose; and I will take the rudder and supply your room.” To whom the yawning pilot, half asleep: “Do you bid me trust the treacherous deep, the harlot smiles of her dissembling face, and commit the Trojan race to her faith? Shall I believe the Siren South again, and, often betrayed, not know the monster main?” He said: his fastened hands kept the rudder, and, fixed on heaven, his eyes repelled invading sleep. The god was wroth, and threw at his temples a branch dipped in Lethe, and drunk with Stygian dew: the pilot, vanquished by the divine power, soon closed his swimming eyes, and lay supine. Scarcely were his limbs extended at their length, when the god, insulting with superior strength, fell heavy on him, plunged him in the sea, and, with the stern, tore away the rudder. Headlong he fell, and, struggling in the main, cried out for helping hands, but cried in vain. The victor daemon mounted obscure in air, while the ship sailed without the pilot's care. On Neptune's faith the floating fleet relied; but what the man forsook, the god supplied, and the navy flew secure over the dangerous deep; it glided by the Sirens' cliffs, a shelvy coast, long infamous for ships and sailors lost, and white with bones. The impetuous ocean roared, and rocks bellowed back from the sounding shores. The watchful hero felt the knocks, and found the tossing vessel sailing on shoaly ground. Sure of his pilot's loss, he himself took the helm, and steered aloof, and shunned the shelf. Inwardly he grieved, and, groaning from his breast, deplored his death; and thus expressed his pain: “For trusting in seas, and in the flattering sky, your naked corpse is doomed to lie on shores unknown.”

The god who slides down to Palinurus at the helm.
