I sing of arms and of the man who, forced by fate and by the unrelenting hatred of haughty Juno, was expelled and exiled from the Trojan shore. He endured long labors both by sea and land, and fought a doubtful war before he won the realm of Latium and built the destined town. He restored his banished gods to their sacred rites, and established a secure succession in his line, from which came the race of Alban fathers and the long glories of majestic Rome. O Muse, tell me the causes and the crimes! What goddess was provoked, and what kindled her hatred? For what offense did the Queen of Heaven begin to persecute so brave and just a man, entangling his anxious life in endless cares, exposing him to want, and hurrying him into wars? While the pious prince lamented his fate, fierce Boreas drove against his flying sails and tore the sheets; the raging billows rose, and lifted the tossing vessels to the skies. The shivering oars could not sustain the blow; the galley gave way at the side and turned her prow, while those astern, descending down the steep, saw the boiling deep through yawning waves. Three ships were carried off by the southern blast, and dashed with fury on the hidden shoals—rocks which the Ausonian sailors knew: when they rose above the flood and showed their broad backs, they called them the Altars. Three more ships fierce Eurus, in his angry mood, dashed on the shallows of the shifting sand, and left them stranded in mid-ocean. Orontes' ship, that bore the Lycian crew—a horrid sight, even in the hero's view—was overwhelmed from stem to stern; the trembling pilot, torn from his rudder, was hurled headlong; three times the ship was tossed around, then broke apart at once, and was lost in the deep. Here and there above the waves were seen weapons, pictures, precious goods, and floating men. Even the stoutest vessel gave way to the storm, and sucked in the rushing sea through loosened planks. Ilioneus was her captain; and old Alethes, faithful Achates, and young bold Abas suffered no less. Their ships, with gaping seams, let in the flood of brine.

Young Lycus and Helenor alone escaped; saved (how, they knew not) from the steepy leap. Helenor, the elder of the two, by birth on one side royal, and on one a son of earth, whom Licymnia bore to the Lydian king, and sent her boasted bastard to the war (a privilege which none but freemen share). His arms were slight, a sword and silver shield; no marks of honor charged its empty field. As light as he fell, so light the youth arose, and, rising, found himself amidst his foes; no flight was left, nor hopes to force his way. Emboldened by despair, he stood at bay; and, like a stag, whom all the troop of eager huntsmen and invading hounds surround, resolved on death, he dissipates his fears, and bounds aloft against the pointed spears. So dares the youth, secure of death, and throws his dying body on his thickest foes. But Lycus, swifter of foot by far, ran, doubled, wound, and turned amidst the war; he sprang to the walls, and left his foes behind, and snatched at the beam he first could find; looked up, and leaped aloft at all the stretch, in hopes to reach the helping hand of some kind friend. But Turnus followed hard his hunted prey (his spear had almost reached him in the way, short of his reins, and scarce a span behind). "Fool," said the chief, "though fleeter than the wind, could you presume to escape, when I pursue?" He said, and drew the trembling dastard down by the feet; at the tug he fell; vast ruins came along, rent from the smoking walls. Thus on some silver swan, or timorous hare, Jove's bird comes souring down from upper air; her crooked talons truss the fearful prey; then out of sight she soars, and wings her way. So the grim wolf seizes the tender lamb, in vain lamented by the bleating dam.

A young Trojan who escapes the burning tower and is run down by Turnus.

The jolly crew, forgetful of the past, shared the quarry and hurried their plentiful dinner. Some stripped off the skin; some divided up the spoil; limbs, still trembling, boiled in the cauldrons; some broiled the steaming entrails over the fire. Stretched at ease on the grassy turf, they dined, restoring their strength with meat and cheering their souls with wine. Their hunger thus appeased, their thoughts turned to the doubtful fortune of their absent friends. Alternate hopes and fears possessed their minds, whether to count them dead or still distressed. Above the rest, Aeneas mourned the fate of brave Orontes, and the uncertain state of Gyas, Lycus, and Amycus. The day, but not their sorrows, ended thus.

A Trojan captain given up for lost after the storm.

## modern-en · amycus-huntsman · 9:49

"But do not hope," said Turnus, "when I strike, to shun your fate: our force is not alike, nor is your steel tempered by the Lemnian god." Then rising, he stood at his utmost stretch, and aimed from high: the full descending blow cleaved the broad front and beardless cheeks in two. Down sank the giant with a thundering sound: his ponderous limbs oppressed the trembling ground; blood, brains, and foam gushed from the gaping wound; the keen steel divided scalp, face, and shoulders, and the shared visage hung on equal sides. The Trojans fled from their approaching fate; and had the victor then secured the gate, and unclosed the bars to his troops without, one lucky day would have ended all his wars. But boiling youth, and blind desire of blood, pushed on his fury to pursue the crowd. Hamstrung behind, unhappy Gyges died; then Phalaris was added to his side. He drew the pointed javelins from the dead, and threw their friends' arms against their fellows. Strong Halys stood in vain; weak Phlegys fled; Saturnia, still at hand, supplied new force and fire. Then Halius, Prytanis, Alcander fell—engaged against the foes who scaled the wall: but whom they feared without, they found within. At last, though late, he was seen by Lynceus. He called new succors, and assaulted the prince; but his force was weak, and their defense was vain. Turned to the right, the hero drew his sword, and at one blow slew the bold aggressor. He lopped the neck; and, with a stroke so strong, the helm flew off, and bore the head along. Next him, he killed the huntsman Amycus, skilled in envenomed darts and in poison. Then Clytius fell beneath his fatal spear, and Cretheus, whom the Muses held so dear: he fought with courage, and he sang the fight; arms were his business, verses his delight.

A Trojan huntsman, skilled in poisoned darts, killed by Turnus in the camp.

## modern-en · alethes · 1:9

While the pious prince lamented his fate, fierce Boreas drove against his flying sails and tore the sheets; the raging billows rose, and lifted the tossing vessels to the skies. The shivering oars could not sustain the blow; the galley gave way at the side and turned her prow, while those astern, descending down the steep, saw the boiling deep through yawning waves. Three ships were carried off by the southern blast, and dashed with fury on the hidden shoals—rocks which the Ausonian sailors knew: when they rose above the flood and showed their broad backs, they called them the Altars. Three more ships fierce Eurus, in his angry mood, dashed on the shallows of the shifting sand, and left them stranded in mid-ocean. Orontes' ship, that bore the Lycian crew—a horrid sight, even in the hero's view—was overwhelmed from stem to stern; the trembling pilot, torn from his rudder, was hurled headlong; three times the ship was tossed around, then broke apart at once, and was lost in the deep. Here and there above the waves were seen weapons, pictures, precious goods, and floating men. Even the stoutest vessel gave way to the storm, and sucked in the rushing sea through loosened planks. Ilioneus was her captain; and old Alethes, faithful Achates, and young bold Abas suffered no less. Their ships, with gaping seams, let in the flood of brine.

The oldest of the Trojan counsellors, who blesses Nisus and Euryalus.

## modern-en · capys · 1:12

First, good Achates, with repeated strokes of clashing flints, struck their hidden fire. A short flame caught; a bed of withered leaves received the dying sparks as they fell. Kindled into life, they rose in fiery fumes and, fed with stronger fuel, mounted to the skies. The Trojans, dripping wet, either stood around the cheerful blaze or lay along the ground. Some dried their grain, spoiled with brine, ground it between stones, and prepared to dine. Aeneas climbed the mountain's airy brow and took a prospect of the seas below, hoping to spy Capys from there, or Antheus, or to see the streamers of Caicus flying. No vessels were in view; but on the plain three stately stags, with branching heads, led a lordly train; the more ignoble herd followed their stately steps, grazing slowly along. He halted; and while they fed in security below, he took the quiver and the trusty bow that Achates was used to carry. First he laid the leaders low, and then pierced the rest; nor did he cease from his arrows until seven mighty bodies stained the shaded plain with their blood. For the seven ships he made an equal share, and returned to the port in triumph from the hunt. He broached the jars of generous wine—Acestes' gift, when the fleet left his Trinacrian shores—and prepared for the feast, sharing the wine equally with the venison. While he dealt it round, the pious chief allayed the common grief with cheerful words: "Endure, and conquer! Jove will soon dispose our past and present sufferings to future good. With me you have survived the rocks of Scylla, and defied the inhuman Cyclops and his den. What greater ills can you endure after that? Take courage again and put away care; an hour will come when it will be a pleasure to recall your past sorrows, as blessings sent by Fate. Through various hazards and events we move to Latium and the realms foreordained by Jove. There we are called (that is the promise of the skies), where Trojan kingdoms may rise once again. Endure the hardships of your present state; live, and keep yourselves for a better fate."

A Trojan captain.

## modern-en · capys-alban · 6:28

Thus having said, the father spirit led the priestess and his son through swarms of shades, and took a rising ground, from which to see the long procession of his progeny. “Survey,” the sire pursued, “this airy throng, as they pass along, offered to your view. These are the Italian names, which fate will join with ours, and graft upon the Trojan line. Observe the youth who appears first in sight, and holds the nearest station to the light; already he seems to snuff the vital air, and leans just forward, on a shining spear: he is Silvius, your last-begotten race, but sent first in order, to fill your place; an Alban name, but mixed with Dardan blood, born in the covert of a shady wood: fair Lavinia, your surviving wife, shall breed him in groves, to lead a solitary life. In Alba he shall fix his royal seat, and, born a king, shall beget a race of kings. Then Procas, honor of the Trojan name, Capys, and Numitor, of endless fame. After these, a second Silvius appears; Silvius Aeneas, for he bears your name; equally renowned for arms and justice, who, late restored, shall be crowned in Alba. How great they look! How vigorously they wield their weighty lances, and sustain the shield! But those who appear crowned with oaken wreaths shall rear the Gabian walls and strong Fidena; shall found Nomentum, Bola, with Pometia; and raise Collatian towers on rocky ground. All these shall then be towns of mighty fame, though now they lie obscure, and as lands without a name. See Romulus the great, born to restore the crown which once his injured grandsire wore. A priestess of your blood shall bear this prince, and he shall appear in arms like his sire. Two rising crests adorn his royal head; born from a god, himself born to godhead: his sire already signs him for the skies, and marks the seat amidst the deities. Auspicious chief! Your race, in times to come, shall spread the conquests of imperial Rome. Rome, whose ascending towers shall invade heaven, enveloping earth and ocean in her shade; high as the Mother of the Gods in place, and proud, like her, of an immortal race. Then, when in pomp she makes the Phrygian round, with golden turrets crowned on her temples; a hundred gods supply her sweeping train; all her offspring, and all command the sky.

An Alban king in the parade of Aeneas’s descendants.

## modern-en · bitias-carthage · 1:37

Now, when the rage of hunger was appeased, the meat removed, and every guest was pleased, the golden bowls were crowned with sparkling wine, and cheerful cries resounded through the palace. From gilded roofs hung lamps displayed nocturnal beams that rivaled the day. The queen commanded that a golden bowl, shining with divine gems, should be crowned with wine—the bowl which Belus and all the Tyrian line had used. Then, when silence had been proclaimed through the hall, she spoke: "O hospitable Jove, we invoke your sacred name and power with solemn rites; bless this auspicious hour for both nations! So may the Trojan and the Tyrian line be joined in lasting concord from this day. You, Bacchus, god of joys and friendly cheer, and you, gracious Juno, both be present here! And you, my lords of Tyre, address your vows to Heaven with mine, to ratify the peace." Then she took the goblet crowned with nectar (sprinkling the first libations on the ground), and raised it to her mouth with sober grace. Then, after sipping, she offered it to the next in place. It was Bitias whom she called, a thirsty soul; he took the challenge, embraced the bowl, and with pleasure swallowed the gold, nor did he cease to draw until he saw the bottom of the cup. The goblet went around; Iopas brought his golden lyre, and sang what ancient Atlas had taught him: the various labors of the wandering moon, and whence the eclipses of the sun proceed; the origin of men and beasts; and whence the rains arise, and fires dispense their warmth; and how the fixed and wandering stars dispose their influence; what shakes the solid earth; what cause delays the summer nights and shortens winter days. The Tyrians praised the song with peals of shouts, and those peals were echoed by the Trojan throng. The unhappy queen prolonged the night with talk, and drank large drafts of love with vast delight. She inquired much of Priam, and more of Hector; then asked what arms the swarthy Memnon wore, and what troops he had landed on the Trojan shore; the steeds of Diomede varied the discourse, and fierce Achilles, with his matchless force. At length, as fate and her ill stars required, she desired to hear the whole series of the war. "Relate fully, my godlike guest," she said, "the Grecian stratagems, the town betrayed, the fatal issue of so long a war, your flight, your wanderings, and your woes. For, since your men have been distressed on every sea and every coast, and your navy tossed, seven times the sun has seen either tropic, the winter has been banished, and the spring renewed."

A Tyrian lord at Dido’s feast, the first to take up the challenge of the cup.

## modern-en · bitias-trojan · 9:43

Pandarus and Bitias, thunderbolts of war, whom Hiera bore to bold Alcanor on Ida's top, two youths of height and size like firs that rise on their mother mountain, presuming on their force, unbarred the gates, and of their own accord invited the war. With fates averse, against their king's command, armed, on the right and on the left they stood, and flanked the passage: they wore shining steel, and waving crests appeared above their heads. Thus two tall oaks that adorn the banks of the Po lift up to heaven their unshorn leafy heads, and, overpressed with nature's heavy load, dance to the whistling winds, and nod at each other. In flows a tide of Latians, when they see the gate set open, and the passage free; bold Quercens, with rash Tmarus, rushing on, Equicolus, who shone in bright armor, and Haemon first; but soon repulsed they flew, or died in the well-defended pass. These were fired with success, and those with rage, and each at length engaged on equal terms. Drawn from their lines, and issuing on the plain, the Trojans maintained the fight hand to hand.

A giant Trojan, son of Alcanor and the nymph Hiera, who opens the camp gate and dies for it.

## modern-en · pandarus-lycian · 5:21

This done, Aeneas ordered, for the close, the strife of archers with contending bows. He raised with his own hands, on the shore, the mast that Sergesthus' shattered galley had borne. They tied a fluttering dove upon the top, the living mark at which their arrows would fly. The rival archers advanced in a line, to receive their turn of shooting from chance. A helmet held their names; the lots were drawn: on the first scroll was read Hippocoon. The people shouted. On the next was found young Mnestheus, lately crowned with naval honors. The third contained Eurytion's noble name, your brother, Pandarus, and next in fame, whom Pallas urged to confound the treaty, and to send a feathered wound among the Greeks. Acestes remained last at the bottom, whom not his age restrained from youthful sports. Soon all with vigor bent their trusty bows, and each chose his arrow from the quiver. Hippocoon's was the first: with forceful sway it flew, and, whizzing, cut the liquid way. Fixed in the mast the feathered weapon stood: the fearful pigeon fluttered in her bonds, and the tree trembled, and the shouting cries of the pleased people rent the vaulted skies. Then Mnestheus drove his arrow to the head, with lifted eyes, and took his aim above, but made a glancing shot, and missed the dove; yet missed so narrowly that he cut the cord that fastened by the foot the flitting bird. The captive thus released, she flew away, and beat with clapping wings the yielding skies. With his bow already bent, Eurytion stood; and, having first invoked his brother god, he sped his winged shaft with eager haste. The fatal message reached her as she fled: she left her life aloft; she struck the ground, and rendered back the weapon in the wound. Acestes, grudging at his lot, remained, without a prize to gratify his pains. Yet, shooting upward, he sent his shaft, to show an archer's art, and boast his twanging bow. The feathered arrow gave a dire portent, from which later augurs judge events. Chafed by the speed, it fired; and, as it flew, drew a trail of following flames ascending: kindling, they mounted, and marked the shiny way; like falling meteors they played across the skies, and vanished into wind, or decayed in a blaze. The Trojans and Sicilians wildly stared, and, trembling, turned their wonder into prayer. The Dardan prince put on a smiling face, and embraced Acestes closely; then, honoring him with gifts above the rest, turned the bad omen, and did not confess his fears. “The gods,” said he, “have wrought this miracle, and ordered you the prize without the lot. Accept this goblet, rough with figured gold, which Thracian Cisseus gave my sire of old: receive this pledge of ancient amity, which I justly give to my second sire.” He said this, and, with the trumpets' cheerful sound, proclaimed him victor, and crowned him with laurel. Nor did good Eurytion envy him the prize, though he had transfixed the pigeon in the skies. He who cut the line was graced with the second gifts; the third was his whose arrow pierced the mast.

The Lycian archer who broke the truce at Troy, named as Eurytion’s brother.

## modern-en · helymus · 5:2

Now, when the following morning had chased away the flying stars, and light had restored the day, Aeneas called the Trojan troops around, and thus addressed them from a rising ground: “Offspring of heaven, divine Dardanian race! The sun, revolving through the ethereal space, has filled the shining circle of the year since this isle first held my father's ashes: and now the rising day renews the year; a day forever sad, forever dear. I would celebrate this with annual games, with gifts piled on altars, and holy flames, though banished to Gaetulia's barren sands, caught on Grecian seas, or on hostile lands. But since this happy storm has driven our fleet (not, as I judge, without the will of Heaven) upon these friendly shores and flowery plains, which hide Anchises and his blessed remains, let us with joy perform his due honors, and pray for prosperous winds, to renew our voyage; let us pray that in towns and temples of our own, the name of great Anchises may be known, and that yearly games may spread the gods' renown. Acestes, of the Trojan race, is pleased to grace our sports with royal gifts: the king bestows two steers on every ship; his gods and ours shall share in your equal vows. Besides, if, nine days hence, the rosy morn shall adorn the skies with unclouded light, that day I mean to grace with solemn sports: light galleys shall run a watery race on the seas; some shall contend in swiftness for the goal, and others try to bend the twanging bow; the strong, armed with iron gauntlets, shall stand opposed in combat on the yellow sand. Let all be present at the prepared games, and let the joyful victors await the just reward. But now assist the rites, crowned with garlands.” He said this, and first bound his brows with myrtle. Then Helymus, led by his example, and old Acestes, each adorned his head; so too did young Ascanius, with a sprightly grace, tie his temples, and all the Trojan race.

A Sicilian of Acestes’ following who runs in the foot race.

## modern-en · panopes · 5:11

From there the Trojan hero bent his way into the neighboring plain, penned in with mountains, whose sides were shaded with surrounding wood. Full in the midst of this fair valley stood a native theater, which, rising slow by just degrees, overlooked the ground below. High on a sylvan throne the leader sat; a numerous train attended in solemn state. Here those who delighted in the rapid course were invited by the desire of honor and the prize. The rival runners stood without order; the Trojans mingled with the Sicilian band. First appeared Nisus, with Euryalus; Euryalus was a boy of blooming years, crowned with sprightly grace and equal beauty; Nisus, renowned for his friendship to the youth. Diores next, of Priam's royal race; then Salius joined with Patron, took their place; but Patron had his birth in Arcadia, and Salius his from Acarnanian earth; then two Sicilian youths, whose names were these: swift Helymus, and lovely Panopes: both jolly huntsmen, both bred in the forest, and acknowledging old Acestes as their head; with several others of more ignoble name, whom time has not delivered over to fame.

A Sicilian huntsman of Acestes’ following.

## modern-en · entellus · 5:17

Acestes, fired with just disdain to see the palm usurped without a victory, reproached Entellus thus, who sat beside him, and heard and saw, unmoved, the Trojan's pride: “Once, but in vain, a champion of renown, can you so tamely bear the ravished crown, a prize borne in triumph before your sight, and shun, for fear, the danger of the fight? Where the spoil that filled your house, and the fame that filled our isle?” Entellus thus replied: “My soul is still the same, unmoved with fear, and moved with martial fame; but my chill blood is curdled in my veins, and scarcely the shadow of a man remains. Then haughty Dares appeared in the lists; stalking he strode, bearing his head erect: his nervous arms wielded the weighty gauntlets, and loud applause echoed through the field. ## modern-en · hippocoon · 5:21

This done, Aeneas ordered, for the close, the strife of archers with contending bows. He raised with his own hands, on the shore, the mast that Sergesthus' shattered galley had borne. They tied a fluttering dove upon the top, the living mark at which their arrows would fly. The rival archers advanced in a line, to receive their turn of shooting from chance. A helmet held their names; the lots were drawn: on the first scroll was read Hippocoon. The people shouted. On the next was found young Mnestheus, lately crowned with naval honors. The third contained Eurytion's noble name, your brother, Pandarus, and next in fame, whom Pallas urged to confound the treaty, and to send a feathered wound among the Greeks. Acestes remained last at the bottom, whom not his age restrained from youthful sports. Soon all with vigor bent their trusty bows, and each chose his arrow from the quiver. Hippocoon's was the first: with forceful sway it flew, and, whizzing, cut the liquid way. Fixed in the mast the feathered weapon stood: the fearful pigeon fluttered in her bonds, and the tree trembled, and the shouting cries of the pleased people rent the vaulted skies. Then Mnestheus drove his arrow to the head, with lifted eyes, and took his aim above, but made a glancing shot, and missed the dove; yet missed so narrowly that he cut the cord that fastened by the foot the flitting bird. The captive thus released, she flew away, and beat with clapping wings the yielding skies. With his bow already bent, Eurytion stood; and, having first invoked his brother god, he sped his winged shaft with eager haste. The fatal message reached her as she fled: she left her life aloft; she struck the ground, and rendered back the weapon in the wound. Acestes, grudging at his lot, remained, without a prize to gratify his pains. Yet, shooting upward, he sent his shaft, to show an archer's art, and boast his twanging bow. The feathered arrow gave a dire portent, from which later augurs judge events. Chafed by the speed, it fired; and, as it flew, drew a trail of following flames ascending: kindling, they mounted, and marked the shiny way; like falling meteors they played across the skies, and vanished into wind, or decayed in a blaze. The Trojans and Sicilians wildly stared, and, trembling, turned their wonder into prayer. The Dardan prince put on a smiling face, and embraced Acestes closely; then, honoring him with gifts above the rest, turned the bad omen, and did not confess his fears. “The gods,” said he, “have wrought this miracle, and ordered you the prize without the lot. Accept this goblet, rough with figured gold, which Thracian Cisseus gave my sire of old: receive this pledge of ancient amity, which I justly give to my second sire.” He said this, and, with the trumpets' cheerful sound, proclaimed him victor, and crowned him with laurel. Nor did good Eurytion envy him the prize, though he had transfixed the pigeon in the skies. He who cut the line was graced with the second gifts; the third was his whose arrow pierced the mast.

A Trojan whose lot is drawn first in the archery contest.

Thus marching on in military pride, shouts of applause resounded from side to side. They wore their helmets adorned with laurel wreaths, each brandishing aloft a cornel spear. Young Priam led the first; a lovely boy, whose grandsire was the unhappy king of Troy; his race was known to fame in after times, adding new honors to the Latian name; and well the royal boy became his Thracian steed. ## modern-en · nautes · 5:32

But doubtful thoughts divided the hero's heart: whether he should still reside in Sicily, forgetful of his fates, or tempt the main, in hope of gaining the promised Italy. Then Nautes, old and wise, to whom alone Pallas had foreshown the will of Heaven; versed in portents, experienced, and inspired to tell events, and what the fates required; thus while he stood, inclined to neither part, relieved his laboring mind with cheerful words: “O goddess-born, resigned in every state, bear with patience, push with prudence your fate. By suffering well, we subdue our Fortune; flee when she frowns, and, when she calls, pursue. Your friend Acestes is of Trojan kind; to him disclose the secrets of your mind: trust in his hands your old and useless train; they are too numerous for the ships that yet remain: the feeble, the old, those indulgent of their ease, the dames who dread the dangers of the seas, with all the dastard crew, who dare not stand the shock of battle with your foes by land. Here you may build a common town for all, and, from Acestes' name, call it Acesta.” These reasons, joined with his friend's experience, encouraged him much, but more disturbed his mind.

The old Trojan seer who advises leaving the weary behind in Sicily.

## modern-en · beroe · 5:27

The goddess, great in mischief, viewed their pains, and restrained her heavenly limbs in a woman's form. In face and shape she became old Beroe, Doryclus' wife, a venerable dame, once blessed with riches, and a mother's name. Thus changed, she ran amidst the crying crowd, mingled with the matrons, and began these words: “O wretched we, whom neither the Grecian power, nor the flames, destroyed in Troy's unhappy hour! O wretched we, reserved by cruel fate, beyond the ruins of the sinking state! Now seven revolving years are wholly run, since we began this unprosperous voyage; since, tossed from shores to shores, from lands to lands, inhospitable rocks and barren sands, wandering in exile through the stormy sea, we search in vain for flying Italy. Now cast by fortune on this kindred land, what should withstand our rest and rising walls, or hinder us from fixing our banished band here? O country lost, and gods redeemed in vain, if we still remain in endless exile! Shall we no more renew the Trojan walls, or view the streams of some dissembled Simois? Haste, join with me, to consume the unhappy fleet! Cassandra bids it; and I declare her doom. In sleep I saw her; she supplied my hands (for this I more than dreamt) with flaming brands: ‘With these,' she said, ‘destroy these wandering ships: these are your fated seats, and this your Troy.' Time calls you now; employ the precious hour: do not slack the good presage, while Heaven inspires our minds to dare, and gives the ready fires. See! Neptune's altars minister their brands: the god is pleased; the god supplies our hands.” Then she drew a flaming fire from the pile, and, tossed in air, threw it amidst the galleys.

Doryclus’s aged wife, whose shape Iris takes to fire the Trojan ships.

## modern-en · pyrgo · 5:28

Wrapped in amazement, the matrons wildly stared; then Pyrgo, revered for her hoary hair, Pyrgo, the nurse of Priam's numerous race, cried: “This is no Beroe, though she belies her face! What terrors arise from her frowning brow! Behold a goddess in her ardent eyes! What rays are seen around her heavenly face! Mark her majestic voice, and more than mortal bearing! I just left Beroe, whom, pined with pain, her age and anguish detain from these rites,” she said. The matrons, seized with new amazement, rolled their malignant eyes, and gazed upon the navy. They feared, and hoped, and obeyed neither part: they hoped the fated land, but feared the fatal way. The goddess, having done her task below, mounted up on equal wings, and bent her painted bow. Struck with the sight, and seized with divine rage, the matrons prosecuted their mad design: they shrieked aloud; they snatched, with impious hands, the food of altars; fires and flaming brands. Green boughs and saplings, mingled in their haste, and smoking torches, they cast on the ships. The flame, unstopped at first, gained more fury, and Vulcan rode at large with loosened reins: triumphant he soared to the painted sterns, and seized, in this way, the banks and crackling oars. Eumelus was the first to bear the news, while they still crowded the rural theater. Then, what they heard was witnessed by their eyes: a storm of sparkles and of flames arose. Ascanius took the alarm, while he still led his early warriors on his prancing steed, and, spurring on, soon overpassed his equals; nor could his frightened friends reclaim his haste. As soon as the royal youth appeared in view, he sent his voice before him as he flew: “What madness moves you, matrons, to destroy the last remainders of unhappy Troy? You burn not hostile fleets, but your own hopes, and turn your fatal fury on your friends. Behold your own Ascanius!” While he said this, he drew his glittering helmet from his head, in which he had led the youths to sportful arms. By this, Aeneas and his train appeared; and now the women, seized with shame and fear, dispersed, and took their flight to woods and caverns, abhorred their actions, and avoided the light; they acknowledged their friends, and found their error, and shook the goddess from their altered mind.

The old nurse of Priam’s children, who sees through Iris’s disguise.

## modern-en · acmon · 10:8

The Aeneans wished in vain for their wanted chief, hopeless of flight, more hopeless of relief. Thin on the towers they stood; and even those few were a feeble, fainting, and dejected crew. ## modern-en · caeneus-underworld · 6:16

Not far from there, the Mournful Fields appear, so called from lovers who inhabit there. The souls whom that unhappy flame invades, in secret solitude and myrtle shades, make endless moans, and, pining with desire, lament too late their unextinguished fire. Here he found Procris, and Eriphyle here, baring her breast, yet bleeding with the wound made by her son. He saw Pasiphaë there, with Phaedra's ghost, a foul incestuous pair. There Laodamia, with Evadne, moves, unhappy both, but loyal in their loves: Caeneus, once a woman, and once a man, but ending in the sex she first began. Not far from these stood Phoenician Dido, fresh from her wound, her bosom bathed in blood; whom when the Trojan hero hardly knew, obscure in shades, and with a doubtful view, (doubtful as he who sees, through dusky night, or thinks he sees, the moon's uncertain light,) he first approached the sullen shade with tears; and, as his love inspired him, thus he said: “Unhappy queen! Then is the common breath of rumor true, in your reported death, and I, alas, the cause? By Heaven, I vow, and all the powers that rule the realms below, unwilling I forsook your friendly state, commanded by the gods, and forced by fate. Those gods, that fate, whose unresisted might has sent me to these regions void of light, through the vast empire of eternal night. Nor did I dare to presume that, pressed with grief, my flight should urge you to this dire relief. Stay, stay your steps, and listen to my vows: this is the last interview that fate allows!” In vain he thus attempted to move her mind with tears, and prayers, and late-repenting love. Disdainfully she looked; then, turning round, she fixed her eyes unmoved upon the ground, and regarded what he said and swore no more than the deaf rocks, when the loud billows roar; but she whirled away, to shun his hateful sight, hid in the forest and the shades of night; then sought Sichaeus through the shady grove, who answered all her cares, and equaled all her love.

A shade in the fields of mourning, once a woman and once a man.

## modern-en · helenor · 9:34

Young Lycus and Helenor alone escaped; saved (how, they knew not) from the steepy leap. Helenor, the elder of the two, by birth on one side royal, and on one a son of earth, whom Licymnia bore to the Lydian king, and sent her boasted bastard to the war (a privilege which none but freemen share). His arms were slight, a sword and silver shield; no marks of honor charged its empty field. As light as he fell, so light the youth arose, and, rising, found himself amidst his foes; no flight was left, nor hopes to force his way. Emboldened by despair, he stood at bay; and, like a stag, whom all the troop of eager huntsmen and invading hounds surround, resolved on death, he dissipates his fears, and bounds aloft against the pointed spears. So dares the youth, secure of death, and throws his dying body on his thickest foes. But Lycus, swifter of foot by far, ran, doubled, wound, and turned amidst the war; he sprang to the walls, and left his foes behind, and snatched at the beam he first could find; looked up, and leaped aloft at all the stretch, in hopes to reach the helping hand of some kind friend. But Turnus followed hard his hunted prey (his spear had almost reached him in the way, short of his reins, and scarce a span behind). "Fool," said the chief, "though fleeter than the wind, could you presume to escape, when I pursue?" He said, and drew the trembling dastard down by the feet; at the tug he fell; vast ruins came along, rent from the smoking walls. Thus on some silver swan, or timorous hare, Jove's bird comes souring down from upper air; her crooked talons truss the fearful prey; then out of sight she soars, and wings her way. So the grim wolf seizes the tender lamb, in vain lamented by the bleating dam.

A Lydian king’s bastard son by the slave Licymnia, who leaps from the burning tower and dies fighting.

## modern-en · idaeus-trojan · 9:29

Meanwhile the Trojans ran, where danger called; they lined their trenches, and they manned their walls. In front they stood extended to the left; safe was the right, surrounded by the flood. But, casting a frightful view from their towers, they saw the faces, which too well they knew, though then disguised in death, and smeared all over with obscene filth, and dropping putrid gore. Soon hasty fame bore through the sad city the mournful message to the mother's ears. An icy cold benumbed her limbs; she shook; the blood forsook her cheeks, and her hand forsook the web. She ran round the ramparts amidst the war, nor feared the flying darts; she rent her hair, and filled the liquid air with loud laments. "So, then, my loved Euryalus appears! Thus looks the prop of my declining years! Was it on this face my famished eyes I fed? Ah, how unlike the living is the dead! And could you leave me, cruel, thus alone? Not one kind kiss from a departing son! No look, no last adieu before he went, in an ill-boding hour, to slaughter sent! Cold on the ground, and pressing foreign clay, he lies, a prey to Latian dogs and fowls! Nor was I near to close his dying eyes, to wash his wounds, to weep his obsequies, to call his crying friends about his corpse, or spread the mantle (made for other ends) on his dear body, which I wove with care, nor did I spare my daily pains or nightly labor. Where shall I find his corpse? What earth sustains his dismembered trunk, and his cold remains? For this, alas, I left my needful ease, exposed my life to winds and winter seas! If any pity touches Rutulian hearts, here empty all your quivers, all your darts; or, if they fail, you, Jove, conclude my woe, and send me thunderstruck to the shades below!" Her shrieks and clamors pierced the Trojans' ears, unmanned their courage, and augmented their fears; nor could young Ascanius sustain the sight, nor old Ilioneus restrain his tears, but Actor and Idaeus were jointly sent, to bear the madding mother to her tent.

A Trojan sent with Actor to carry Euryalus’s mother away.

But Trivia kept her care, Hippolytus, alone in secret shades, unknown to fate, and called him Virbius in the Egerian grove, where then he lived obscure, but safe from Jove. For this reason, from Trivia's temple and her wood, horses that shed their master's blood are driven, affrighted by the monsters of the flood. His son, the second Virbius, retained his father's art, and reined warrior steeds.

Hippolytus’s son, named for his father’s second life, who comes to the war from Aricia’s groves.

At first, while fortune favored neither side, the fight was tried with clubs and burning brands; but now, both parties reinforced, the fields were bright with flaming swords and brazen shields. A shining harvest was displayed by either host, and each shot against the sun with equal rays. Thus, when a black-browed gust begins to rise, white foam at first boils on the curled ocean; then roars the main, and the billows mount the skies, until, fully blown by the fury of the storm, the muddy bottom is thrown over the clouds. Almon fell first, old Tyrrheus' eldest care, pierced with an arrow from the distant war: the flying weapon stood fixed in his throat, and stopped his breath, and drank his vital blood. Huge heaps of slain rose about the body; among the rest, rich Galesus lies, a good old man, who had in vain preached peace amidst the madness of the unruly train: five herds, five bleating flocks, filled his pastures; his lands were tilled by a hundred yoke of oxen.

But if we still have fresh recruits in store, if our confederates can afford us more; if the contended field we bravely fought, and a bloodless victory was not bought; their losses equaled ours; and, for their slain, they filled the shining plain with equal fires—why, unforced, should we so tamely yield, and, before the trumpet sounds, resign the field? Good unexpected, and evils unforeseen, appear by turns, as fortune shifts the scene: some, raised aloft, come tumbling down amain; then fall so hard, they bound and rise again. If Diomede refuses to lend his aid, the great Messapus yet remains our friend: Tolumnius, who foretells events, is ours; the Italian chiefs and princes join their powers; nor least in number, nor last in name, your own brave subjects have embraced your cause. Above the rest, the Volscian Amazon contains an army in herself alone, and heads a squadron, terrible to sight, with glittering shields, bright in brazen armor. Yet, if the foe demand a single fight, and I alone withstand the public peace; if you consent, he shall not be refused, nor shall he find a hand unused to victory. Let this new Achilles take the field, with fated armor, and with Vulcanian shield! For you, my royal father, and my fame, I, Turnus, not the least of all my name, devote my soul. He calls me hand to hand, and I alone will answer his demand. Drances shall rest secure, and neither share the danger, nor divide the prize of war."

The Latins’ augur, who reads the omen and throws the spear that breaks the truce.

## modern-en · camers · 10:43

On Lycas and Antaeus next he ran, two chiefs of Turnus, who led his van. They fled for fear; with these, he chased along Camers the yellow-locked, and Numa the strong; both great in arms, and both were fair and young. Camers was son to Volscens lately slain, surpassing all the Latian train in wealth, and in Amycla had fixed his silent easy reign. And, as Aegaeon, when he strove with heaven, stood opposite in arms to mighty Jove; moved all his hundred hands, provoked the war, defied the forky lightning from afar; at fifty mouths his flaming breath expires, and flash for flash returns, and fires for fires; in his right hand he wields as many swords, and takes the thunder on as many shields: with strength like his, the Trojan hero stood; and soon the fields were strewed with falling corpses, when once his falchion had found the taste of blood. With fury scarce to be conceived, he flew against Niphaeus, whom four coursers drew. They, when they saw the fiery chief advance, and pushing his pointed lance at their chests, wheeled with so swift a motion, mad with fear, that they threw their master headlong from the chair. They stare, they start, nor stop their course, before they bear the bounding chariot to the shore.

A rich young Latin, Volscens’s son, killed by Aeneas.

## modern-en · volscens · 9:25

But they had not passed far, before they spied three hundred horse, with Volscens for their guide. The queen had sent a legion to King Turnus; but the swift horse forestalled the slower foot, and now, advancing, sought the leader's tent. They saw the pair; for, through the doubtful shade, the shining helm of Euryalus betrayed them, on which the moon played in full reflection. "It is not for nothing," cried Volscens from the crowd, "that these men go there." Then he raised his voice aloud: "Stand! Stand! Why thus in arms? And whither bent? From where, to whom, and on what errand sent?" Silent, they scudded away, and hasted their flight to neighboring woods, and trusted themselves to night. The speedy horse beset all the passages, and spurred their smoking steeds to cross their way, and watched each entrance of the winding wood. Black was the forest: it stood thick with beech, horrid with fern, and intricate with thorn; few paths of human feet, or tracks of beasts, were worn. The darkness of the shades, his heavy prey, and fear, misled the younger from his way. But Nisus hit the turns with happier haste, and, thoughtless of his friend, passed the forest, and the Alban plains (so called from Alba's name), where King Latinus then stabled his oxen; till, at length, turning, he stood his ground, and missed his friend, and cast his eyes around: "Ah, wretch!" he cried, "where have I left behind the unhappy youth? Where shall I hope to find him? Or what way shall I take?" Again he ventured back, and trod the mazes of his former track. He winds the wood, and, listening, heard the noise of tramping coursers, and the riders' voices. The sound approached; and suddenly he viewed the foes enclosing, and his friend pursued, forelaid and taken, while he strove in vain to gain the shelter of the friendly shades. What should he next attempt? What arms employ, what fruitless force, to free the captive boy? Or should he, desperate, rush and lose his life, oppressed with odds, in such unequal strife?

The Latin cavalry commander who kills Euryalus and is killed by Nisus.

## modern-en · rhamnes · 9:22

First they passed the trenches; then they took their way where their proud foes lay in pitched pavilions—fatal to many, before they themselves were slain. They found the careless host dispersed upon the plain, who, gorged, and drunk with wine, supinely snored. Unharnessed chariots stood along the shore: amidst the wheels and reins, the goblet by, a medley of debauch and war, they lay. Observing this, Nisus showed his friend the sight: "Behold a conquest gained without a fight. Occasion offers, and I stand prepared; there lies our way; be you upon the guard, and look around, while I securely go, and hew a passage through the sleeping foe." Softly he spoke; then, striding, took his way, with his drawn sword, to where haughty Rhamnes lay; his head raised high on tapestry beneath, and heaving from his breast, he drew his breath; a king and prophet, beloved by King Turnus; but fate cannot be removed by prescience. Him and his sleeping slaves he slew; then he spied where Remus, with his rich retinue, lay. His armor-bearer first, and next he killed his charioteer, entrenched between the wheels and his beloved horses; last he invaded their lord: full on his neck he drove the fatal sword; the gasping head flew off; a purple flood flowed from the trunk, that weltered in the blood, which, dispersed by the spurning heels, besprinkled the bed and bedewed the ground. Lamus the bold, and Lamyrus the strong, he slew, and then Serranus, fair and young. The youth had retired from dice and wine to rest, and puffed the fumy god out of his breast: even then he dreamt of drink and lucky play—more lucky, had it lasted till the day. The famished lion thus, with hunger bold, overleaps the fences of the nightly fold, and tears the peaceful flocks: with silent awe, trembling they lie, and pant beneath his paw.

An augur and Turnus’s favourite, killed asleep by Nisus.

## modern-en · remus-brother · 1:17

"Daughter, dismiss your fears. The fates of your descendants stand fixed and unchanged, as you desire. You shall behold the Lavinian walls you wish for; and when Aeneas, ripe for heaven, is called by fate, you shall bear him up, sublime, to me. No counsel has reversed my firm decree. And lest new fears disturb your happy state, know that I have searched the mystic rolls of Fate. Your son (nor is the appointed season far off) shall wage successful war in Italy, tame fierce nations in the bloody field, impose sovereign laws, and build cities, until, every foe subdued, the sun has run its annual race three times through the signs. This is his appointed time. Then Ascanius, now called Iulus, shall begin his reign. He shall wear the crown for thirty rolling years, and then shall transfer the seat from Lavinium, and with hard labor shall build Alba Longa. The throne shall be filled by his successors for three hundred more years, and then Ilia the fair shall be seen, a priestess and a queen, who, filled with the seed of Mars, shall in due time bring forth twin boys at a single birth. A tawny wolf shall suckle the royal babes. Then Romulus shall gain his grandfather's throne, shall found towers of war, shall call the people Romans, and the city Rome. To them I assign no bounds of empire, nor term of years to their immortal line. Even haughty Juno, who now turmoils earth, seas, and heaven, and Jove himself, with endless broils, shall be reconciled at last, and join her friendly power to cherish and advance the Trojan line. The subject world shall acknowledge Rome's dominion, and lying prostrate shall adore the nation of the toga. An age is ripening in revolving fate when Troy shall overturn the Grecian state, and her conquering sons shall call for sweet revenge, to crush the people who conspired at her fall. Then Caesar shall arise from the Julian stock, whose empire shall be bounded only by ocean, and whose fame only by the skies; whom, laden with eastern spoils, our heaven, the just reward of human toils, shall securely receive with divine rites, and incense shall rise before his sacred shrine. Then dire debate and impious war shall cease, and the stern age shall be softened into peace. Then banished Faith shall return once more, and Vestal fires shall burn in hallowed temples; and Remus with Quirinus shall sustain the righteous laws, and restrain fraud and force. Janus himself shall stand before his shrine and guard the dreadful gates, with bolts and iron bars: within remains Fury, imprisoned, bound in brazen chains; high on a trophy of useless weapons he sits, and threatens the world with vain alarms."

Romulus’s brother, named in the promise of a Rome at peace.

## modern-en · rhoetus · 9:23

Nor with less rage did Euryalus employ the wrathful sword, or destroy fewer foes; but on the ignoble crowd his fury flew; he slew Fadus, Hebesus, and Rhoetus. ## modern-en · caedicus · 9:24

Now they arrived where Messapus had quartered. The fires were fainting there, and just alive; the warrior horses, tied in order, fed. Nisus observed the discipline, and said: "Our eager thirst of blood may betray us both; see the scattered streaks of dawning day, foe to nocturnal thefts. No more, my friend; let our glutted execution end here. We have made a lane through slaughtered bodies." Bold Euryalus, though loth, obeyed. They found a precious load of arms, and arras, and of plate; but these they left behind. Yet, fond of gaudy spoils, the boy would stay to make the rich caparison his prey, which lay on the steed of conquered Rhamnes. Nor did his eyes less longingly behold the girdle-belt, with nails of burnished gold. This present Caedicus the rich had bestowed on Remulus, when first they vowed friendship, and, though absent, joined in hospitable ties; he, dying, bequeathed the prize to his heir, until, oppressed by the conquering Ardean troops, he fell; and they possessed the glorious gift. These glittering spoils (now made the victor's gain) he fitted to his body, but fitted in vain: he found Messapus' helm among the rest, and laced it on, and wore the waving crest. Proud of their conquest, and prouder of their prey, they left the camp, and took the ready way.

A rich man who gave Remulus the golden belt that Euryalus takes.

## modern-en · sulmo · 9:26

Resolved at length, he shook his pointed spear; and, casting on the moon a mournful look: "Guardian of groves, and goddess of the night, fair queen," he said, "direct my dart aright. If ever my pious father, for my sake, made grateful offerings on your altars, or I increased them with my sylvan toils, and hung your holy roofs with savage spoils, grant me to scatter these." Then from his ear he poised, and aimed, and launched the trembling spear. The deadly weapon, hissing from the grove, drove impetuously on the back of Sulmo; pierced his thin armor, drank his vital blood, and left the broken wood within his body. He staggers round; his eyeballs roll in death, and with short sobs he gasps away his breath. All stood amazed—a second javelin flew with equal strength, and quivered through the skies. This forced its way through your temples, Tagus, and warmly buried itself in the brainpan. Fierce Volscens foamed with rage, and, gazing round, descried not him who gave the fatal wound, nor knew where to fix revenge: "But you," he cried, "shall pay for both," and at the prisoner flew with his drawn sword. Then, struck with deep despair, the lover could not bear that cruel sight, but rushed from his covert into open view, and sent his voice before him as he flew: "Me! Me!" he cried—"turn all your swords alone on me—the fact is confessed, the fault my own. He neither could nor dared, the guiltless youth: you moon and stars, bear witness to the truth! His only crime (if friendship can offend) is too much love to his unhappy friend." Too late he speaks: the sword, guided by fury, driven with full force, had pierced his tender sides. Down fell the beauteous youth: the yawning wound gushed out a purple stream, and stained the ground. His snowy neck reclined upon his breast, like a fair flower pressed by the keen plowshare; like a white poppy sinking on the plain, whose heavy head is overcharged with rain. Despair, and rage, and vengeance justly vowed, drove Nisus headlong onto the hostile crowd. He seeks Volscens; on him alone he bends: borne back, and hemmed in by his surrounding friends, onward he pressed, and kept him still in sight; then whirled his sword aloft with all his might: the unerring steel descended while he spoke, pierced his wide mouth, and broke through his weasand. Dying, he slew; and, staggering on the plain, with swimming eyes he sought his lover slain; then quietly fell on his bleeding bosom, content, in death, to be revenged so well.

A Rutulian speared in the back during the night pursuit.

Then from his ear he poised, and aimed, and launched the trembling spear. The deadly weapon, hissing from the grove, drove impetuously on the back of Sulmo; pierced his thin armor, drank his vital blood, and left the broken wood within his body. He staggers round; his eyeballs roll in death, and with short sobs he gasps away his breath. All stood amazed—a second javelin flew with equal strength, and quivered through the skies. This forced its way through your temples, Tagus, and warmly buried itself in the brainpan. Fierce Volscens foamed with rage, and, gazing round, descried not him who gave the fatal wound, nor knew where to fix revenge: "But you," he cried, "shall pay for both," and at the prisoner flew with his drawn sword. Then, struck with deep despair, the lover could not bear that cruel sight, but rushed from his covert into open view, and sent his voice before him as he flew: "Me! Me!" he cried—"turn all your swords alone on me—the fact is confessed, the fault my own. He neither could nor dared, the guiltless youth: you moon and stars, bear witness to the truth! His only crime (if friendship can offend) is too much love to his unhappy friend." Too late he speaks: the sword, guided by fury, driven with full force, had pierced his tender sides. Down fell the beauteous youth: the yawning wound gushed out a purple stream, and stained the ground. His snowy neck reclined upon his breast, like a fair flower pressed by the keen plowshare; like a white poppy sinking on the plain, whose heavy head is overcharged with rain. Despair, and rage, and vengeance justly vowed, drove Nisus headlong onto the hostile crowd. He seeks Volscens; on him alone he bends: borne back, and hemmed in by his surrounding friends, onward he pressed, and kept him still in sight; then whirled his sword aloft with all his might: the unerring steel descended while he spoke, pierced his wide mouth, and broke through his weasand. Dying, he slew; and, staggering on the plain, with swimming eyes he sought his lover slain; then quietly fell on his bleeding bosom, content, in death, to be revenged so well.

A Rutulian killed beside Sulmo.

## modern-en · antiphates · 9:44

Fierce Turnus fought in another quarter, when suddenly the unhoped-for news was brought that the foes had left the fastness of their place, had prevailed in fight, and had his men in chase. He quit the attack, and, to prevent their fate, ran to where the giant brothers guarded the gate. The first he met was Antiphates the brave, but base-begotten on a Theban slave, son of Sarpedon. He slew him: the deadly dart found passage through his breast, and pierced his heart. The Italian cornel stood fixed in the wound, warmed in his lungs, and in his vital blood. Aphidnus next, and Erymanthus, died, and Meropes, and the gigantic size of Bitias, threatening with his ardent eyes. Not by the feeble dart he fell oppressed (a dart would have been lost within that roomy breast), but from a knotted lance, large, heavy, strong, which roared like thunder as it whirled along; not two bull hides could withstand the impetuous force, nor coat of double mail, with scales of gold. Down sank the monster bulk, and pressed the ground; his arms and clattering shield sounded on the vast body. Not with less ruin than the Bajan mole, raised on the seas to control the surges, comes tumbling down at once the rocky wall; the stones, disjointed, fall prone into the deep from the vast pile; the scattered ocean flies; black sands, discolored froth, and mingled mud arise; the frighted billows roll, and seek the shores; then Prochyta trembles, then Ischia roars; Typhoeus, thrown beneath by Jove's command, astonished at the flaw that shakes the land, soon shifts his weary side, and, scarce awake, with wonder feels the weight press lighter on his back.

Sarpedon’s bastard son by a Theban slave, the first man Turnus meets inside the camp.

## modern-en · quercens · 9:43

Pandarus and Bitias, thunderbolts of war, whom Hiera bore to bold Alcanor on Ida's top, two youths of height and size like firs that rise on their mother mountain, presuming on their force, unbarred the gates, and of their own accord invited the war. With fates averse, against their king's command, armed, on the right and on the left they stood, and flanked the passage: they wore shining steel, and waving crests appeared above their heads. Thus two tall oaks that adorn the banks of the Po lift up to heaven their unshorn leafy heads, and, overpressed with nature's heavy load, dance to the whistling winds, and nod at each other. In flows a tide of Latians, when they see the gate set open, and the passage free; bold Quercens, with rash Tmarus, rushing on, Equicolus, who shone in bright armor, and Haemon first; but soon repulsed they flew, or died in the well-defended pass. These were fired with success, and those with rage, and each at length engaged on equal terms. Drawn from their lines, and issuing on the plain, the Trojans maintained the fight hand to hand.

A Rutulian who rushes the open gate.

## modern-en · clytius · 9:49

"But do not hope," said Turnus, "when I strike, to shun your fate: our force is not alike, nor is your steel tempered by the Lemnian god." Then rising, he stood at his utmost stretch, and aimed from high: the full descending blow cleaved the broad front and beardless cheeks in two. Down sank the giant with a thundering sound: his ponderous limbs oppressed the trembling ground; blood, brains, and foam gushed from the gaping wound; the keen steel divided scalp, face, and shoulders, and the shared visage hung on equal sides. The Trojans fled from their approaching fate; and had the victor then secured the gate, and unclosed the bars to his troops without, one lucky day would have ended all his wars. But boiling youth, and blind desire of blood, pushed on his fury to pursue the crowd. Hamstrung behind, unhappy Gyges died; then Phalaris was added to his side. He drew the pointed javelins from the dead, and threw their friends' arms against their fellows. Strong Halys stood in vain; weak Phlegys fled; Saturnia, still at hand, supplied new force and fire. Then Halius, Prytanis, Alcander fell—engaged against the foes who scaled the wall: but whom they feared without, they found within. At last, though late, he was seen by Lynceus. He called new succors, and assaulted the prince; but his force was weak, and their defense was vain. Turned to the right, the hero drew his sword, and at one blow slew the bold aggressor. He lopped the neck; and, with a stroke so strong, the helm flew off, and bore the head along. Next him, he killed the huntsman Amycus, skilled in envenomed darts and in poison. Then Clytius fell beneath his fatal spear, and Cretheus, whom the Muses held so dear: he fought with courage, and he sang the fight; arms were his business, verses his delight.

A Trojan killed by Turnus inside the camp.

## modern-en · lucagus · 10:44

Now Lucagus and Liger scour the plains, with two white steeds; but Liger holds the reins, and Lucagus maintains the lofty seat: bold brethren both. The former waved in air his flaming sword: Aeneas couched his spear, unused to threats, and more unused to fear. Then Liger thus: "Your confidence is vain to escape from here, as from the Trojan plain: these are not the steeds that Diomede bestrode, nor is this the chariot where Achilles rode; nor is Venus' veil here, nor Neptune's shield; your fatal hour is come, and this the field." Thus Liger vainly vaunts: the Trojan peer returned his answer with his flying spear. As Lucagus bends to lash his horses, prone to the wheels, and protends his left foot, prepared for fight, the fatal dart arrives, and drives through the borders of his buckler; it passed through and pierced his groin: the deadly wound cast him from his chariot, and rolled him on the ground. Whom the chief thus upbraids with scornful spite: "Blame not the slowness of your steeds in flight; no vain shadows forced their swift retreat; but you yourself forsake your empty seat." He said, and seized the loosened rein at once; for Liger lay already on the plain, by the same shock. Then, stretching out his hands, the recreant thus demands his wretched life: "Now, by yourself, O more than mortal man! By her and him from whom your breath began, who formed you thus divine, I beg you, spare this forfeit life, and hear your suppliant's prayer." This much he spoke, and more he would have said; but the stern hero turned aside his head, and cut him short: "I hear another man; you did not talk thus before the fight began. Now take your turn; and, as a brother should, attend your brother to the Stygian flood." Then through his breast he sent his fatal sword, and the soul issued at the gaping vent.

A Latin who fights from the chariot his brother Liger drives; killed by Aeneas.

A thousand youths obeyed brave Massicus, borne in the Tiger through the foaming sea; brought from Asium and Cosa by his care; for arms, they bear light quivers, bows, and shafts. ## modern-en · mimas · 10:52

Beneath his feet fell haughty Hebrus dead, then Latagus, and Palmus as he fled. At Latagus he flung a weighty stone: his face was flattened, and his helmet rang. ## modern-en · orsilochus · 11:36

Twice were the Tuscans masters of the field, twice by the Latins, in their turn, repelled. Ashamed at length, they ran to the third charge; both hosts resolved, and mingled man to man. Now dying groans are heard; the fields are strewn with falling bodies, and are drunk with blood. Arms, horses, men, lie together in heaps: the fight is confused, and the cry more confused. Orsilochus, who did not dare to press too near strong Remulus, drove his spear at a distance, and stuck the steel beneath his horse's ear. The fiery steed, impatient of the wound, curvets, and, springing upward with a bound, casts his helpless lord backward on the ground. Catillus first pierced Iolas; then he drew his reeking lance, and threw it at Herminius, the mighty champion of the Tuscan crew. His neck and throat were unarmed, his head was bare, but shaded with a length of yellow hair: secure, he fought, exposed on every part, a spacious mark for swords and for the flying dart. The feathered wound came across his shoulders; transfixed he fell, and doubled to the ground. The sands are sanguine dyed with streaming blood, and death with honor sought on either side.

A Trojan who does not dare face Camilla and is killed by her.

## modern-en · butes-boxer · 5:16

Then haughty Dares appeared in the lists; stalking he strode, bearing his head erect: his nervous arms wielded the weighty gauntlets, and loud applause echoed through the field. Dares alone used to stand in combat against mighty Paris, hand to hand; the same, at Hector's funerals, undertook gigantic Butes, of the Amycian stock, and, by the stroke of his resistless hand, stretched the vast bulk upon the yellow sand. Such was Dares; and such he strode along, and drew the wonder of the gazing throng. Phoenician Dido rules the growing state; she fled from Tyre to escape her brother's hate. Great were her wrongs, her story full of fate, which I will briefly tell. Sichaeus, famous for his wealth and brother to the Punic throne, possessed fair Dido's bed; and both hearts were wounded at once with an equal dart. Her father gave her, a spotless maid; Pygmalion then held the Tyrian scepter—a man who despised both divine and human laws. Then strife arose, and cursed gold was its cause. The monarch, blinded by the desire for wealth, stealthily attacked his brother with steel, made him bleed before the sacred altar, and long concealed the cruel deed from her. He daily coined some tale, some new pretense, to soothe his sister and delude her mind. At length, in the dead of night, the ghost of her unhappy husband appeared. The specter stared, and with erected eyes bared his bloody breast; he told her of the cruel altars and his fate, revealed the dire secret of his house, and warned the widow to flee, with her household gods, to remote abodes. Finally, to support her on so long a journey, he showed her where his hidden treasure lay. Admonished thus, and seized with mortal fear, the queen provided companions for her flight. ## modern-en · ganymede · 1:2

Far opposite the mouth of the Tiber, an ancient town was seated by the sea—a Tyrian colony, its people hardened for war and devoted to trade. Its name was Carthage, and Juno loved it more than her own Argos or the Samian shore. Here she kept her chariot; and here, if Heaven favored her, she planned to set the seat of imperial power. Yet she had heard an ancient rumor circulating among the gods, that in times to come the Trojan race would ruin her Carthage and throw down her towers, and that this race, not content with that, would lay the yoke of sovereign rule upon the necks of all nations. She brooded on this, and feared it was fated. Nor could she forget the recent war she had waged for conquered Greece against the Trojan state. Besides, long-standing causes were working in her mind, and secret seeds of envy remained: deep in her heart lay the verdict of partial Paris, her own beauty disdained, the grace bestowed on ravished Ganymede, the glories of Electra, and her own wronged bed. Each was a cause in itself, and all together kindled vengeance in her haughty mind. For these reasons, far distant from the coast of Latium, she drove the remnants of the Trojan host, and for seven long years the unhappy wandering company were tossed by storms and scattered through the seas. So much time, so much toil, was required to found the Roman name—so vast a frame demanded such long labor.

The Trojan boy carried up to serve Jove, one of Juno’s standing grievances.

## modern-en · agamemnon · 1:25

In the very center of the town stood a venerable wood, thick with trees. The Tyrians, landing near this holy ground and digging here, had found a prosperous omen: from beneath the earth they drew out a horse's head, which foreshadowed their growth and future fortune. Juno, the foundress, had given them this fated sign of a fruitful soil and a brave people. Here Sidonian Dido built and consecrated Juno's temple with solemn state, enriched with gifts and with a golden shrine; but the goddess made the place still more divine. On brazen steps the marble threshold rose, and brazen plates enclosed the cedar beams. The rafters were crowned with brazen coverings, and the lofty doors sounded on brazen hinges. What Aeneas first beheld in this place revived his courage and drove away his fear. For while, awaiting the queen, he raised his wondering eyes and gazed around the temple, admiring the fortune of the rising town, the competing artists, and the fame of their art, he saw, in order painted on the wall, all that had befallen unhappy Troy: the wars that fame had blown around the world, every scene true to life, every leader known. There he sees Agamemnon, and here Priam, and fierce Achilles, who defies them both. He stopped, and weeping, said: "O friend! Even here monuments of Trojan suffering appear! Our known disasters fill even foreign lands: see there, where old unhappy Priam stands! Even the mute walls relate the warrior's fame, and Trojan griefs stir Tyrian pity!" He said, and his tears found a ready passage, as he devoured with his eyes the scenes so well depicted, and fed his mind with an empty picture. For there he saw the fainting Greeks yielding, and there the trembling Trojans quitting the field, pursued by fierce Achilles across the plain as he drove his high chariot over the slain. Next came the tents of Rhesus, and his grief was renewed, their white sails betraying them to nightly view, and wakeful Diomede, whose cruel sword slew the sentries and did not spare their slumbering lord; then he took the fiery steeds before they tasted the food of Troy or drank from the river Xanthus. Elsewhere he saw where Troilus defied Achilles, and tried unequal combat; then, where the boy, disarmed, with loosened reins, was hurried over the plain by his horses, hung by the neck and hair, and dragged around, the hostile spear still sticking in his wound, inscribing the dusty ground with tracks of blood. Meanwhile the Trojan matrons, oppressed with woe, went in long procession to the temple of Pallas, hoping to reconcile their heavenly enemy. They wept, beat their breasts, tore their hair, and bore richly embroidered vests as offerings; but the stern goddess stood unmoved by prayer. Three times Achilles dragged Hector's corpse around the Trojan walls, whom he had slain in combat. Here Priam was suing; and there, for sums of gold, the lifeless body of his son was being sold. So sad an object, and so well expressed, drew sighs and groans from the grieving hero's breast, to see the figure of his lifeless friend, and his old father stretching out his helpless hand. He saw himself also amid the Grecian train, mingled in the bloody battle on the plain; and he knew swarthy Memnon in his armor, his pompous ensigns, and his Indian crew. There was Penthesilea, leading an Amazonian race to war with haughty grace; in their right hands they wielded a pointed dart, and their left sustained the lunar shield for defense. She threw a golden belt across her breast, and alone among the press she provoked a thousand foes, daring to oppose her maiden arms to manly force.

The Greek commander at Troy.

“A greater omen, and of worse portent, tormented our unwary minds with fear, contributing to the dire event. Laocoön, chosen by lot that year to be Neptune's priest, was making solemn sacrifice of a bull, when, dreadful to behold, we saw from the sea two serpents, side by side, parting the waters and sweeping smoothly along the swelling tide. They raised their flaming crests above the waves; their bellies seemed to burn the seas below; their speckled tails steered their course, and on the sounding shore the flying billows were driven. Now they held the strand, now the plain; their ardent eyes were filled with bloody streaks; their nimble tongues they brandished as they came, and licked their hissing jaws, which sputtered flame. We fled, amazed. They took their destined way and made straight for Laocoön and his children. First they wound around his tender boys, and with sharpened fangs ground their limbs and bodies. The wretched father, running to their aid with pious but vain haste, they next invaded. Twice their winding coils rolled about his waist; twice they folded about his gasping throat. The priest, thus doubly choked, was overtopped by their crests, as they rode in triumph over his head. With both hands he labored at the knots; his holy fillets were stained by their blue venom; his roaring filled the flitting air around him. So, when an ox receives a glancing wound, he breaks his bonds, flies from the fatal altar, and breaks the yielding skies with his loud bellowing. Their task performed, the serpents left their prey and made their way to the tower of Pallas. There they couched at her feet, protected by her great shield and extended spear. Amazement seized us all; the general cry proclaimed that Laocoön had justly been doomed to die, for his hand had withstood the will of Pallas, and had dared to violate the sacred wood. All voted to admit the steed, that vows might be paid and incense offered to the offended maid. A spacious breach was made; the town lay bare. Some prepared hoisting levers, some the wheels, which were fastened to the horse's feet; the rest hauled the unwieldy beast along with cables. Each called on his fellow for help; at last the fatal fabric mounted the walls, big with destruction. Boys crowned with chaplets, and choirs of virgins, sang and danced around it. Thus raised aloft, and then descending down, it passed in over our heads and threatened the town. O sacred city, built by hands divine! O valiant heroes of the Trojan line! Four times it struck: as often the clashing sound of arms was heard, and inward groans rebounded. Yet, mad with zeal, and blinded by our fate, we hauled along the horse in solemn state, and placed the dire portent within the tower. Cassandra cried out, and cursed the unhappy hour; she foretold our fate; but by the gods' decree, all heard her, and none believed the prophecy. We adorned the temples with branches, and in jollity we wasted the day ordained to be our last. Meanwhile the rapid heavens rolled down the light, and night rushed upon the shaded ocean. Our men, feeling secure, kept no guards nor sentries, but easy sleep compelled their weary limbs. The Greeks had embarked their naval forces from Tenedos, and sought our well-known shores, safe under cover of the silent night, and guided by the imperial galley's light. Then Sinon, favored by the partial gods, unlocked the horse and opened its dark abode, restoring to vital air our hidden foes, who joyfully rose from their long confinement. Bold Tysander, and Sthenelus their guide, and dire Ulysses slid down the cable. Then Thoas, Athamas, and Pyrrhus hastened; nor was the Podalirian hero the last, nor injured Menelaus, nor the famed Epeus, who had framed the fatal engine. A nameless crowd followed; they joined forces to invade the town, which was oppressed with sleep and wine. The few they found awake first met their fate; then they unbarred the gates to their comrades.

Conducted to the grove, Aeneas first broke the silence, and thus addressed the king: "Best of the Greeks, to whom, by fate's command, I bear these peaceful branches in my hand, undaunted I approach you, though I know your birth is Grecian, and your land my foe; though your ancient lineage came from Atreus, and both the brother kings claim your kindred; yet my self-conscious worth, your high renown, your virtue, blown through the neighboring nations, our fathers' mingled blood, and Apollo's voice, have led me hither, less by need than by choice. Our founder Dardanus, as fame has sung, and as the Greeks acknowledge, sprang from Electra: Electra came from the loins of Atlas; Atlas, whose head sustains the starry frame. Your sire is Mercury, whom long before fair Maia bore on cold Cyllene's top. Maia the fair, if we rely on fame, was Atlas' daughter, who sustains the sky. Thus from one common source our streams divide; ours is the Trojan, yours the Arcadian side. Raised by these hopes, I sent no news before, nor asked your leave, nor did I implore your faith; but I come, without a pledge, as my own ambassador. The same Rutulians who pursue the Trojan race with arms are equal foes to you. Our host expelled, what further force can stay the victor troops from universal sway? Then will they stretch their power athwart the land, and command either sea from side to side. Receive our offered faith, and give us yours; ours is a generous and experienced line: we do not lack hearts or bodies for the war; we are cautious in council, and daring in the field."

Father of the two brother kings.

## modern-en · calchas · 2:3

“His fear at last dismissed, he said: ‘Whatever my fate decrees, my words shall be sincere: I neither can nor dare disown my birth. Greece is my country, Sinon is my name. Though plunged by Fortune's power into misery, it is not in Fortune's power to make me lie. If the name of Palamedes has reached you—not unknown to fame—who suffered from the malice of the times, accused and sentenced for imaginary crimes because he sought to prevent these fatal wars, whose death the wretched Greeks too late lament—I, then a boy, was committed to his care by my father, who was poor and had no other means. He was my kinsman and his companion in the war. While Fortune favored him, while his counsel ruled the court, I too made some figure there; my name was not obscure, nor was I without my share of fame. But when Ulysses, with his deceitful arts, made his impression on the people's hearts and forged a treason in my patron's name—I speak of things too widely known by fame—my kinsman fell. Then I, without support, mourned his loss in private and left the court. Mad as I was, I could not bear his fate with silent grief, but loudly blamed the state and cursed the direful author of my woes. Word of it got back; and from this my ruin rose. I swore that if indulgent Heaven would once more land me safely on my native shore, I would avenge his death doubly. This stirred the murderer's hate; soon the effects of malice from so proud a man followed. Ambiguous rumors he spread through the camp, and sought by treachery to take my devoted head. He invented new crimes; he left no stone unturned to make my guilt appear and to hide his own, until at last he forced Calchas to speak. But why—why do I dwell on that anxious thought? If it is your aim to take just revenge upon my nation, and to be a Greek is to be your enemy, you already know my name and country: quench your thirst for blood and strike the blow! My death will please both the kingly brothers, and will set the insatiable man of Ithaca at ease.' This fair unfinished tale, these broken starts, raised expectations in our longing hearts, unknowing as we were in Grecian arts. With his former trembling once again renewed, with feigned fear, the villain went on:

The Greek augur whose word Sinon uses to frame his story.
