## modern-en · thymoetes · 2:2

“Compelled by destiny and in despair, the Greeks grew weary of the long war, and with Minerva's help they built a structure which looked like a horse of monstrous height. The sides were planked with pine; they pretended it was made as an offering for their safe return, and this was the vow they paid. So they pretended, but in the hollow side they hid chosen soldiers. They loaded the dread machine with arms within, and stuffed its dark belly with men of iron. In sight of Troy lies Tenedos, an island once famous for wealth while Fortune smiled on Priam's empire, but now a treacherous bay where ships lay exposed to wind and weather. There their fleet was concealed. We thought they had hoisted sail for Greece, and we were relieved of our fears. The Trojans, cooped up within their walls for so long, unbarred their gates and poured out in a throng, like swarming bees, and with delight they surveyed the deserted camp where the Greeks had lain. They pointed out the quarters of the various chiefs: here Phoenix made his abode, here Achilles; here the battles joined, there the navy rode at anchor. Some stared in wonder at the pile, the pile that Pallas had raised to ruin Troy. Thymoetes was first—whether bribed or because Trojan destiny required it—to urge that the ramparts be broken down to lodge the monstrous fabric in the town. But Capys, and the rest of sounder mind, wanted the fatal gift thrown into the flames, or cast into the sea, or at least bored open so its hidden frauds might be explored. The giddy crowd, swayed by their whims, made much noise but said nothing, and split into factions. Then Laocoön, followed by a numerous crowd, came running from the citadel and cried out from a distance: ‘O wretched countrymen! What madness is this? What worse than madness has possessed your brains? Do you think the Greeks have left your coasts? Are Ulysses' tricks no better known than this? Either this hollow fabric encloses our secret foes within its blind recess, or it is an engine raised above the town to overlook the walls and then to batter them down. Something is surely planned, by fraud or force. Trust not their presents, and do not admit the horse.' Having said this, he hurled his forceful spear against the steed, which, hissing as it flew, pierced through the yielding planks of jointed wood and stood trembling in the hollow belly. The pierced sides returned a rattling sound, and the groans of the Greeks enclosed within came issuing through the wound. And had Heaven not decreed Troy's fall, or had men not been fated to be blind, enough was said and done to inspire a better mind. Then our lances would have pierced the treacherous wood, and the Trojan towers and Priam's empire would still stand. Meanwhile, with shouts, Trojan shepherds brought a captive Greek in chains before the king—one taken so that he might take; one who had given himself up as prey, to impose on their belief and betray Troy; fixed on his purpose, determined either to die undaunted or to deceive us. Around the captive, tides of Trojans flowed; all pressed to see, and some insulted the foe. Now hear how well the Greeks disguised their tricks; behold a nation compressed into one man. Trembling the wretch stood, unarmed and bound; he stared and rolled his haggard eyes around, and then said: ‘Alas! What land remains, what sea is open to receive unhappy me? What fate awaits a wretched fugitive, scorned by my foes, abandoned by my friends?' He said this, and sighed, and cast a rueful eye: our pity was kindled, and our passions died. We urged the youth to defend himself, and to tell us freely what he was and where he came from, what news he could bring. We longed to know what to believe from a captive foe.

The Trojan who urges bringing the horse inside.

## modern-en · cassandra · 2:8

“A greater omen, and of worse portent, tormented our unwary minds with fear, contributing to the dire event. Laocoön, chosen by lot that year to be Neptune's priest, was making solemn sacrifice of a bull, when, dreadful to behold, we saw from the sea two serpents, side by side, parting the waters and sweeping smoothly along the swelling tide. They raised their flaming crests above the waves; their bellies seemed to burn the seas below; their speckled tails steered their course, and on the sounding shore the flying billows were driven. Now they held the strand, now the plain; their ardent eyes were filled with bloody streaks; their nimble tongues they brandished as they came, and licked their hissing jaws, which sputtered flame. We fled, amazed. They took their destined way and made straight for Laocoön and his children. First they wound around his tender boys, and with sharpened fangs ground their limbs and bodies. The wretched father, running to their aid with pious but vain haste, they next invaded. Twice their winding coils rolled about his waist; twice they folded about his gasping throat. The priest, thus doubly choked, was overtopped by their crests, as they rode in triumph over his head. With both hands he labored at the knots; his holy fillets were stained by their blue venom; his roaring filled the flitting air around him. So, when an ox receives a glancing wound, he breaks his bonds, flies from the fatal altar, and breaks the yielding skies with his loud bellowing. Their task performed, the serpents left their prey and made their way to the tower of Pallas. There they couched at her feet, protected by her great shield and extended spear. Amazement seized us all; the general cry proclaimed that Laocoön had justly been doomed to die, for his hand had withstood the will of Pallas, and had dared to violate the sacred wood. All voted to admit the steed, that vows might be paid and incense offered to the offended maid. A spacious breach was made; the town lay bare. Some prepared hoisting levers, some the wheels, which were fastened to the horse's feet; the rest hauled the unwieldy beast along with cables. Each called on his fellow for help; at last the fatal fabric mounted the walls, big with destruction. Boys crowned with chaplets, and choirs of virgins, sang and danced around it. Thus raised aloft, and then descending down, it passed in over our heads and threatened the town. O sacred city, built by hands divine! O valiant heroes of the Trojan line! Four times it struck: as often the clashing sound of arms was heard, and inward groans rebounded. Yet, mad with zeal, and blinded by our fate, we hauled along the horse in solemn state, and placed the dire portent within the tower. Cassandra cried out, and cursed the unhappy hour; she foretold our fate; but by the gods' decree, all heard her, and none believed the prophecy. We adorned the temples with branches, and in jollity we wasted the day ordained to be our last. Meanwhile the rapid heavens rolled down the light, and night rushed upon the shaded ocean. Our men, feeling secure, kept no guards nor sentries, but easy sleep compelled their weary limbs. The Greeks had embarked their naval forces from Tenedos, and sought our well-known shores, safe under cover of the silent night, and guided by the imperial galley's light. Then Sinon, favored by the partial gods, unlocked the horse and opened its dark abode, restoring to vital air our hidden foes, who joyfully rose from their long confinement. Bold Tysander, and Sthenelus their guide, and dire Ulysses slid down the cable. Then Thoas, Athamas, and Pyrrhus hastened; nor was the Podalirian hero the last, nor injured Menelaus, nor the famed Epeus, who had framed the fatal engine. A nameless crowd followed; they joined forces to invade the town, which was oppressed with sleep and wine. The few they found awake first met their fate; then they unbarred the gates to their comrades.

Priam’s daughter, whose true prophecies Apollo doomed to be disbelieved.

## modern-en · coroebus · 2:13

“I heard him; and Heaven, which inspires well-born souls, prompted me through lifted swords and rising fires to run where clashing arms and clamor called, and to rush undaunted to defend the walls. Ripheus and Iphitus engaged at my side, one renowned for valor, the other for age. Dymas and Hypanis, knowing my motion and bearing by moonlight, drew to my party, along with young Coroebus, who had been led by love to win renown and the bed of fair Cassandra, and had lately brought his troops to Priam's aid—warned in vain by the prophetic maid. When I saw them resolved to fall in arms, and that one spirit animated all, I said: ‘Brave souls! But brave, alas, in vain: come, finish what our cruel fates ordain. You see the desperate state of our affairs, and heaven's protecting powers are deaf to our prayers. The passive gods behold the Greeks defile their temples, and abandon their own abodes to the spoiler. We, a feeble few, conspire to save a sinking town, engulfed in fire. Then let us fall, but fall amidst our foes: despair of life shows the means of living.' So bold a speech encouraged their desire for death, and added fuel to their fire.

Cassandra’s suitor, killed at Pallas’s altar on the night Troy fell.

## modern-en · pantheus · 2:12

“Pantheus, Apollo's priest, a sacred name, had escaped the Grecian swords and passed through the flames. Loaded with relics, he fled to my doors, and led his tender grandson by the hand. ‘What hope is there, O Pantheus? Where can we run? Where make a stand? And what may still be done?' Hardly had I said this when Pantheus, with a groan, replied: ‘Troy is no more, and Ilium was a town! The fatal day, the appointed hour, has come, when wrathful Jove's irrevocable doom transfers the Trojan state to Grecian hands. The fire consumes the town, the foe commands; and armed hosts, an unexpected force, break from the bowels of the fatal horse. Within the gates proud Sinon is flinging the flames; and foes press in from outside—a thousand others, whom I fear to name, more than ever came from Argos or Mycenae. They have divided their parties to several posts; some block the narrow streets, some scour the wide. They kill the bold and surprise the unwary; whoever fights finds death, and death finds him who flees. The wardens of the gate can scarcely maintain the unequal combat, and resist in vain.'

Apollo’s priest on the citadel, who brings Aeneas the household gods.

## modern-en · androgeos · 2:14

“As hungry wolves, with raging appetite, scour through the fields, not fearing the stormy night—their whelps at home await the promised food, and long to wet their dry jaws in blood—so we rushed forth at once, resolved to die, resolved in death to try the last extremes. We left the narrow lanes behind, and dared the unequal combat in the public square. Night was our friend; our leader was despair. What tongue can tell the slaughter of that night? What eyes can weep its sorrows and affright? An ancient and imperial city fell; the streets were filled with frequent funerals; houses and holy temples floated in blood, and hostile nations made a common flood. Not only Trojans fell; but in their turn the vanquished triumphed, and the victors mourned. Our men took new courage from despair and night; the fortune was confused, the fight was confused. All parts resounded with tumult, plaints, and fears; and grisly Death appeared in sundry shapes. Androgeos fell among us with his band; he thought we were Greeks newly come to land. ‘From where,' he said, ‘my friends, this long delay? You loiter while the spoils are being borne away. Our ships are laden with Trojan store, and you, like truants, have come too late ashore.' He said this, but soon corrected his mistake, realizing from our doubtful answers. Amazed, he would have shunned the unequal fight; but we, being more numerous, intercepted his flight. As when some peasant in a bushy brake unwarily treads on a snake, and starts aside astonished, when he sees its rising crest, blue neck, and rolling eyes—so Androgeos, surprised, fled from our arms. In vain; for we surrounded him and his, possessed with fear and unfamiliar with the ground, and found them an easy conquest. Thus Fortune smiled on our first endeavor. Then Coroebus, beguiled by youthful hopes, swollen with success and a daring mind, fatally designed this new invention. ‘My friends,' he said, ‘since Fortune shows the way, it is fitting to obey the auspicious guide. Why has she bestowed these Grecian arms on us, but for their destruction and the Trojans' good? Then let us change shields, and bear their devices: let fraud supply the want of force in war. They furnish us the arms.' Having said this, he dressed himself in dead Androgeos' spoils—his upper vest, his painted buckler, and his plumy crest. Likewise Ripheus, Dymas, all the Trojan train, laid down their own attire, and stripped the slain. Mingled with the Greeks, we went on with ill foreboding, flattering ourselves with hopes of glutting our greedy rage. Unknown, we assaulted whomever we blindly met, and strewed the street with Grecian corpses. Thus, while we defeated their straggling parties, some retreated to the shore and safer ships; and some, oppressed with a more ignoble fear, climbed back into the hollow horse, and panted in secret there.

The Greek captain who mistakes Aeneas’s band for his own men.

## modern-en · peneleus · 2:16

“Thus, when the rival winds try their quarrel, contending for the kingdom of the sky—south, east, and west, borne on airy coursers—the whirlwind gathers, and the woods are torn; then Nereus strikes the deep, the billows rise, and, mixed with ooze and sand, pollute the skies. The troops we had at first scattered reappeared from various quarters, and closed in behind us. They first observed, and betrayed to the rest, our different speech, and surveyed our borrowed arms. Oppressed with odds, we fell. Coroebus fell first, at Pallas' altar, pierced by Peneleus. Then Ripheus followed, in the unequal fight, the most just of his word, most observant of the right—but Heaven judged otherwise. Dymas met the same fate, with Hypanis, mistaken by their friends. Nor did your miter, Pantheus, nor the bands of awful Phoebus, save you from impious hands. You Trojan flames, bear witness to what I performed and what I suffered there; I avoided no sword in the fatal strife, exposed to death, prodigal of life. Bear witness, you heavens: I live not by my own fault; I strove to earn the death I sought. But, when I could not fight and would have died, I was borne off to a distance by the growing tide. Old Iphitus and I were hurried from there, with Pelias wounded and defenseless. New clamors rang from the besieged palace; we ran to die, or to relieve the king. So hot was the assault, so high the tumult rose, as our men defended and the Greeks attacked, that it seemed as if all the Dardan and Argive race had been crammed into that narrow space; or as if all the rest of Ilium were void of fear, and tumult, war, and slaughter were only there. Their shields cast in a tortoise formation, the foes, advancing in safety, rose to the turrets. Some mounted scaling ladders; others, bolder, climbed upward by posts and pillars. With their left hand they gripped their bucklers in the ascent, while with their right they seized the battlement. From their demolished towers the Trojans threw huge heaps of stones, which, falling, crushed the foe; and heavy beams and rafters from the sides (such arms their last necessity provides), and gilded roofs, came tumbling down from on high, the marks of state and ancient royalty. The guards below, fixed in the pass, attended the charge undaunted, and defended the gate. Renewed in courage, with recovered breath, a second time we ran to tempt our death, to clear the palace of the foe, to relieve the weary who still fought, and to avenge the dead.

The Greek who kills Coroebus at Pallas’s altar.

## modern-en · polites · 2:18

“Perhaps you may inquire Priam's fate. When he saw his regal town on fire, his ruined palace, and his entering foes—on every side inevitable woes—he put on his disused armor upon his aged limbs, decayed like them; a late and useless aid. His feeble shoulders could scarcely sustain the weight; loaded, not armed, he crept along in pain, despairing of success, ambitious to be slain. Uncovered, but by heaven, there stood in view an altar; near the hearth an old laurel tree grew, whose boughs encompassed the household gods and shaded the holy ground. Here Hecuba, with all her helpless train of dames, had sought shelter, but sought in vain. Driven like a flock of doves along the sky, they hugged the images, and fled to their altars. When the Queen beheld her trembling lord, and saw a heavy sword hanging by his side, ‘What rage,' she cried, ‘has seized my husband's mind? What arms are these, and for what use designed? These times require other aids! Were Hector here, even Hector would now appear in vain, like Priam. With us you shall find one common shelter, or you shall be joined with us in one common fate.' She said this, and, embracing the poor old man with a last salute, placed him by the laurel. Behold! Polites, one of Priam's sons, pursued by Pyrrhus, came running for safety. Amazed and hurt, he fled through swords and foes, through empty courts and open galleries. Pyrrhus, urging him with his lance, pursued him, and often reached him, and renewed his thrusts. The youth, transfixed, with lamentable cries expired before his wretched parent's eyes. When Priam saw him gasping at his feet, the fear of death gave place to nature's law; and, shaking more with anger than with age, ‘The gods,' he said, ‘requite your brutal rage! As surely they will, barbarian, surely they must, if there are gods in heaven, and if the gods are just—you who take an insolent delight in wrongs; who have infected a father's sight with a son's death. Not he, whom lying fame and you conspire to call your father, not he, your vaunted sire, so used my wretched age. He feared the gods, he heard the laws of nature and of nations. He cheered my sorrows; and, for sums of gold, he sold the bloodless body of my Hector; he pitied the woes a parent suffered, and sent me back in safety from his tent.'

Priam’s son, run down and killed in front of his parents.

## modern-en · polydorus · 3:2

“Against our coast appeared a spacious land, once ruled by the fierce Lycurgus—Thracia was the name; the people were bold in war; their fields were vast, and tillage was their care, a hospitable realm while Fate was kind, bound to Troy in friendship and religion. I landed; with luckless omens I then adored their gods, and drew a line along the shore; I laid the deep foundations of a wall, and named the city Aenos, from myself. To Dionaean Venus I paid my vows, and to all the powers that aid rising labors; a bull I laid on Jove's imperial altar. Not far off, a rising hillock stood in view; sharp myrtles and cornel trees grew on its sides. There, while I went to crop the sylvan scenes, and to shade our altar with their leafy greens, I pulled a plant—with horror I relate a prodigy so strange and full of fate. The rooted fibers rose, and from the wound black bloody drops distilled upon the ground. Mute and amazed, my hair stood with terror; fear shrank my sinews and congealed my blood. Mastering myself once again, I tried another plant: it too gushed with the same sanguine dye. Then, fearing guilt for some unknown offense, I atoned the Dryads with prayers and vows, and all the sisters of the woods, and especially the God of Arms, who rules the Thracian coast, that they, or he, would avert these omens, release our fears, and impart better signs. Cleared in mind, as I thought, and at last fully determined to learn the cause, I tugged with all my strength: I bent my knees against the ground; once more the violated myrtle ran with gore. Scarcely do I dare to tell the sequel: from the womb of wounded earth, and from the caverns of the tomb, a groan, as of a troubled ghost, renewed my fright, and then these dreadful words ensued: ‘Why do you thus rend my buried body? O spare the corpse of your unhappy friend! Spare to pollute your pious hands with blood. These tears do not distill from wounded wood; every drop this living tree contains is kindred blood, which ran in Trojan veins. O flee from this unhospitable shore, warned by my fate; for I am Polydorus! Here loads of lances, steeped in my blood, have shot upward again, renewed by my blood.'

Priam’s youngest son, murdered for his gold in Thrace; his voice comes out of the ground. Dryden calls him Polydore.

## modern-en · idomeneus · 3:7

“All were concerned to know what place the god had assigned, and where he had determined our abode. My father, long revolving in his mind the race and lineage of the Trojan kind, thus answered their demands: ‘You princes, hear your pleasing fortune, and dispel your fear. The fruitful isle of Crete, well known to fame, of old sacred to Jove's imperial name, lies in the mid ocean, with large command, and on its plains a hundred cities stand. Another Ida rises there; and from thence we derive our Trojan ancestry. From there, as is divulged by certain fame, old Teucer came to the Rhoetean shores; there he fixed, and there chose the seat of empire, before Ilium and the Trojan towers arose. In humble vales they built their soft abodes, until Cybele, the mother of the gods, with tinkling cymbals charmed the Idaean woods; she taught secret rites and ceremonies, and brought savage lions to the yoke. Let us explore the land which Heaven appoints; let us appease the winds, and seek the Gnossian shore. If Jove assists our fleet's passage, the third propitious dawn shall discover Crete.' Having said this, he laid the sacrifices on smoking altars for the gods: a bull, an oblation due to Neptune; another bull slain for bright Apollo; a milk-white ewe to please the western winds, and one coal-black to calm the stormy seas. Before this, a flying rumor had been spread that fierce Idomeneus had fled from Crete, expelled and exiled; that the coast was free from foreign or domestic enemy.

The Cretan king driven out of his own country, which leaves Crete open.

## modern-en · anius · 3:6

“Anius, the priest and king, crowned with laurel, his hoary locks bound with purple fillets, who saw my sire ascending the Delian shore, came forth with eager haste to meet his friend. He invited him to his palace; and, in sign of ancient love, they joined their plighted hands. Then I went to the temple of the god, and thus, before the shrine, I presented my vows: ‘Give, O Thymbraeus, give a resting place to the sad relics of the Trojan race; a seat secure, a region of their own, a lasting empire, and a happier town. Where shall we fix? Where shall our labors end? Whom shall we follow, and what fate await? Let not my prayers find a doubtful answer; but in clear auguries unveil your mind.' Scarcely had I said this when he shook the holy ground, the laurels, and the lofty hills around; and from the tripod a bellowing sound rushed out. We fell prostrate, acknowledging the present god, who gave this answer from his dark abode: ‘Undaunted youths, go, seek that mother earth from which your ancestors derive their birth. The soil that sent you forth shall in her old bosom embrace her ancient race again. Through the wide world the house of Aeneas shall reign, and children's children shall sustain the crown.' Thus Phoebus disclosed our future fates: a mighty tumult, mixed with joy, arose.

The priest-king of Delos, Anchises’ old guest-friend.

## modern-en · deiphobus · 2:11

“Now peals of shouts came thundering from afar—cries, threats, and loud laments, and mingled war. The noise approached, though our palace stood apart from the streets, encompassed by a wood. Louder and yet louder I heard the alarms of human cries distinct, and the clash of arms. Fear broke my sleep; I stayed no longer, but mounted the terrace, and from there surveyed the town, listening to what the frightful sounds conveyed. So, when a flood of fire is driven by wind, it rolls crackling and mows down the standing corn; or when deluges descend upon the plains, they sweep over the yellow ear, and destroy the labor of oxen and the peasant's gains; they uproot the forest oaks, and carry away flocks, folds, and trees, and undistinguished prey. The shepherd climbs the cliff and sees from afar the wasteful ravage of the watery war. Then Hector's warning was manifestly confirmed, and Grecian frauds appeared in open light. The palace of Deiphobus rose in smoky flames, and caught fire from its neighbors. Ucalegon's house burned next; the seas were bright with a splendor not their own, and shone with Trojan light. New clamors and new clangors now arose, the sound of trumpets mingled with battle cries. Seized with frenzy, I ran to meet the alarms, resolved on death, resolved to die in arms; but first to gather friends, with them to oppose, if fortune favored, and to drive back the foes. I was spurred on by my own courage, fired by my country, and inspired by a sense of honor and revenge.

Priam’s son, whose house burns first, and whose mutilated shade Aeneas meets below.

## modern-en · sthenelus · 2:8

“A greater omen, and of worse portent, tormented our unwary minds with fear, contributing to the dire event. Laocoön, chosen by lot that year to be Neptune's priest, was making solemn sacrifice of a bull, when, dreadful to behold, we saw from the sea two serpents, side by side, parting the waters and sweeping smoothly along the swelling tide. They raised their flaming crests above the waves; their bellies seemed to burn the seas below; their speckled tails steered their course, and on the sounding shore the flying billows were driven. Now they held the strand, now the plain; their ardent eyes were filled with bloody streaks; their nimble tongues they brandished as they came, and licked their hissing jaws, which sputtered flame. We fled, amazed. They took their destined way and made straight for Laocoön and his children. First they wound around his tender boys, and with sharpened fangs ground their limbs and bodies. The wretched father, running to their aid with pious but vain haste, they next invaded. Twice their winding coils rolled about his waist; twice they folded about his gasping throat. The priest, thus doubly choked, was overtopped by their crests, as they rode in triumph over his head. With both hands he labored at the knots; his holy fillets were stained by their blue venom; his roaring filled the flitting air around him. So, when an ox receives a glancing wound, he breaks his bonds, flies from the fatal altar, and breaks the yielding skies with his loud bellowing. Their task performed, the serpents left their prey and made their way to the tower of Pallas. There they couched at her feet, protected by her great shield and extended spear. Amazement seized us all; the general cry proclaimed that Laocoön had justly been doomed to die, for his hand had withstood the will of Pallas, and had dared to violate the sacred wood. All voted to admit the steed, that vows might be paid and incense offered to the offended maid. A spacious breach was made; the town lay bare. Some prepared hoisting levers, some the wheels, which were fastened to the horse's feet; the rest hauled the unwieldy beast along with cables. Each called on his fellow for help; at last the fatal fabric mounted the walls, big with destruction. Boys crowned with chaplets, and choirs of virgins, sang and danced around it. Thus raised aloft, and then descending down, it passed in over our heads and threatened the town. O sacred city, built by hands divine! O valiant heroes of the Trojan line! Four times it struck: as often the clashing sound of arms was heard, and inward groans rebounded. Yet, mad with zeal, and blinded by our fate, we hauled along the horse in solemn state, and placed the dire portent within the tower. Cassandra cried out, and cursed the unhappy hour; she foretold our fate; but by the gods' decree, all heard her, and none believed the prophecy. We adorned the temples with branches, and in jollity we wasted the day ordained to be our last. Meanwhile the rapid heavens rolled down the light, and night rushed upon the shaded ocean. Our men, feeling secure, kept no guards nor sentries, but easy sleep compelled their weary limbs. The Greeks had embarked their naval forces from Tenedos, and sought our well-known shores, safe under cover of the silent night, and guided by the imperial galley's light. Then Sinon, favored by the partial gods, unlocked the horse and opened its dark abode, restoring to vital air our hidden foes, who joyfully rose from their long confinement. Bold Tysander, and Sthenelus their guide, and dire Ulysses slid down the cable. Then Thoas, Athamas, and Pyrrhus hastened; nor was the Podalirian hero the last, nor injured Menelaus, nor the famed Epeus, who had framed the fatal engine. A nameless crowd followed; they joined forces to invade the town, which was oppressed with sleep and wine. The few they found awake first met their fate; then they unbarred the gates to their comrades.

One of the Greeks who comes out of the horse.

## modern-en · demoleus · 5:9

Mnestheus was declared the second victor; and, summoned there, he shared the second prize. A coat of mail, which brave Demoleus bore—more brave Aeneas tore from his shoulders in single combat on the Trojan shore—was ordained for Mnestheus to possess: in war for his defense, for ornament in peace. The gift was rich, and glorious to behold, but yet so ponderous with its plates of gold, that scarcely two servants could sustain the weight; yet, loaded thus, Demoleus over the plain had pursued and lightly seized the Trojan train. The third, succeeding to the last reward, shared two goodly bowls of massy silver, with prominent figures, and richly wrought, and two brass cauldrons brought from Dodona.

A Greek from whom Aeneas took a coat of mail.

## modern-en · cisseus · 5:21

This done, Aeneas ordered, for the close, the strife of archers with contending bows. He raised with his own hands, on the shore, the mast that Sergesthus' shattered galley had borne. They tied a fluttering dove upon the top, the living mark at which their arrows would fly. The rival archers advanced in a line, to receive their turn of shooting from chance. A helmet held their names; the lots were drawn: on the first scroll was read Hippocoon. The people shouted. On the next was found young Mnestheus, lately crowned with naval honors. The third contained Eurytion's noble name, your brother, Pandarus, and next in fame, whom Pallas urged to confound the treaty, and to send a feathered wound among the Greeks. Acestes remained last at the bottom, whom not his age restrained from youthful sports. Soon all with vigor bent their trusty bows, and each chose his arrow from the quiver. Hippocoon's was the first: with forceful sway it flew, and, whizzing, cut the liquid way. Fixed in the mast the feathered weapon stood: the fearful pigeon fluttered in her bonds, and the tree trembled, and the shouting cries of the pleased people rent the vaulted skies. Then Mnestheus drove his arrow to the head, with lifted eyes, and took his aim above, but made a glancing shot, and missed the dove; yet missed so narrowly that he cut the cord that fastened by the foot the flitting bird. The captive thus released, she flew away, and beat with clapping wings the yielding skies. With his bow already bent, Eurytion stood; and, having first invoked his brother god, he sped his winged shaft with eager haste. The fatal message reached her as she fled: she left her life aloft; she struck the ground, and rendered back the weapon in the wound. Acestes, grudging at his lot, remained, without a prize to gratify his pains. Yet, shooting upward, he sent his shaft, to show an archer's art, and boast his twanging bow. The feathered arrow gave a dire portent, from which later augurs judge events. Chafed by the speed, it fired; and, as it flew, drew a trail of following flames ascending: kindling, they mounted, and marked the shiny way; like falling meteors they played across the skies, and vanished into wind, or decayed in a blaze. The Trojans and Sicilians wildly stared, and, trembling, turned their wonder into prayer. The Dardan prince put on a smiling face, and embraced Acestes closely; then, honoring him with gifts above the rest, turned the bad omen, and did not confess his fears. “The gods,” said he, “have wrought this miracle, and ordered you the prize without the lot. Accept this goblet, rough with figured gold, which Thracian Cisseus gave my sire of old: receive this pledge of ancient amity, which I justly give to my second sire.” He said this, and, with the trumpets' cheerful sound, proclaimed him victor, and crowned him with laurel. Nor did good Eurytion envy him the prize, though he had transfixed the pigeon in the skies. He who cut the line was graced with the second gifts; the third was his whose arrow pierced the mast.

The Thracian who gave Anchises a figured goblet.

## modern-en · marcellus · 6:30

He paused; and, while they viewed the passing spirits with wondering eyes, thus renewed his speech: “See great Marcellus! How, untired in toils, he moves with manly grace, how rich with regal spoils! When his country, threatened with alarms, requires his courage and his conquering arms, he shall more than once affright the Punic bands; shall kill the Gaulish king in single fight; then move to the Capitol in triumph, and the third spoils shall grace Feretrian Jove.” Aeneas here beheld, of form divine, a godlike youth shining in glittering armor, keeping equal pace with great Marcellus; but his eyes were gloomy, his face dejected. He saw, and, wondering, asked his airy guide, what he was and from whence, who pressed the hero's side: “His son, or one of his illustrious name? How like the former, and almost the same! Observe the crowds that compass him around; all gaze, and all admire, and raise a shouting sound: but hovering mists are spread around his brows, and night, with sable shades, involves his head.” “Seek not to know,” the ghost replied with tears, “the sorrows of your sons in future years. This youth (the blissful vision of a day) shall just be shown on earth, and snatched away. The gods had raised the Roman state too high, had their gifts been as permanent as great. What groans of men shall fill the Martian field! How fierce a blaze his flaming pile shall yield! What funeral pomp shall floating Tiber see, when, rising from his bed, he views the sad solemnity! No youth shall give equal hopes of glory, no youth afford so great a cause to grieve; the Trojan honor, and the Roman boast, admired when living, and adored when lost! Mirror of ancient faith in early youth! Undaunted worth, inviolable truth! No foe, unpunished, in the fighting field shall dare you, foot to foot, with sword and shield; much less in arms oppose your matchless force, when your sharp spurs shall urge your foaming horse. Ah! Could you break through fate's severe decree, a new Marcellus shall arise in you! Bring full canisters of fragrant lilies, mixed with the purple roses of the spring; let me strew his body with funeral flowers; this gift which parents owe to their children, this unavailing gift, at least, I may bestow!” Thus having said, he led the hero round the confines of the blessed Elysian ground; which when Anchises had shown to his son, and fired his mind to mount the promised throne, he tells him the future wars, ordained by fate; the strength and customs of the Latian state; the prince, and people; and forearms his care with rules, to push his fortune, or to bear.

The young Roman in the parade of souls whose early death the poem mourns.

## modern-en · caesar · 1:17

"Daughter, dismiss your fears. The fates of your descendants stand fixed and unchanged, as you desire. You shall behold the Lavinian walls you wish for; and when Aeneas, ripe for heaven, is called by fate, you shall bear him up, sublime, to me. No counsel has reversed my firm decree. And lest new fears disturb your happy state, know that I have searched the mystic rolls of Fate. Your son (nor is the appointed season far off) shall wage successful war in Italy, tame fierce nations in the bloody field, impose sovereign laws, and build cities, until, every foe subdued, the sun has run its annual race three times through the signs. This is his appointed time. Then Ascanius, now called Iulus, shall begin his reign. He shall wear the crown for thirty rolling years, and then shall transfer the seat from Lavinium, and with hard labor shall build Alba Longa. The throne shall be filled by his successors for three hundred more years, and then Ilia the fair shall be seen, a priestess and a queen, who, filled with the seed of Mars, shall in due time bring forth twin boys at a single birth. A tawny wolf shall suckle the royal babes. Then Romulus shall gain his grandfather's throne, shall found towers of war, shall call the people Romans, and the city Rome. To them I assign no bounds of empire, nor term of years to their immortal line. Even haughty Juno, who now turmoils earth, seas, and heaven, and Jove himself, with endless broils, shall be reconciled at last, and join her friendly power to cherish and advance the Trojan line. The subject world shall acknowledge Rome's dominion, and lying prostrate shall adore the nation of the toga. An age is ripening in revolving fate when Troy shall overturn the Grecian state, and her conquering sons shall call for sweet revenge, to crush the people who conspired at her fall. Then Caesar shall arise from the Julian stock, whose empire shall be bounded only by ocean, and whose fame only by the skies; whom, laden with eastern spoils, our heaven, the just reward of human toils, shall securely receive with divine rites, and incense shall rise before his sacred shrine. Then dire debate and impious war shall cease, and the stern age shall be softened into peace. Then banished Faith shall return once more, and Vestal fires shall burn in hallowed temples; and Remus with Quirinus shall sustain the righteous laws, and restrain fraud and force. Janus himself shall stand before his shrine and guard the dreadful gates, with bolts and iron bars: within remains Fury, imprisoned, bound in brazen chains; high on a trophy of useless weapons he sits, and threatens the world with vain alarms."

The ruler promised to rise from the Julian line.

## modern-en · numitor · 6:28

Thus having said, the father spirit led the priestess and his son through swarms of shades, and took a rising ground, from which to see the long procession of his progeny. “Survey,” the sire pursued, “this airy throng, as they pass along, offered to your view. These are the Italian names, which fate will join with ours, and graft upon the Trojan line. Observe the youth who appears first in sight, and holds the nearest station to the light; already he seems to snuff the vital air, and leans just forward, on a shining spear: he is Silvius, your last-begotten race, but sent first in order, to fill your place; an Alban name, but mixed with Dardan blood, born in the covert of a shady wood: fair Lavinia, your surviving wife, shall breed him in groves, to lead a solitary life. In Alba he shall fix his royal seat, and, born a king, shall beget a race of kings. Then Procas, honor of the Trojan name, Capys, and Numitor, of endless fame. After these, a second Silvius appears; Silvius Aeneas, for he bears your name; equally renowned for arms and justice, who, late restored, shall be crowned in Alba. How great they look! How vigorously they wield their weighty lances, and sustain the shield! But those who appear crowned with oaken wreaths shall rear the Gabian walls and strong Fidena; shall found Nomentum, Bola, with Pometia; and raise Collatian towers on rocky ground. All these shall then be towns of mighty fame, though now they lie obscure, and as lands without a name. See Romulus the great, born to restore the crown which once his injured grandsire wore. A priestess of your blood shall bear this prince, and he shall appear in arms like his sire. Two rising crests adorn his royal head; born from a god, himself born to godhead: his sire already signs him for the skies, and marks the seat amidst the deities. Auspicious chief! Your race, in times to come, shall spread the conquests of imperial Rome. Rome, whose ascending towers shall invade heaven, enveloping earth and ocean in her shade; high as the Mother of the Gods in place, and proud, like her, of an immortal race. Then, when in pomp she makes the Phrygian round, with golden turrets crowned on her temples; a hundred gods supply her sweeping train; all her offspring, and all command the sky.

An Alban king in the parade of Aeneas’s descendants.

## modern-en · tullus · 6:29

“Now fix your sight, and stand intent, to see your Roman race, and the Julian progeny. The mighty Caesar awaits his vital hour, impatient for the world, and grasps his promised power. But next behold the youth of form divine, Caesar himself, exalted in his line; Augustus, often promised, and long foretold, sent to the realm that Saturn ruled of old; born to restore a better age of gold. Africa and India shall obey his power; he shall extend his propagated sway beyond the solar year, without the starry way, where Atlas turns the rolling heavens around, and his broad shoulders are crowned with their lights. At his foreseen approach, already quake the Caspian kingdoms and the Maeotian lake: their seers behold the tempest from afar, and threatening oracles denounce the war. Nile hears him knocking at his sevenfold gates, and seeks his hidden spring, and fears his nephew's fates. Nor did Hercules know more lands or labors, not even when he slew the brazen-footed hind, freed Erymanthus from the foaming boar, and dipped his arrows in Lernaean gore; nor Bacchus, turning from his Indian war, drawn triumphant in his car by tigers, descending from Nisus' top to the plains, with curling vines around his purple reins. And do we yet doubt, through dangers, to pursue the paths of honor, and a crown in view? But who is the man, who appears from afar? His head crowned with olive, his hand bears a censer, his hoary beard and holy vestments bring his lost idea back: I know the Roman king. He shall ordain new laws for peaceful Rome, called from his humble abode to sustain a scepter. Next in dignity him, Tullus succeeds, an active prince, and prone to martial deeds. He shall prepare his troops for fighting fields, disused to toils, and triumphs of war. By dint of sword he shall increase his crown, and scour his armor from the rust of peace. Whom Ancus follows, with a fawning air, but vain within, and proudly popular. Next view the Tarquin kings, the avenging sword of Brutus, justly drawn, and Rome restored. He first renews the rods and severe axe, and gives the consuls royal robes to wear. His sons, who seek to sustain the tyrant, and long for arbitrary lords again, are scourged with ignominy, in open sight; he dooms them to deserved death, asserting public right. Unhappy man, to break the pious laws of nature, pleading in his children's cause! However the doubtful fact is understood, it is love of honor, and his country's good: the consul, not the father, sheds the blood. Behold Torquatus pursuing the same track; and, next, view the two devoted Decii: the Drusian line, Camillus loaded home with standards well redeemed, and foreign foes overcome. The pair you see shine in equal armor, now, friends below, joined in close embraces; but, when they leave the shady realms of night, and, clothed in bodies, breathe your upper light, they shall pursue each other with mortal hate: what wars, what wounds, what slaughter shall ensue! From the Alpine heights the father first descends; his daughter's husband awaits him on the plain: his daughter's husband arms his eastern friends. Embrace again, my sons, be foes no more; nor stain your country with her children's gore! And you, the first, lay down your lawless claim, you, of my blood, who bear the Julian name! Another comes, who shall ride in triumph, and guide his chariot to the Capitol, from conquered Corinth, rich with Grecian spoils. And yet another, famed for warlike toils, shall impose the Roman laws on Argos, and avenge the Trojan cause on the Greeks; he shall drag their Achillean race in chains; he shall vindicate his ancestors' disgrace, and Pallas, for her violated place. Great Cato there, for gravity renowned, and conquering Cossus go crowned with laurels. Who can omit the Gracchi? Who can declare the Scipios' worth, those thunderbolts of war, the double bane of Carthage? Who can see, without esteem for virtuous poverty, severe Fabricius, or cease to admire the plowman consul in his coarse attire? Tired as I am, the Fabii claim my praise; and you, great hero, greatest of your name, ordained in war to save the sinking state, and, by delays, to put a stop to fate! Let others better mold the running mass of metals, and inform the breathing brass, and soften into flesh a marble face; plead better at the bar; describe the skies, and tell when the stars descend, and when they rise. But, Rome, it is yours alone, with awful sway, to rule mankind, and make the world obey, disposing peace and war by your own majestic way; to tame the proud, to free the fettered slave: these are imperial arts, and worthy of you.”

An early Roman king in the parade of souls.

And do we yet doubt, through dangers, to pursue the paths of honor, and a crown in view? But who is the man, who appears from afar? His head crowned with olive, his hand bears a censer, his hoary beard and holy vestments bring his lost idea back: I know the Roman king. He shall ordain new laws for peaceful Rome, called from his humble abode to sustain a scepter. Next in dignity him, Tullus succeeds, an active prince, and prone to martial deeds. He shall prepare his troops for fighting fields, disused to toils, and triumphs of war. By dint of sword he shall increase his crown, and scour his armor from the rust of peace. Whom Ancus follows, with a fawning air, but vain within, and proudly popular. Next view the Tarquin kings, the avenging sword of Brutus, justly drawn, and Rome restored. He first renews the rods and severe axe, and gives the consuls royal robes to wear. His sons, who seek to sustain the tyrant, and long for arbitrary lords again, are scourged with ignominy, in open sight; he dooms them to deserved death, asserting public right. Unhappy man, to break the pious laws of nature, pleading in his children's cause! However the doubtful fact is understood, it is love of honor, and his country's good: the consul, not the father, sheds the blood. Behold Torquatus pursuing the same track; and, next, view the two devoted Decii: the Drusian line, Camillus loaded home with standards well redeemed, and foreign foes overcome. The pair you see shine in equal armor, now, friends below, joined in close embraces; but, when they leave the shady realms of night, and, clothed in bodies, breathe your upper light, they shall pursue each other with mortal hate: what wars, what wounds, what slaughter shall ensue! From the Alpine heights the father first descends; his daughter's husband awaits him on the plain: his daughter's husband arms his eastern friends. Embrace again, my sons, be foes no more; nor stain your country with her children's gore! And you, the first, lay down your lawless claim, you, of my blood, who bear the Julian name! Another comes, who shall ride in triumph, and guide his chariot to the Capitol, from conquered Corinth, rich with Grecian spoils. And yet another, famed for warlike toils, shall impose the Roman laws on Argos, and avenge the Trojan cause on the Greeks; he shall drag their Achillean race in chains; he shall vindicate his ancestors' disgrace, and Pallas, for her violated place. Great Cato there, for gravity renowned, and conquering Cossus go crowned with laurels. Who can omit the Gracchi? Who can declare the Scipios' worth, those thunderbolts of war, the double bane of Carthage? Who can see, without esteem for virtuous poverty, severe Fabricius, or cease to admire the plowman consul in his coarse attire? Tired as I am, the Fabii claim my praise; and you, great hero, greatest of your name, ordained in war to save the sinking state, and, by delays, to put a stop to fate! Let others better mold the running mass of metals, and inform the breathing brass, and soften into flesh a marble face; plead better at the bar; describe the skies, and tell when the stars descend, and when they rise. But, Rome, it is yours alone, with awful sway, to rule mankind, and make the world obey, disposing peace and war by your own majestic way; to tame the proud, to free the fettered slave: these are imperial arts, and worthy of you.”

The Roman renowned for gravity, seen in the parade of souls.

## modern-en · hercules · 3:28

“From here Tarentum's bay appeared in view, renowned for Hercules, if fame be true. Just opposite, Lacinian Juno stands; the Caulonian towers, and the Scylacaean strands, feared for shipwrecks. Then we spied Mount Aetna, known by the smoky flames that cloud the sky. Far off we heard the waves with surly sound attack the rocks, and the rocks rebound their groans. The billows broke upon the sounding strand, and rolled the rising tide, impure with sand. Then thus said Anchises, old in experience: ‘That is Charybdis, which the seer foretold, and those are the promised rocks! Bear off to sea!' With haste the frightened mariners obeyed. First Palinurus veered to larboard; then all the fleet steered by his example. We rode aloft to heaven on ridgy waves, then descended to hell when they divided; and three times our galleys knocked the stony ground, and three times the hollow rocks returned the sound, and three times we saw the stars, that stood round with dews. The flagging winds forsook us with the sun; and, weary, we ran on Cyclopian shores. The port is capacious, and secure from wind, and is joined to the foot of thundering Aetna. By turns she rolls a pitchy cloud on high; by turns hot embers fly from her entrails, and flakes of mounting flames, that lick the sky. Often massy rocks are thrown from her bowels, and, shivered by the force, come piecemeal down. Often liquid lakes of burning sulphur flow, fed from the fiery springs that boil below. Enceladus, they say, transfixed by Jove, came tumbling from above with blasted limbs; and where he fell, the avenging father drew this flaming hill, and threw it on his body. As often as he turns his weary sides, he shakes the solid isle, and smoke hides the heavens. In shady woods we passed the tedious night, where bellowing sounds and groans affrighted our souls, of which no cause was offered to the sight; for not one star was kindled in the sky, nor could the moon supply her borrowed light; for misty clouds enveloped the firmament, the stars were muffled, and the moon was pent.

The hero who killed Cacus on the future site of Rome, worshipped there ever since. The poem also calls him Alcides.

## modern-en · cacus · 8:9

But when the rage of hunger was repressed, Evander thus spoke to his royal guest: "These rites, these altars, and this feast, O king, spring from no vain fears or superstition, nor from blind devotion, nor from blinder chance, nor from heady zeal, or brutal ignorance; but, saved from danger, we recompense the labors of a god with a grateful sense. See, from afar, yon rock that mates the sky, about whose feet such heaps of rubbish lie—such undigested ruin; bleak and bare, how desert it stands now, exposed in air! It was once a robber's den, enclosed around with living stone, and deep beneath the ground. The monster Cacus, more than half a beast, possessed this hold, impervious to the sun. The pavement was ever foul with human gore; heads, and their mangled members, hung on the door. Vulcan begot this plague; and, like his sire, he belched black clouds, and flakes of livid fire. Time, long expected, eased us of our load, and brought the needful presence of a god. The avenging force of Hercules arrived in triumph from Spain, Geryon slain: the giant lived three times, and three times lived in vain. Alcides drove his prize, the lowing herds, near Tiber's bank, to graze in the shady grove. Allured with hope of plunder, and intent on robbing by force and circumventing by fraud, the brutal Cacus, as they strayed by chance, conveyed four oxen and four fair kine from there; and, lest the printed footsteps might be seen, he dragged them backwards to his rocky den. The reversed tracks gave a lying notice, and led the searcher backward from the cave.

The fire-breathing monster of the Aventine cave, killed by Hercules.

## modern-en · geryon · 6:11

Just in the gate and in the jaws of hell, revengeful Cares and sullen Sorrows dwell, and pale Diseases, and repining Age, Want, Fear, and Famine's unresisted rage; here Toils, and Death, and Death's half-brother, Sleep, terrible forms to view, keep their sentry; with the anxious Pleasures of a guilty mind, deep Frauds before, and open Force behind; the Furies' iron beds; and Strife, that shakes her hissing tresses and unfolds her snakes. Full in the midst of this infernal road, an elm displays her dusky arms abroad: the God of Sleep there hides his heavy head, and empty dreams are spread on every leaf. Of various forms, unnumbered specters more, Centaurs, and double shapes, besiege the door. Before the passage, horrid Hydra stands, and Briareus with all his hundred hands; Gorgons, Geryon with his triple frame; and vain Chimaera vomits empty flame. The chief unsheathed his shining steel, prepared, though seized with sudden fear, to force the guard, offering his brandished weapon at their face; had not the Sibyl stopped his eager pace, and told him what those empty phantoms were: forms without bodies, and impassive air. Hence to deep Acheron they took their way, whose troubled eddies, thick with ooze and clay, are whirled aloft, and lost in Cocytus. There Charon stands, who rules the dreary coast: a sordid god: down from his hoary chin a length of beard descends, uncombed, unclean; his eyes, like hollow furnaces on fire; a girdle, foul with grease, binds his obscene attire. He spreads his canvas; with his pole he steers; he bears the freights of flitting ghosts in his thin bottom. He looked old in years; yet in his years were seen a youthful vigor and autumnal green. An airy crowd came rushing where he stood, which filled the margin of the fatal flood: husbands and wives, boys and unmarried maids, and the more majestic shades of mighty heroes, and youths, entombed before their fathers' eyes, with hollow groans, and shrieks, and feeble cries. Thick as the leaves in autumn strew the woods, or fowls, forced by winter, forsake the floods, and wing their hasty flight to happier lands; such, and so thick, the shivering army stood, and pressed for passage with extended hands. Now these, now those, the surly boatman bore: the rest he drove to a distance from the shore. The hero, who beheld with wondering eyes the tumult mixed with shrieks, laments, and cries, asked of his guide what the rude concourse meant; why the thronging people bent toward the shore; what forms of law were used among the ghosts; why some were ferried over, and some refused.

The triple-bodied giant Hercules killed in Spain.

## modern-en · potitius · 8:10

"Meanwhile the herdsman hero shifted his place, to find fresh pasture and untrodden grass. The beasts, who missed their mates, filled all around with bellowings, and the rocks restored the sound. One heifer, who had heard her love complain, roared from the cave, and made the project vain. Alcides found the fraud; with rage he shook, and tossed about his head his knotted oak. Swift as the winds, or the flight of Scythian arrows, he climbed the aerial height with eager haste. Then first we saw the monster mend his pace; fear in his eyes, and paleness in his face, confessed the god's approach. Trembling he sprang, as if terror had increased his feet with wings; nor did he stay for stairs, but threw his body down the depth, drew the door over his back (the door, a rib of living rock; with pains his father had hewn it out, and bound it with iron chains); he broke the heavy links, the mountain closed, and opposed bars and levers to his foe. The wretch had hardly made his dungeon fast, when the fierce avenger came with bounding haste; he surveyed the mouth of the forbidden hold, and rolled his raging eyes here and there. He gnashed his teeth; and three times he compassed, with winged speed, the circuit of the ground. Three times at the cavern's mouth he pulled in vain, and, panting, three times desisted from his pain. A pointed flinty rock, all bare and black, grew gibbous from behind the mountain's back; owls, ravens, all ill omens of the night, built their nests here, and winged their flight hither. The leaning head hung threatening over the flood, and nodded to the left. The hero stood adverse, with planted feet, and, from the right, tugged at the solid stone with all his might. Thus heaved, the fixed foundations of the rock gave way; heaven echoed at the rattling shock. Tumbling, it choked the flood: on either side the banks leaped backward, and the streams divided; the sky shrunk upward with unusual dread, and trembling Tiber dived beneath his bed. The court of Cacus stood revealed to sight; the cavern glared with new-admitted light. So the pent vapors, with a rumbling sound, heave from below, and rend the hollow ground; a sounding cleft succeeds; and from on high the gods with hate beheld the nether sky: the ghosts repined at violated night, cursed the invading sun, and sickened at the sight. The graceless monster, caught in open day, enclosed, and in despair to fly away, howled horribly from underneath, and filled his hollow palace with unmanly yells. The hero stood above, and from afar plied him with darts, and stones, and distant war. He, from his huge mouth and nostrils, expired black clouds of smoke, amidst his father's fires, gathering, with each repeated blast, the night, to make aim uncertain, and sight erring. The wrathful god then plunged from above, and, where the sparkles drove in thickest waves, there he alighted; he waded through fumes, and groped his way, half singed, half stifled, till he grasped his prey. He found the monster, spewing fruitless flames; he squeezed his throat; he writhed his neck around, and bound his crippled members in a knot; then from their sockets tore his burning eyes. Rolled on a heap, the breathless robber lay. The doors, unbarred, received the rushing day, and thorough lights disclosed the ravished prey. The bulls, redeemed, breathed the open air again. Next, by the feet, they dragged him from his den. The wondering neighborhood, with glad surprise, beheld his shaggy breast, his giant size, his mouth that flamed no more, and his extinguished eyes. From that auspicious day, with rites divine, we worship at the hero's holy shrine. Potitius first ordained these annual vows; the Pinarian house were added as priests, who raised this altar in the sacred shade, where the honors forever due shall forever be paid. For these deserts, and for this high virtue shown, you warlike youths, crown your heads with garlands; fill high the goblets with a sparkling flood, and with deep draughts invoke our common god."

The founder of Hercules’ annual rites at Rome.

## modern-en · evadne · 6:16

Not far from there, the Mournful Fields appear, so called from lovers who inhabit there. The souls whom that unhappy flame invades, in secret solitude and myrtle shades, make endless moans, and, pining with desire, lament too late their unextinguished fire. Here he found Procris, and Eriphyle here, baring her breast, yet bleeding with the wound made by her son. He saw Pasiphaë there, with Phaedra's ghost, a foul incestuous pair. There Laodamia, with Evadne, moves, unhappy both, but loyal in their loves: Caeneus, once a woman, and once a man, but ending in the sex she first began. Not far from these stood Phoenician Dido, fresh from her wound, her bosom bathed in blood; whom when the Trojan hero hardly knew, obscure in shades, and with a doubtful view, (doubtful as he who sees, through dusky night, or thinks he sees, the moon's uncertain light,) he first approached the sullen shade with tears; and, as his love inspired him, thus he said: “Unhappy queen! Then is the common breath of rumor true, in your reported death, and I, alas, the cause? By Heaven, I vow, and all the powers that rule the realms below, unwilling I forsook your friendly state, commanded by the gods, and forced by fate. Those gods, that fate, whose unresisted might has sent me to these regions void of light, through the vast empire of eternal night. Nor did I dare to presume that, pressed with grief, my flight should urge you to this dire relief. Stay, stay your steps, and listen to my vows: this is the last interview that fate allows!” In vain he thus attempted to move her mind with tears, and prayers, and late-repenting love. Disdainfully she looked; then, turning round, she fixed her eyes unmoved upon the ground, and regarded what he said and swore no more than the deaf rocks, when the loud billows roar; but she whirled away, to shun his hateful sight, hid in the forest and the shades of night; then sought Sichaeus through the shady grove, who answered all her cares, and equaled all her love.

A shade in the fields of mourning.

Disdainfully she looked; then, turning round, she fixed her eyes unmoved upon the ground, and regarded what he said and swore no more than the deaf rocks, when the loud billows roar; but she whirled away, to shun his hateful sight, hid in the forest and the shades of night; then sought Sichaeus through the shady grove, who answered all her cares, and equaled all her love.

A shade in the fields of mourning.

## modern-en · theseus · 6:1

He said this, and wept; then spread his sails before the winds, and at length reached the Cumaean shore. The anchors dropped, and his crew moored the vessels. They turned their heads to sea, their sterns to land, and greeted the Italian strand with greedy joy. Some struck their fiery seed from clashing flints; some gathered sticks to feed the kindled flames, or searched for hollow trees, and felled the woods, or traced the discovered floods through valleys. Thus, while they fulfilled their several charges, the pious prince ascended the sacred hill where Phoebus is adored, and sought the shade that hid from sight his venerable maid. Deep in a cave the Sibyl makes her abode; from there she returns full of fate, and of the god. Through Trivia's grove they walked; and now they beheld, and now entered, the temple roofed with gold. When Daedalus, to flee the Cretan shore, bore his heavy limbs on jointed pinions (the first who sailed in air, as Fame sings), he came at length to the Cumaean coast, and alighting here, built this costly frame. Inscribed to Phoebus, he hung on high the steerage of his wings that cut the sky: then over the lofty gate his art embossed Androgeos' death, and the offerings to his ghost; the seven youths yearly sent from Athens, to meet the fate appointed by revengeful Crete. And next to these the dreadful urn was placed, in which the destined names were cast by lots: the mournful parents stood around in tears, and rising Crete appeared against their shore. There too, in living sculpture, might be seen the mad affection of the Cretan queen; then how she cheated her bellowing lover's eye; the rushing leap, the doubtful progeny, the lower part a beast, a man above, the monument of their polluted love. Not far from there he engraved the wondrous maze, with a thousand doors, a thousand winding ways: here dwells the monster, hid from human view, not to be found, but by the faithful clue; until the kind artist, moved with pious grief, lent this last relief to the loving maid, and described all those erring paths so well that Theseus conquered and the monster fell. Here hapless Icarus would have found his part, had not the father's grief restrained his art. Twice he tried to cast his son in gold; twice from his hands he dropped the forming mold.

The hero seated for ever in the underworld.

## modern-en · minos · 6:15

No sooner had they landed, than in his den they found the triple porter of the Stygian sound, grim Cerberus, who soon began to rear his crested snakes, and armed his bristling hair. The prudent Sibyl had prepared beforehand a sop, steeped in honey, to charm the guard; which, mixed with powerful drugs, she cast before his greedy grinning jaws, just opened to roar. With three enormous mouths he gaped; and straightway, pressed with hunger, devoured the pleasing bait. Long draughts of sleep enslaved his monstrous limbs; he reeled, and, falling, filled the spacious cave. The keeper charmed, the chief without delay passed on, and took the irremeable way. Before the gates, the cries of babes newly born, whom fate had torn from their tender mothers, assaulted his ears: then those, whom the form of laws condemned to die, when traitors judged their cause. Nor do they lack lots, nor judges to review the wrongful sentence, and award a new. Minos, the strict inquisitor, appears; and hears lives and crimes, with his assessors. He rolls the blended balls round in his urn, absolves the just, and dooms the guilty souls. The next, in place and punishment, are they who prodigally throw their souls away; fools, who, repining at their wretched state, and loathing anxious life, suborned their fate. With late repentance now they would retrieve the bodies they forsook, and wish to live; they desire to bear their pains and poverty, to view the light of heaven, and breathe the vital air: but fate forbids; the Stygian floods oppose, and with circling streams enclose the captive souls.

The judge who shakes the urn over the silent shades.

The hero, looking on the left, spied a lofty tower, and strong on every side with treble walls, which Phlegethon surrounds, whose fiery flood bounds the burning empire; and, pressed between the rocks, the bellowing noise resounds. Wide is the fronting gate, and, raised on high with adamantine columns, threatens the sky. Vain is the force of man, and vain of Heaven, to crush the pillars which sustain the pile. Sublime on these a tower of steel is reared; and dire Tisiphone there keeps the ward, girt in her sanguine gown, by night and day, observant of the souls that pass the downward way. From there are heard the groans of ghosts, the pains of sounding lashes and of dragging chains. The Trojan stood astonished at their cries, and asked his guide from where those yells arose; and what the crimes, and what the tortures were, and the loud laments that rent the liquid air.

The Fury who keeps the gate of Tartarus.

Vast is the throng of these; nor less the train of lustful youths, for foul adultery slain: hosts of deserters, who sold their honor, and basely broke their faith for bribes of gold. All these remain within the dungeon's depth, despairing pardon, and expecting pain. Ask not what pains; nor seek further to know their process, or the forms of law below. Some roll a weighty stone; some, laid along, and bound with burning wires, on spokes of wheels are hung. Unhappy Theseus, doomed forever there, is fixed by fate on his eternal chair; and wretched Phlegyas warns the world with cries (could warning make the world more just or wise): ‘Learn righteousness, and dread the avenging deities.' Others have sold their country to tyrants, imposing foreign lords for foreign gold; some have repealed old laws, made new statutes, not as the people pleased, but as they paid; with incest some profaned their daughters' bed: all dared the worst of ills, and, what they dared, attained. Had I a hundred mouths, a hundred tongues, and throats of brass, inspired with iron lungs, I could not repeat half those horrid crimes, nor half the punishments those crimes have met. But let us haste to pursue our voyage: the walls of Pluto's palace are in view; the gate, and iron arch above it, stands on anvils labored by the Cyclops' hands. Before the Fates allow our further way, here we must fix on high the golden bough.”

The shade who cries out a warning to learn justice.

Thus, from the dark recess, the Sibyl spoke, and the resisting air the thunder broke; the cave rebellowed, and the temple shook. At length her fury fell, her foaming ceased, and, ebbing in her soul, the god decreased. Then thus the chief: “No terror is new to my view, no frightful face of danger can be new. Inured to suffer, and resolved to dare, the Fates, beyond my power, shall be beyond my care. This let me crave, since near your grove the road to hell lies open, and the dark abode which Acheron surrounds, the innavigable flood; conduct me through the regions void of light, and lead me longing to my father's sight. For him, I have sought a thousand dangers, and, rushing where the thickest Grecians fought, brought the sacred burden safe on my back. He, for my sake, endured the raging ocean, and the wrath of Heaven, my still auspicious guide, and bore beyond the strength that decrepit age supplied. Often, since he breathed his last, in the dead of night his reverend image has stood before my sight; charging me to seek his holy shade below; conducted there by your unerring aid. But you, if pious minds are won by prayers, oblige the father, and protect the son. Yours is the power; nor has Proserpine in vain made you priestess of her nightly reign. If Orpheus, armed with his enchanting lyre, could inspire the ruthless king with pity, and redeem his wife from the shades below; if Pollux, offering his alternate life, could free his brother, and can daily go by turns aloft, and by turns descend below: why do I name Theseus, or his greater friend, who trod the downward path, and could ascend upward? No less than theirs is my lineage from Jove; my mother is greater, my descent the same.” So prayed the Trojan prince, and, while he prayed, laid his hand upon the holy altar.

The Thracian singer, seen among the blessed in his long robe.

## modern-en · memnon · 1:25

In the very center of the town stood a venerable wood, thick with trees. The Tyrians, landing near this holy ground and digging here, had found a prosperous omen: from beneath the earth they drew out a horse's head, which foreshadowed their growth and future fortune. Juno, the foundress, had given them this fated sign of a fruitful soil and a brave people. Here Sidonian Dido built and consecrated Juno's temple with solemn state, enriched with gifts and with a golden shrine; but the goddess made the place still more divine. On brazen steps the marble threshold rose, and brazen plates enclosed the cedar beams. The rafters were crowned with brazen coverings, and the lofty doors sounded on brazen hinges. What Aeneas first beheld in this place revived his courage and drove away his fear. For while, awaiting the queen, he raised his wondering eyes and gazed around the temple, admiring the fortune of the rising town, the competing artists, and the fame of their art, he saw, in order painted on the wall, all that had befallen unhappy Troy: the wars that fame had blown around the world, every scene true to life, every leader known. There he sees Agamemnon, and here Priam, and fierce Achilles, who defies them both. He stopped, and weeping, said: "O friend! Even here monuments of Trojan suffering appear! Our known disasters fill even foreign lands: see there, where old unhappy Priam stands! Even the mute walls relate the warrior's fame, and Trojan griefs stir Tyrian pity!" He said, and his tears found a ready passage, as he devoured with his eyes the scenes so well depicted, and fed his mind with an empty picture. For there he saw the fainting Greeks yielding, and there the trembling Trojans quitting the field, pursued by fierce Achilles across the plain as he drove his high chariot over the slain. Next came the tents of Rhesus, and his grief was renewed, their white sails betraying them to nightly view, and wakeful Diomede, whose cruel sword slew the sentries and did not spare their slumbering lord; then he took the fiery steeds before they tasted the food of Troy or drank from the river Xanthus. Elsewhere he saw where Troilus defied Achilles, and tried unequal combat; then, where the boy, disarmed, with loosened reins, was hurried over the plain by his horses, hung by the neck and hair, and dragged around, the hostile spear still sticking in his wound, inscribing the dusty ground with tracks of blood. Meanwhile the Trojan matrons, oppressed with woe, went in long procession to the temple of Pallas, hoping to reconcile their heavenly enemy. They wept, beat their breasts, tore their hair, and bore richly embroidered vests as offerings; but the stern goddess stood unmoved by prayer. Three times Achilles dragged Hector's corpse around the Trojan walls, whom he had slain in combat. Here Priam was suing; and there, for sums of gold, the lifeless body of his son was being sold. So sad an object, and so well expressed, drew sighs and groans from the grieving hero's breast, to see the figure of his lifeless friend, and his old father stretching out his helpless hand. He saw himself also amid the Grecian train, mingled in the bloody battle on the plain; and he knew swarthy Memnon in his armor, his pompous ensigns, and his Indian crew. There was Penthesilea, leading an Amazonian race to war with haughty grace; in their right hands they wielded a pointed dart, and their left sustained the lunar shield for defense. She threw a golden belt across her breast, and alone among the press she provoked a thousand foes, daring to oppose her maiden arms to manly force.

The swarthy warrior in the Carthaginian frescoes.

He spoke, and hurled his quivering spear against the mountain's side, with all the strength of a god. The pitying hero paid some pious tears, and followed the flitting shade with his eyes, then took the forward way, ordained by fate, and, with his guide, attained the farther fields, where, severed from the rest, the warrior souls remained. The gladsome ghosts, in circling troops, attended, and beheld their friend with unwearied eyes; delighted to hover near, and longed to know what business brought him to the realms below. But the Argive chiefs, and Agamemnon's train, when his refulgent arms flashed through the shady plain, fled from his well-known face, with their wonted fear, as when his thundering sword and pointed spear had driven them headlong to their ships, and gleaned the routed rear. ## modern-en · antenor · 1:15

"O King of Gods and Men, whose awful hand scatters thunder on the seas and land, and disposes all things with absolute command! How could my pious son incense your power? Or what, alas, was vanished Troy's offense? Our hope of Italy is not only lost, tossed on various seas by various tempests, but we are shut out from every shore and barred from every coast. You once promised a divine progeny of Romans rising from the Trojan line, who in time to come should hold the world in awe, and give law to land and ocean. How is your decree reversed, which eased my care when Troy was ruined in that cruel war? Then I could balance fates against fates; but now, when Fortune still pursues her former blow, what can I hope? What worse can still come? What end has your will decreed to these labors? Antenor was able to pass safely from the midst of Grecian hosts, and pierce the Illyrian coasts, where Timavus rages as it rolls down from the heights and empties through nine channels. At length he founded the happy seat of Padua, and gave his Trojans a secure retreat; there he established their arms, renewed their name, and now rules in peace, crowned with fame. But we, descended from your sacred line, entitled to your heaven and your divine rites, are banished from earth; and, because of the wrath of one, removed from Latium and the promised throne. Are these our scepters? Are these our due rewards? And is this how Jove keeps his plighted word?"

The Trojan who escaped and founded Padua, cited as a precedent by Venus.
