Meanwhile Aeneas lay in the shadows of night. Care seized his soul, and sleep forsook his eyes. But when the sun restored the cheerful day, he rose to survey the coast and country, anxious and eager to discover more. It looked a wild and uncultivated shore; but whether mankind or beasts alone possessed this new-found region was still unknown. Beneath a ledge of rocks he hid his fleet. Tall trees surrounded the mountain's shady sides; the overhanging brow above provided a safe retreat. Armed with two pointed darts, he left his friends, and true Achates attended on his steps. Behold, in the deep recesses of the wood, his goddess mother stood before his eyes—a huntress in dress and bearing, clothed as a maid, but her air proclaimed a queen. Her knees were bare, and knots tied up her garments; her hair was loose, and played upon the wind; her hand supported a bow, and her quiver hung behind. She seemed a virgin of the Spartan blood: in such attire Harpalyce bestrode her Thracian courser, outstripping the rapid flood. "Ho, strangers," she said, "have you lately seen one of my sisters, dressed as I am, who crossed the lawn, or strayed in the forest? A painted quiver at her back she bore; she wore a spotted lynx's hide, and at full cry pursued the tusky boar."

The Thracian huntress Venus is compared to.

## modern-en · iopas · 1:37

Now, when the rage of hunger was appeased, the meat removed, and every guest was pleased, the golden bowls were crowned with sparkling wine, and cheerful cries resounded through the palace. From gilded roofs hung lamps displayed nocturnal beams that rivaled the day. The queen commanded that a golden bowl, shining with divine gems, should be crowned with wine—the bowl which Belus and all the Tyrian line had used. Then, when silence had been proclaimed through the hall, she spoke: "O hospitable Jove, we invoke your sacred name and power with solemn rites; bless this auspicious hour for both nations! So may the Trojan and the Tyrian line be joined in lasting concord from this day. You, Bacchus, god of joys and friendly cheer, and you, gracious Juno, both be present here! And you, my lords of Tyre, address your vows to Heaven with mine, to ratify the peace." Then she took the goblet crowned with nectar (sprinkling the first libations on the ground), and raised it to her mouth with sober grace. Then, after sipping, she offered it to the next in place. It was Bitias whom she called, a thirsty soul; he took the challenge, embraced the bowl, and with pleasure swallowed the gold, nor did he cease to draw until he saw the bottom of the cup. The goblet went around; Iopas brought his golden lyre, and sang what ancient Atlas had taught him: the various labors of the wandering moon, and whence the eclipses of the sun proceed; the origin of men and beasts; and whence the rains arise, and fires dispense their warmth; and how the fixed and wandering stars dispose their influence; what shakes the solid earth; what cause delays the summer nights and shortens winter days. The Tyrians praised the song with peals of shouts, and those peals were echoed by the Trojan throng. The unhappy queen prolonged the night with talk, and drank large drafts of love with vast delight. She inquired much of Priam, and more of Hector; then asked what arms the swarthy Memnon wore, and what troops he had landed on the Trojan shore; the steeds of Diomede varied the discourse, and fierce Achilles, with his matchless force. At length, as fate and her ill stars required, she desired to hear the whole series of the war. "Relate fully, my godlike guest," she said, "the Grecian stratagems, the town betrayed, the fatal issue of so long a war, your flight, your wanderings, and your woes. For, since your men have been distressed on every sea and every coast, and your navy tossed, seven times the sun has seen either tropic, the winter has been banished, and the spring renewed."

The long-haired bard who sings at Dido’s feast.

## modern-en · cupid · 1:35

But Venus, anxious for her son's affairs, tried new counsels and prepared new designs: that Cupid should assume the shape and face of sweet Ascanius, and his sprightly grace; that he should bring the presents in her nephew's stead, and shed the gentle poison into Eliza's veins. For she feared the double-tongued Tyrians greatly, and knew the town was under Juno's care. These thoughts broke her golden slumbers in the night, and, so alarmed, she spoke thus to winged Love: "My son, my strength, whose mighty power alone controls the Thunderer on his awful throne, to you your much-afflicted mother flies, and relies on your help and your faith. You know, my son, how Jove's vengeful wife attempts your brother's life by force and fraud, and you have often mourned with me his sufferings. Dido now detains him with blandishments; but I suspect the town where Juno reigns. For this reason it is needful to forestall her craft, and fire the proud Phoenician's heart with love—a love so violent, so strong, so certain, that neither age can change it nor art can cure it. How this may be done, hear now my mind. Ascanius is planned by his father to come from the port, laden with presents, to gratify the queen and win the court. I mean to plunge the boy in a pleasing sleep, and, having carried him off, to keep him in the Idalian bowers, or on lofty Cythera, so that the sweet deceit may pass unseen, and no one prevent the trick. You take his form and shape. I beg the grace for only one night's revolving space: yourself a boy, assume a boy's dissembled face; so that when, in the fervor of the feast, the Tyrian queen hugs and caresses you on her breast, and, with sweet kisses, clasps you in her arms, you may infuse your venom into her veins." The God of Love obeyed, and set aside his bow and quiver and his feathered pride; he walked as Iulus in his mother's sight, and took delight in the sweet resemblance.

Venus’s son, sent to Carthage in Ascanius’s shape to fire Dido with love.

## modern-en · cyclops · 1:12

First, good Achates, with repeated strokes of clashing flints, struck their hidden fire. A short flame caught; a bed of withered leaves received the dying sparks as they fell. Kindled into life, they rose in fiery fumes and, fed with stronger fuel, mounted to the skies. The Trojans, dripping wet, either stood around the cheerful blaze or lay along the ground. Some dried their grain, spoiled with brine, ground it between stones, and prepared to dine. Aeneas climbed the mountain's airy brow and took a prospect of the seas below, hoping to spy Capys from there, or Antheus, or to see the streamers of Caicus flying. No vessels were in view; but on the plain three stately stags, with branching heads, led a lordly train; the more ignoble herd followed their stately steps, grazing slowly along. He halted; and while they fed in security below, he took the quiver and the trusty bow that Achates was used to carry. First he laid the leaders low, and then pierced the rest; nor did he cease from his arrows until seven mighty bodies stained the shaded plain with their blood. For the seven ships he made an equal share, and returned to the port in triumph from the hunt. He broached the jars of generous wine—Acestes' gift, when the fleet left his Trinacrian shores—and prepared for the feast, sharing the wine equally with the venison. While he dealt it round, the pious chief allayed the common grief with cheerful words: "Endure, and conquer! Jove will soon dispose our past and present sufferings to future good. With me you have survived the rocks of Scylla, and defied the inhuman Cyclops and his den. What greater ills can you endure after that? Take courage again and put away care; an hour will come when it will be a pleasure to recall your past sorrows, as blessings sent by Fate. Through various hazards and events we move to Latium and the realms foreordained by Jove. There we are called (that is the promise of the skies), where Trojan kingdoms may rise once again. Endure the hardships of your present state; live, and keep yourselves for a better fate."

The one-eyed giants of Sicily; Polyphemus is their most famous. Dryden spells the singular Polypheme.

## modern-en · polyphemus · 3:30

“‘Ulysses did not bear their fate unavenged, nor was he thoughtless of his own unhappy state; for, gorged with flesh, and drunk with human wine, while the giant lay fast asleep, supine, snoring aloud, and belching from his maw his indigested foam, and morsels raw; we prayed; we cast the lots, and then surrounded the monstrous body, stretched along the ground. Each of us, as he could approach him, lent a hand to bore his eyeball with a flaming brand. Beneath his frowning forehead lay his eye; for the vast frame supplied only one; but it was a globe so large it filled his front, like the sun's disk or like a Grecian shield. The stroke succeeded; and down the pupil bent: this vengeance followed for our slaughtered friends. But haste, unhappy wretches, haste to flee! Cut your cables, and rely on your oars! Such, and as vast as Polyphemus appears, this hated island bears a hundred more: like him, they shut their woolly sheep in caves; like him, they keep their herds on the mountain tops; like him, with mighty strides, they stalk from steep to steep. And now three moons have renewed their sharpened horns since, obscure from view in woods and wilds, I have dragged my loathsome days in mortal fright, and lodged by night in deserted caverns; often from the rocks I see a dreadful sight of the huge Cyclops, like a walking tree. From afar I hear his thundering voice resound, and his trampling feet that shake the solid ground. Cornels and savage berries of the wood, and roots and herbs, have been my meager food. While all around I cast my longing eyes, I saw your happy ships appear at last. On those I fixed my hopes, to these I run; it is all I ask, to shun this cruel race; you yourselves bestow what other death you please.'

First, good Achates, with repeated strokes of clashing flints, struck their hidden fire. A short flame caught; a bed of withered leaves received the dying sparks as they fell. Kindled into life, they rose in fiery fumes and, fed with stronger fuel, mounted to the skies. The Trojans, dripping wet, either stood around the cheerful blaze or lay along the ground. Some dried their grain, spoiled with brine, ground it between stones, and prepared to dine. Aeneas climbed the mountain's airy brow and took a prospect of the seas below, hoping to spy Capys from there, or Antheus, or to see the streamers of Caicus flying. No vessels were in view; but on the plain three stately stags, with branching heads, led a lordly train; the more ignoble herd followed their stately steps, grazing slowly along. He halted; and while they fed in security below, he took the quiver and the trusty bow that Achates was used to carry. First he laid the leaders low, and then pierced the rest; nor did he cease from his arrows until seven mighty bodies stained the shaded plain with their blood. For the seven ships he made an equal share, and returned to the port in triumph from the hunt. He broached the jars of generous wine—Acestes' gift, when the fleet left his Trinacrian shores—and prepared for the feast, sharing the wine equally with the venison. While he dealt it round, the pious chief allayed the common grief with cheerful words: "Endure, and conquer! Jove will soon dispose our past and present sufferings to future good. With me you have survived the rocks of Scylla, and defied the inhuman Cyclops and his den. What greater ills can you endure after that? Take courage again and put away care; an hour will come when it will be a pleasure to recall your past sorrows, as blessings sent by Fate. Through various hazards and events we move to Latium and the realms foreordained by Jove. There we are called (that is the promise of the skies), where Trojan kingdoms may rise once again. Endure the hardships of your present state; live, and keep yourselves for a better fate."

## modern-en · charybdis · 3:19

“‘When, having parted from here, the wind that waits ready for Sicily shall bear you to the straits where proud Pelorus opens a wider way, tack to larboard, and stand off to sea: veer starboard from sea and land. The Italian shore and fair Sicilia's coast were one, before an earthquake caused the flaw: the roaring tides broke the passage that divides land from land; and where the lands retired, the rushing ocean rides. Distinguished by the straits, on either hand, rising cities now stand in long order, and fruitful fields—so much can time invade the moldering work that beauteous Nature made. Far on the right, foul Scylla hides her dogs; Charybdis, roaring on the left, presides, and in her greedy whirlpool sucks the tides; then spouts them up from below; driven with fury, the waves mount up and wash the face of heaven. But Scylla from her den, with open jaws, draws the sinking vessel into her eddy, then dashes it on the rocks. A human face and virgin bosom hide her tail's disgrace: her obscene parts descend below the waves, enclosed by dogs, and ending in a dolphin. It is safer, then, to bear aloof to sea, and coast Pachynus, though with more delay, than once to view misshapen Scylla near, and to hear the loud yell of watery wolves.

The whirlpool on the left of the strait, which swallows and spews the sea three times a day.

## modern-en · chimaera · 6:11

Just in the gate and in the jaws of hell, revengeful Cares and sullen Sorrows dwell, and pale Diseases, and repining Age, Want, Fear, and Famine's unresisted rage; here Toils, and Death, and Death's half-brother, Sleep, terrible forms to view, keep their sentry; with the anxious Pleasures of a guilty mind, deep Frauds before, and open Force behind; the Furies' iron beds; and Strife, that shakes her hissing tresses and unfolds her snakes. Full in the midst of this infernal road, an elm displays her dusky arms abroad: the God of Sleep there hides his heavy head, and empty dreams are spread on every leaf. Of various forms, unnumbered specters more, Centaurs, and double shapes, besiege the door. Before the passage, horrid Hydra stands, and Briareus with all his hundred hands; Gorgons, Geryon with his triple frame; and vain Chimaera vomits empty flame. The chief unsheathed his shining steel, prepared, though seized with sudden fear, to force the guard, offering his brandished weapon at their face; had not the Sibyl stopped his eager pace, and told him what those empty phantoms were: forms without bodies, and impassive air. Hence to deep Acheron they took their way, whose troubled eddies, thick with ooze and clay, are whirled aloft, and lost in Cocytus. There Charon stands, who rules the dreary coast: a sordid god: down from his hoary chin a length of beard descends, uncombed, unclean; his eyes, like hollow furnaces on fire; a girdle, foul with grease, binds his obscene attire. He spreads his canvas; with his pole he steers; he bears the freights of flitting ghosts in his thin bottom. He looked old in years; yet in his years were seen a youthful vigor and autumnal green. An airy crowd came rushing where he stood, which filled the margin of the fatal flood: husbands and wives, boys and unmarried maids, and the more majestic shades of mighty heroes, and youths, entombed before their fathers' eyes, with hollow groans, and shrieks, and feeble cries. Thick as the leaves in autumn strew the woods, or fowls, forced by winter, forsake the floods, and wing their hasty flight to happier lands; such, and so thick, the shivering army stood, and pressed for passage with extended hands. Now these, now those, the surly boatman bore: the rest he drove to a distance from the shore. The hero, who beheld with wondering eyes the tumult mixed with shrieks, laments, and cries, asked of his guide what the rude concourse meant; why the thronging people bent toward the shore; what forms of law were used among the ghosts; why some were ferried over, and some refused.

The fire-breathing monster, seen at the gate of hell and blazoned on Turnus’s crest.

## modern-en · typhoeus · 8:11

This said, Evander twined a double wreath, and poplars black and white bound his temples. Then he filled his ample bowl. With like design the rest invoked the gods, with sprinkled wine. Meanwhile the sun descended from the skies, and the bright evening star began to rise. And now the priests, Potitius at their head, involved in the skins of beasts, led the long procession; they held high the flaming tapers in their hands, as custom had prescribed their holy bands. Then they loaded the tables with a second course, and offered to the god with full chargers. The Salii sang, and censed his altars round with Saban smoke, their heads bound with poplar: one choir of the old, another of the young, to dance, and to bear the burden of the song. The lay recorded the labors and the praises, and all the immortal acts of Hercules: first, how the mighty babe, when swathed in bands, strangled the serpents with his infant hands; then, as he grew in years and matchless force, he overthrew the Oechalian walls, and the Trojan. Besides, they related a thousand hazards procured by Juno's and by Eurystheus' hate: "Your hands, unconquered hero, could subdue the cloud-born Centaurs and the monster crew; neither did the bull withstand your resistless arm, nor he, the roaring terror of the wood. The triple porter of the Stygian seat, with lolling tongue, lay fawning at your feet, and, seized with fear, forgot his mangled meat. The infernal waters trembled at your sight; no face of danger, O god, could affright you; neither huge Typhoeus, nor the unnumbered snake, increased with hissing heads, in Lerna's lake. Hail, Jove's undoubted son! An added grace to heaven and to the great author of your race! Receive the grateful offerings which we pay, and smile propitious on your solemn day!" In such verses they sang; above the rest, the den and death of Cacus crowned the feast. The woods conveyed the sound to the hollow vales, the vales to the hills, and the hills rebounded the notes. The rites performed, the cheerful train retired.

A monster named among the terrors Hercules did not fear.

## modern-en · trojans · 1:0

The Trojans, after a seven years' voyage, set sail for Italy, but are overtaken by a dreadful storm, which Aeolus raises at the request of Juno. The tempest sinks one ship and scatters the rest. Neptune drives off the winds and calms the sea. Aeneas, with his own ship and six more, arrives safe at an African port. Venus complains to Jupiter of her son's misfortunes. Jupiter comforts her, and sends Mercury to secure him a kind reception among the Carthaginians. Aeneas, going out to discover the country, meets his mother in the shape of a huntress, who conveys him in a cloud to Carthage, where he sees his friends whom he thought lost, and receives a kind welcome from the queen. Dido, by a device of Venus, begins to feel a passion for him, and, after some conversation, asks to hear the history of his adventures since the siege of Troy, which becomes the subject of the two following books.

Aeneas’s people, the survivors of Troy; also called Dardans, Phrygians and Teucrians.

## modern-en · latins · 5:25

The unfledged commanders and their martial train first made the circuit of the sandy plain around their sires, and, at the appointed sign, drawn up in beautiful order, formed a line. The second signal sounded, the troop divided into three distinguished parts, with three distinguished guides. Again they closed, and once again they parted; troop to troop opposed, and line to line. They met; they wheeled; they threw their darts afar with harmless rage and well-dissembled war. Then in a round the mingled bodies ran: flying they followed, and pursuing shunned; broken, they broke; and, rallying, they renewed the military show in other forms. At last, in order, undiscerned they joined, and marched together in a friendly line. And, as the Cretan labyrinth of old, with wandering ways and many a winding fold, involved the weary feet, without redress, in a round error, which denied recess; so fought the Trojan boys in warlike play, turned and returned, and still took a different way. Thus dolphins in the deep chase each other in circles, when they swim around the watery race. This game, these carousels, Ascanius taught; and, building Alba, brought them to the Latins; he showed what he had learned: the Latin sires impart the graceful art to their succeeding sons; from these imperial Rome received the game, which they call Troy, and the troop the Trojan troop.

Latinus’s people, whose land the Trojans are fated to hold.

## modern-en · rutulians · 8:7

Conducted to the grove, Aeneas first broke the silence, and thus addressed the king: "Best of the Greeks, to whom, by fate's command, I bear these peaceful branches in my hand, undaunted I approach you, though I know your birth is Grecian, and your land my foe; though your ancient lineage came from Atreus, and both the brother kings claim your kindred; yet my self-conscious worth, your high renown, your virtue, blown through the neighboring nations, our fathers' mingled blood, and Apollo's voice, have led me hither, less by need than by choice. Our founder Dardanus, as fame has sung, and as the Greeks acknowledge, sprang from Electra: Electra came from the loins of Atlas; Atlas, whose head sustains the starry frame. Your sire is Mercury, whom long before fair Maia bore on cold Cyllene's top. Maia the fair, if we rely on fame, was Atlas' daughter, who sustains the sky. Thus from one common source our streams divide; ours is the Trojan, yours the Arcadian side. Raised by these hopes, I sent no news before, nor asked your leave, nor did I implore your faith; but I come, without a pledge, as my own ambassador. The same Rutulians who pursue the Trojan race with arms are equal foes to you. Our host expelled, what further force can stay the victor troops from universal sway? Then will they stretch their power athwart the land, and command either sea from side to side. Receive our offered faith, and give us yours; ours is a generous and experienced line: we do not lack hearts or bodies for the war; we are cautious in council, and daring in the field."

Turnus’s people, of Ardea.

## modern-en · tyrians · 1:24

They climbed the next rise, and, looking down, now viewed the town at a nearer distance. The prince gazed in wonder at the stately towers, which had lately been huts and rude shepherds' bowers, at the gates and streets, and heard from every side the noise and busy concourse of the marketplace. The toiling Tyrians called to one another to ply their labor. Some extended the wall; some were building the citadel; the brawny throng either dug, or pushed unwieldy stones along. Some chose a spot of ground for their dwellings, which they first marked out and then surrounded with ditches. Some ordained laws; some attended the election of holy senators, chosen by voice. Here some designed a mole; there others laid deep foundations for a theater, and hewed mighty columns from marble quarries for scenery and future display. Their toil and their busy pains were like those of bees in flowery plains, when, winter past and summer scarcely begun, they are called forth to labor in the sun. Some lead their young abroad; some condense their liquid store; some dispense it into the cells; some stand ready at the gate to receive the golden burden, and relieve their returning friends; all combine with united force to drive the lazy drones from the laborious hive. Stung with envy, they watch each other's deeds; the fragrant work proceeds with diligence. "Three times happy you, whose walls already rise!" said Aeneas, and with lifted eyes he gazed upon their lofty towers. Then, entering at the gate (marvelous to relate), concealed in clouds, he mixed unnoticed among the busy throng, was borne along by the tide, and passed along unseen.

Dido’s people, the settlers of Carthage.

## modern-en · greeks · 1:25

In the very center of the town stood a venerable wood, thick with trees. The Tyrians, landing near this holy ground and digging here, had found a prosperous omen: from beneath the earth they drew out a horse's head, which foreshadowed their growth and future fortune. Juno, the foundress, had given them this fated sign of a fruitful soil and a brave people. Here Sidonian Dido built and consecrated Juno's temple with solemn state, enriched with gifts and with a golden shrine; but the goddess made the place still more divine. On brazen steps the marble threshold rose, and brazen plates enclosed the cedar beams. The rafters were crowned with brazen coverings, and the lofty doors sounded on brazen hinges. What Aeneas first beheld in this place revived his courage and drove away his fear. For while, awaiting the queen, he raised his wondering eyes and gazed around the temple, admiring the fortune of the rising town, the competing artists, and the fame of their art, he saw, in order painted on the wall, all that had befallen unhappy Troy: the wars that fame had blown around the world, every scene true to life, every leader known. There he sees Agamemnon, and here Priam, and fierce Achilles, who defies them both. He stopped, and weeping, said: "O friend! Even here monuments of Trojan suffering appear! Our known disasters fill even foreign lands: see there, where old unhappy Priam stands! Even the mute walls relate the warrior's fame, and Trojan griefs stir Tyrian pity!" He said, and his tears found a ready passage, as he devoured with his eyes the scenes so well depicted, and fed his mind with an empty picture. For there he saw the fainting Greeks yielding, and there the trembling Trojans quitting the field, pursued by fierce Achilles across the plain as he drove his high chariot over the slain. Next came the tents of Rhesus, and his grief was renewed, their white sails betraying them to nightly view, and wakeful Diomede, whose cruel sword slew the sentries and did not spare their slumbering lord; then he took the fiery steeds before they tasted the food of Troy or drank from the river Xanthus. Elsewhere he saw where Troilus defied Achilles, and tried unequal combat; then, where the boy, disarmed, with loosened reins, was hurried over the plain by his horses, hung by the neck and hair, and dragged around, the hostile spear still sticking in his wound, inscribing the dusty ground with tracks of blood. Meanwhile the Trojan matrons, oppressed with woe, went in long procession to the temple of Pallas, hoping to reconcile their heavenly enemy. They wept, beat their breasts, tore their hair, and bore richly embroidered vests as offerings; but the stern goddess stood unmoved by prayer. Three times Achilles dragged Hector's corpse around the Trojan walls, whom he had slain in combat. Here Priam was suing; and there, for sums of gold, the lifeless body of his son was being sold. So sad an object, and so well expressed, drew sighs and groans from the grieving hero's breast, to see the figure of his lifeless friend, and his old father stretching out his helpless hand. He saw himself also amid the Grecian train, mingled in the bloody battle on the plain; and he knew swarthy Memnon in his armor, his pompous ensigns, and his Indian crew. There was Penthesilea, leading an Amazonian race to war with haughty grace; in their right hands they wielded a pointed dart, and their left sustained the lunar shield for defense. She threw a golden belt across her breast, and alone among the press she provoked a thousand foes, daring to oppose her maiden arms to manly force.

The army that took Troy; the poem also calls them Grecians, Argives and Danaans.

## modern-en · arcadians · 8:13

Thus, walking on, he spoke, and showed the gate, since called the Carmental by the Roman state, where stood an altar, sacred to the name of old Carmenta, the prophetic dame, who had foretold to her son the Aenean race, sublime in fame, and the imperial place of Rome. Then he showed the forest, which, in after times, fierce Romulus made a sacred refuge for perpetrated crimes; and, with this, the shrine where Pan below the rock had divine rites. Then he told of Argus' death, his murdered guest, whose grave and tomb attest his innocence. Thence he led to the steep Tarpeian rock, now roofed with gold, then thatched with homely reeds. A reverent fear (such superstition reigns among the rude) possessed the swains even then. Some god, they knew—what god, they could not tell—dwelt there amidst the sacred horror. The Arcadians thought him Jove; and they said they saw the mighty Thunderer with majestic awe, who took his shield, and dealt his bolts around, and scattered tempests on the teeming ground. Then they saw two heaps of ruins (once they stood as two stately towns, on either side of the flood), the remains of Saturnia and of Janiculum; each place retained the founder's name. Thus discoursing together, they arrived where poor Evander kept his country court. They viewed the ground of Rome's litigious hall (once oxen lowed, where now the lawyers bawl); then, stooping, they pressed through the narrow gate, when thus the king bespoke his Trojan guest: "Mean as it is, this palace, and this door, received Alcides, then a conqueror. Dare to be poor; accept our homely food, which feasted him, and emulate a god." Then beneath a lowly roof he led the weary prince, and laid him on a bed—the stuffing leaves, overspread with hides of bears. Now night had shed her silver dews around, and with her sable wings embraced the ground, when love's fair goddess, anxious for her son (new tumults rising, and new wars begun), couched with her husband in his golden bed, with these alluring words invokes his aid; and, so that her pleasing speech may move his mind, she inspires each accent with the charms of love: "While cruel fate conspired with Grecian powers to level with the ground the Trojan towers, I asked not aid to restore the unhappy, nor did I implore the succor of your skill; nor did I urge in vain the labors of my lord, to sustain a sinking empire longer, though I owed much to Priam's house, and more, deplored the dangers of Aeneas. But now, by Jove's command, and fate's decree, his race is doomed to reign in Italy. With humble suit I beg your needful art, O power still propitious, that rules my heart! A mother kneels a suppliant for her son. By Thetis and Aurora you were won to forge impenetrable shields, and to grace a less illustrious race with fated arms. Behold what haughty nations are combined against the relics of the Phrygian kind, to destroy my people with fire and sword, and to conquer Venus twice, in conquering Troy." ## modern-en · gauls · 8:23

Meanwhile the mother goddess, crowned with charms, broke through the clouds, and brought the fated arms. Within a winding vale she found her son, retired alone on the cool river's banks. She showed her heavenly form without disguise, and gave herself to his desiring eyes. "Behold," she said, "performed in every part, my promise made, and Vulcan's labored art. Now secure, seek the Latian enemy, and defy haughty Turnus to the field." She said; and, having first embraced her son, she placed the radiant arms beneath an oak. Proud of the gift, he rolled his greedy sight around the work, and gazed with vast delight. He lifts, he turns, he poises, and admires the crested helm, that vomits radiant fires: his hands hold the fatal sword and corslet, one keen with tempered steel, one stiff with gold: both ample, flaming both, and beamy bright; so shines a cloud, when edged with adverse light. He shakes the pointed spear, and longs to try the plated cuisses on his manly thigh; but he most admires the shield's mysterious mold, and the Roman triumphs rising on the gold. For the heavenly smith had wrought these on it, embossed (not untaught in the rolls of future fate)—the wars in order, and the divine race of warriors issuing from the Julian line. The cave of Mars was dressed with mossy greens; there, by the wolf, were laid the martial twins. Intrepid on her swelling dugs they hung; the foster dam lolled out her fawning tongue; they sucked secure, while, bending back her head, she licked their tender limbs, and formed them as they fed. Not far from there new Rome appears, with games projected for the rape of Sabine dames. The pit resounds with shrieks; a war succeeds, for breach of public faith, and unexampled deeds. Here for revenge the Sabine troops contend; the Romans there with arms defend the prey. Wearied with tedious war, at length they cease; and both the kings and kingdoms plight the peace. The friendly chiefs before Jove's altar stand, both armed, each with a charger in his hand: a fatted sow is led for sacrifice, with imprecations on the perjured head. Near this, the traitor Metius, stretched between four fiery steeds, is dragged along the green, by Tullus' doom: the brambles drink his blood, and his torn limbs are left as the vulture's food. There, Porsena brings proud Tarquin to Rome, and would by force restore the banished kings. One tyrant fights for his fellow-tyrant; the Roman youth assert their native rights. Before the town the Tuscan army lies, to win by famine, or by fraud to surprise. Their king, half-threatening, half-disdaining, stood, while Cocles broke the bridge, and stemmed the flood. The captive maids there tempt the raging tide, escaped from their chains, with Cloelia for their guide. High on a rock heroic Manlius stood, to guard the temple, and the temple's god. Then Rome was poor; and there you might behold the palace thatched with straw, now roofed with gold. The silver goose flew there before the shining gate, and, by her cackle, saved the state. She told the Gauls' approach; the approaching Gauls, obscure in night, ascended, and seized the walls. The gold well dissembled their yellow hair, and they wore golden chains on their white necks. Their vests were gold; they wielded long Alpine spears, and their left arm sustained a length of shield. Nearby, the leaping Salian priests advanced; and the mad Luperci danced naked through the streets, in caps of wool; the targets fallen from heaven. Here modest matrons, driven in soft litters, appeared to pay their vows in solemn pomp, and bore odorous gums in their chaste hands. Far hence removed, the Stygian seats are seen; the pains of the damned, and punished Catiline hung on a rock—the traitor; and, around, the Furies hissing from the nether ground.
